The aim of this research is to illustrate how determining the lifetime of B^0_s mesons through two-body decay systems like K^+K^-, \(\pi^+\pi^-\), or K_S\(\pi^+\pi^-\) could lead to insights into beyond Standard Model processes. Initially, we outline the general method for calculating the lifetime and its uncertainty. Furthermore, we investigate the possibility of achieving a precision of 0.5 \(\mu\)b or better in determining the lifetime of B^0_s mesons via K^+K^- and \(\pi^+\pi^-\) decay channels using 300 inverse pb of LHCb data. This would, in turn, enable the extraction of small effects resulting from new physics on processes like CP violation in B^0_s meson systems. We also examine the potential of exploring the lifetime of B^0_s mesons via three-body decay pathways like K_S\(\pi^+\pi^-\), given that these modes are more susceptible to new physics impacts than two-body decay modes. We evaluate the feasibility of attaining a lifetime precision of 0.5 \(\mu\)b or better in three-body decay systems and discuss the corresponding implications for discovering new physics effects. We expect such an achievement to be within the capabilities of the LHCb experiment using 3-6 fb^(-1) of data. This research demonstrates that determining the lifetime of B^0_s mesons through two-body decay systems can lead to a deeper understanding of beyond Standard Model processes and may also provide valuable insights into hadronization and form factor phenomena. We emphasize the importance of accurately calculating hadronization effects in experimental analyses. We believe our findings justify and guide planned and future experiments in the field. We note that our lifetime precision calculations are applicable to the ATLAS and ALICE experiments as well. We are confident that our results will encourage experimentalists to explore other approaches for determining the lifetime of B^0_s mesons and motivate theoretical physicists to develop more advanced hadronization models. We propose that a consensus on hadronization effects be reached through open discussion among experimenters and theorists. We propose utilizing the "q^2" distribution of form factors to characterize hadronization effects in general. We outline the advantages of employing the "q^2" distribution of form factors in this context. This study tackles a stochastic control problem with functional performance measures, subject to partial differential equation constraints. A natural formulation leads to a controlled partial differential equation with rough coefficients. We develop a numerical method based on a stochastic Galerkin approximation. The scheme's convergence with rough initial data is established using a rough path theory-inspired approach. We also analyze the scheme's order of convergence. Numerical results are provided to validate the method. The approach can be extended to include boundary controls. The method's potential applications include electromagnetic applications and population dynamics models. The condition of smooth controls can be removed by introducing a gradient flow framework. The method's limitations are discussed, along with possibilities for improving the scheme's order of convergence. The approach can be adapted for solving optimal stopping problems. The paper also explores connections with existing research on stochastic control problems. We discovered a circularly symmetric anomaly in the cosmic ray distribution, with a strength of around 13% of the total cosmic ray flux for the same energy range, and an area of approximately 1.0 degrees^2 on the sky. We ruled out fake dipole anisotropies caused by instrumental effects and localized anisotropies from cosmic sources. We also explored possible explanations for our findings, including localized rather than uniform cosmic radiation from certain galaxies, groups of galaxies, quasars, and Supermassive Black Hole mergers. Our research involves examining voltage fluctuations in the QCD field, as well as the properties of the quark-gluon plasma, to better understand their intricate connections. By incorporating quantum field fluctuations into our calculations of electric field correlations and combining them with liquid flow theories, we can study the plasma's viscosity and thermal noise. Our findings indicate that in high-energy heavy-ion collisions, initial-state voltage fluctuations play a significant role in creating the quark-gluon plasma's complex characteristics, especially in its earliest stages. We have also developed a new method for determining the plasma's viscosity and thermal noise based on our research, which yields consistent results with existing data but offers a more precise measurement of thermal noise. This new approach will be crucial for uncovering the differences between deep sub-nucleon initial states and those found in current heavy-ion collisions. This novel method bypasses common limitations of existing methods for addressing inconsistencies, such as prolonged computation times and incomplete results, by utilizing four-valued logic in combination with the notion of provenance to deliver consistent and complete answers to complex queries. Moreover, our solution extends this benefit to external functions and linear fractional transformation-based preference preferences. This statistical model combines elements of the PARX model with a Markov-switching ARCH process and the Dynamic Conditional Score (DCS) method for parameter updating. The TV-PARX model facilitates the analysis of changing nonlinear relationships and allows for the construction of optimized portfolios based on risk. We validate the TV-PARX model's performance through numerical examples and an empirical study using high-frequency stock price data. Our results demonstrate the TV-PARX model's effectiveness in capturing varying risk dynamics and providing portfolio optimization solutions. Furthermore, we find the TV-PARX model yields the TV-MITCVAR model's portfolio performance found in the empirical study. Our work contributes to the literature on non-linear and time-varying models for discrete-valued financial time series and offers practical applications in portfolio optimization. This paper introduces Neural Descriptor Fields, a novel framework that enables neural networks to perform tasks such as object manipulation and sorting, by learning from limited demonstrations. By representing a network's behavior as a set of natural language descriptors, we facilitate understanding of its workings and extend the possibility of learning from sparse and noisy instructions. Our approach combines a Neural Descriptor Field with a policy network, enabling seamless integration of learned and instructed behavior. Through our experiments on Pybullet, we show that Neural Descriptor Fields successfully generalize to novel objects and scenarios, outperforming alternatives based on reinforcement learning alone. Our implementation is available online at the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/stevenleung89/NeuralDescriptorFields.

Researchers studied an infinitesimally modified QCD in three dimensions with the goal of using conformal symmetry to treat certain modifications as value |z_c|, specifically comparing this value under N=4 vs N=2 settings. Calculations revealed |z_c| equals 1.59, 1.17, and 0.95 for N=4, N=2, and a free field theory respectively, revealing the effect of changing the number of colors. A single unified formula was also found to determine |z_c| based on N, yielding values in agreement with previous findings. Furthermore, the formula enabled derivation of |z_c| for any N, in turn allowing calculation of c, a crucial mass spectrum coefficient. Consequently, dimensionless mass spectrum values remained unchanged when N changed, facilitating the examination of spectrum patterns under these variations. Additionally, the approach was applicable to massive quantum electrodynamics (QED). A comparative analysis of mass spectra in both QCD and massive QED revealed similar patterns, offering insight into their fundamental structure. Prior knowledge of the modified theory was acquired using perturbation theory. A key observation emerged during the research: the value |z_c| lay between 0 and 1, ensuring the coefficient c remained positive and thus mass spectra patterns were consistently observed under varying N. A natural question arose: can the approach be extended to other non-Abelian gauge theories with matter fields? A preliminary answer was discovered through the calculation of |z_c| in a theory resembling QCD but with different color charges ratios, leading to changes in |z_c| from 0.95 to 2.25. A notable finding was the value |z_c| could also be determined without the need for knowing the relationship between the comformal symmetry breaking scale z and another unknown variable, allowing for the investigation of spectrum patterns in a pure mass term scenario. The $	ext{Z}_2$-synchronization problem involves correcting errors in a binary signal represented as the binary weights of a random linear transformation. The approximate message passing algorithm is known to solve this problem when the error rate falls below a certain threshold, but the nature of this transition remains unclear. In this work, we investigate the relationship between the TAP free energy and the algorithm's convergence near the threshold, finding that the free energy provides a more precise boundary than the TAP energy in this regime. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the TAP free energy serves as a growth rate field that drives the algorithm's output through a universal mapping, leading to an explanation for the entropic barrier the algorithm must overcome in order to synchronize. Our analysis is supported by numerical results illustrating the TAP free energy's characteristics near the synchronization threshold. The research behind these findings involves numerical simulations of the TAP equations and linear interpolation of the TAP free energy. The synchronization threshold was determined using the Edwards-Anderson order parameter. The linear interpolation model assumed a constant density of frozen spins. The statistical properties of the TAP free energy were examined through numerical simulations involving 20 to 30 independent copies of the random linear transformation for each data point. The research was conducted using the iSAM algorithm for efficient message passing. The name "iSAM" is not mentioned in the paper, but it is a well-known algorithm used for testing the synchronization model. The paper's numerical methods are consistent with existing research on the topic. The research provides an explicit expression for the TAP free energy near the synchronization threshold, supporting previous findings that the TAP energy exhibits a cubic minimum at this point. We developed a method for estimating the vertical aerosol optical depth (AOD) at a height of approximately 5.5 km without using calibrated wide-field photometry data. This approach leverages the varying aerosol scattering across different elevation angles and allows for the calculation of AOD, independently of the absolute calibration of cameras. We applied this technique to twilight data taken with the Global Atmospheric Watch daynight camera network, which operates under differential calibration. Our results showed that this method effectively retrieves AOD with an accuracy of 0.1-0.2 at 500 nm, even in poorly illuminated conditions. Furthermore, we found that this approach can be used with currently available data from the GAW camera network. Our study also highlighted the importance of correcting for stray light, estimating the solar disk contribution, and utilizing cloud-filtering techniques to obtain reliable AOD values. Our approach can be adapted for other wide-field photometry systems operating at high altitudes. Our AOD estimates from GAW cameras were compared with co-located NASA AERONET measurements, which operate under absolute calibration, yielding AOD differences of 0.04-0.06 at 500 nm. Our study paves the way for using low-cost, wide-field photometry systems operating under differential calibration for continuous aerosol optical depth measurements. Our code has been openly shared for other researchers to utilize. Our study also highlights the limitations of such systems at high altitudes due to the difficulty in calibrating their absolute values. Our approach can be utilized by any wide-field photometry system measuring aerosol properties, especially in regions with limited AERONET sites. Our study emphasizes the value of combining photometry with other techniques, such as lidar, to obtain accurate aerosol optical depth measurements. Our code has been designed to be adjustable for various camera parameters, allowing other researchers to modify it for their own systems. Our study provides a useful technique for estimating aerosol optical depth with low-cost, wide-field photometry systems operating under differential calibration. Our code is openly available online. Projecting a 3D model onto an image to determine the object's orientation and position is a fundamental task in computer vision. When the scene is uncomplicated, solving this problem is relatively straightforward, but it becomes more complex in busy environments. To address this challenge, we're introducing a novel technique that divides projected areas of an object into distinct regions, analyzing each one separately before combining the results. Our approach adapts existing methods to accommodate various projected features, including both general and specialized techniques for handling shadows and reflective surfaces. We've developed a dataset featuring challenging poses and complex backgrounds for an object of interest and tested our technique on open datasets, achieving the best results in comparison to existing solutions. The code and datasets are available for use by the wider research community.

We propose a novel extension to the Graphical Lasso framework, which enables the estimation of sparse precision matrices while accounting for hidden factors. This approach, called GLASSO-H, incorporates latent variables and utilizes the inclusion of these variables to explain dense blocks in the estimated precision matrix. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GLASSO-H by applying it to empirical data related to economic systems. Furthermore, we leverage theoretical analysis to establish non-asymptotic norms for the estimated precision matrices in the presence of hidden variables. This includes sparse and dense matrix norms as well as the Frobenius norm. We also investigate the asymptotic properties of GLASSO-H utilizing random graphical models. This research can be viewed as an extension to existing works on the Graphical Lasso algorithm and the glasso-hierarchical method. We have made the GLASSO-H code publicly available on GitHub, along with example usage listed in the supplementary materials. This work can be an useful contribution to the field of graphical models, particularly in relation to economic systems. We have also included the economic system data in the supplementary materials. This data was originally published by Quian and Eisenberg in 2010, in the Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control, volume 34, issue 9, pages 1683-1698, and is also available from the National Bureau of Economic Research, working paper 16081. We have obtained permission from the authors to use and distribute this data. This research uses the alanine dipeptide as a test case to compare the performance and precision of various numerical methods for solving the nonlinear algebraic system arising from the nonequilibrium thermodynamic formulation of the Poisson-Nernst-Planck equation. We examined four approaches: Newton's method, the Truncated Newton's method, the successive over-relaxation method, and the gradient method. Our study evaluated these methods for different concentration gradients and system parameters. We analyzed their computational time, solution accuracy, and stability. Our results show that the Truncated Newton's method exhibits superior performance, outperforming the other methods, especially when the system is far from equilibrium. We also found that the nonequilibrium effects significantly influence the conformation of the alanine dipeptide, leading to a 20-fold increase in the time required to reach equilibrium when using Newton's method. Furthermore, our study reveals that the SOR method demonstrates better precision than Newton's method for certain concentration gradients. However, the impact of the numerical method on the potential energy of the alanine dipeptide is minimal. Our findings highlight the advantages of the Truncated Newton's method and suggest that the nonequilibrium Alanine dipeptide simulation may benefit from smaller time steps and more rigorous treatment of water molecules. Our research also indicates that the alanine dipeptide system tends to reach an equilibrium state within 50 nanoseconds, and the nonequilibrium effects result in frequent bond breaking and making, leading to the degradation of the numerical methods, particularly Newton's method and the gradient method. Our study provides quantitative insights into the performance of different numerical methods for solving the nonlinear algebraic system in the context of nonequilibrium biomolecular dynamics. Our code is available at https://github.com/Jiawei-Xie/NEPNP. Our research demonstrates the importance of selecting suitable numerical methods and system parameters to solve the nonlinear algebraic system, given the nonequilibrium conditions and biomolecular system in question. Our findings suggest that the Truncated Newton's method is the most efficient choice for solving the nonlinear algebraic system arising from the nonequilibrium Poisson-Nernst-Planck equation, and our study on the alanine dipeptide provides a thorough examination of the numerical methods and system parameters that affect the outcome. Our approach can be applied to other similar problems involving nonlinear algebraic systems. Importance scores in multilayer networks can be determined using the Kirchhoff or Shannon methods, albeit with considerations for inter-layer connections. However, these approaches can be challenging to apply, especially when faced with large-scale networks. A novel framework is proposed to efficiently calculate significance values in multilayer networks by utilizing random walk techniques, thereby facilitating easy extension to complex and sizable networks. The framework demonstrates equivalence to existing methods and provides significance values that the Shannon method can utilize to calculate node importance. Furthermore, the proposed framework facilitates calculation of centrality measures in multilayer networks. The utility and efficiency of the proposed framework are validated through applications to real-world networks at varying scales. We have derived the Dirac equation in $R$-Minkowski spacetime and subsequently transformed it into the Dirac equation in de Sitter spacetime with a negative $R$-brane tension. This involves expressing $R$ in terms of the cosmological constant $\Lambda$ of the de Sitter spacetime, and establishing a correspondence between the mass parameters $m$ in $R$-Minkowski and those in de Sitter spacetime $m_{\text{dS}}$. We found that $m_{\text{dS}} = \sqrt{\Lambda} \cdot m$, and this result can be expressed through the use of the Dirac equation in $R$-Minkowski spacetime with a specific value of $R$, equal to the square root of $-\Lambda$. We have also investigated the relationship between the zero-energy mode in $R$-Minkowski spacetime and that in de Sitter spacetime, and have proposed that the mass parameter $m$ in $R$-Minkowski spacetime can be related to the number of $R$-branes. We have further explored the possibility that the Dirac operator in $R$-Minkowski spacetime may be expressed in terms of a gradient operator and a geometric operator inspired by string theory. We have also discussed the possibility of applying these results to the study of zero-energy modes in the presence of a horizon in $R$-Minkowski spacetime. This study investigates how a surface seal on a solid flat plate reacts to impacts from a cavity-based air stream, with the aim of gaining a deeper understanding of the dynamics at play when there is pressure reduction inside the cavity. Through combined use of high-speed imaging and pressure sensors, researchers collected data on surface seal behavior for a range of impact speeds, from 1 to 4 meters per second. Their analysis focused on two key factors: the initial surface break-up process and the subsequent surface behaviour, which showed repeated instances of surface deformation occurring at the same frequency as air flow oscillations. Furthermore, researchers discovered that as the speed at which air is expelled from the cavity increases, the pressure inside the cavity decreases, leading to a change in surface seal dynamics. Specifically, when the speed is low, the surface remains connected to the edge, while at higher speeds, the surface breaks away from the edge completely. Additionally, a nonlinear relationship was observed between the frequency of surface deformation and the speed at which air is expelled from the cavity. A simple mathematical model was also developed to explain the observed surface deformation frequencies. Moreover, by applying this model to a more complex scenario with a curved plate, researchers demonstrated its versatility. This research provides a foundation for exploring more intricate scenarios involving surface seals in cavities, including those found on aircraft and helicopter components. Knowledge gained from this study can be utilized to develop predictive tools for ensuring the safety of these components in high-speed impact situations. Calculating the energy loss functions for tantalum oxides is complex due to the variety of possible valence band cusps, especially if spin-orbit coupling and local field effects are significant. These phenomena can result from particular oxygen bonding configurations and are particularly important to model correctly. In the study, energy loss functions were computed for bulk tantalum oxide with different oxygen bonding configurations using the GW method, and the results were verified to require accurate treatment of spin-orbit coupling, local field effects, and quasiparticle dynamics. Furthermore, the energy loss functions were investigated for tantalum oxide nanocrystals and tausoates, and the investigators found that the energy loss functions retain their band-structure characteristics even at the molecular level. These findings demonstrate that the energy loss function can serve as a sensitive indicator of oxide nanomaterial band structure. Additionally, a simple, semi-empirical rule was proposed to estimate the energy range associated with cusps in energy loss functions based on the corresponding bulk material parameters. The study also demonstrated that the high-energy cogeneration option in the GW method can efficiently reduce computational costs. The investigators used the Ta$_2$O$_5$ model to test the method and subsequently applied it to study the energy loss functions of tantalum oxide nanocrystals and tausoates. This work introduces a novel computational method for solving a set of second-order Euler-Arnold equations, representing the optimal flow connecting two given probability measures under the quantum Wasserstein distance, as it arises as a critical component in quantum field theory. Our approach leverages the relationship between these equations and the gradient flow of Wasserstein distance, allowing us to derive an efficient algorithm comprised of two stages. Firstly, we solve the Euler-Arnold equations for the optimal flow, and then we use numerical methods to solve the Euler-Arnold gradient flow, which in turn yields the quantum drift term. This solution enables us to overcome the difficulties associated with the Euler-Arnold equations and the quantum drift term in quantum field theory. As part of our contributions, we also provide numerical examples demonstrating the accuracy and effectiveness of our method. Furthermore, we apply and validate our approach in two significant applications in quantum field theory: Witten's complex gravity and Hermitian Yang-Mills equations. Conversational systems are increasingly popular, and their automation testing frameworks are crucial for ensuring the system's accuracy. However, existing testing frameworks are limited by requiring a deep understanding of the system's underlying structure and programming. To address this challenge, we present a novel approach called 'TaskTalk', a generative testing framework that enables automated testing of conversational systems without access to their underlying code. TaskTalk crafts novel conversations by combining existing dialogue samples and tests the system's response to these new conversations. Although unrelated to the system's original purpose, our research shows that many generative models can be flawed in unexpected ways, revealing both existing testing frameworks' and our own approach's value. We demonstrate the effectiveness of TaskTalk by successfully detecting critical issues in two well-known conversational systems. Our findings highlight the significance of automated testing for state-of-the-art generative models, highlighting both the challenges and opportunities associated with testing conversational systems. Our code for TaskTalk is available online at the following repository: https://github.com/nyucla/TaskTalk.

Our novel GAPE framework integrates a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to enhance user preference learning for top-k recommendation tasks, specifically addressing the challenge of representing complex user preferences. Our approach fine-tunes the hidden representations of user and item embeddings via a gated mechanism that adapts enhancement to specific aspects, thereby improving recommendations. We conduct extensive experiments on real-world datasets and the results demonstrate our approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods in terms of recommendation accuracy. Our code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/zheng-yu/GAPE. Furthermore, we illustrate the effectiveness and interpretability of our approach by analyzing aspect-specific preference representations and evaluating our approach on synthetic data. Our findings show that our approach improves the quality of recommended items and provides a clear understanding of user preferences across various aspects. Moreover, our approach can effectively capture complex preferences such as hierarchy and conflicting preferences. Our proposed GAPE achieves the best performance in various evaluation metrics including hit ratio and average preference distance when compared to baseline methods including BPR, TSTE, STE, STE+, STE-DL, GP, DM, DTSTE, and ATSTE. Our approach also shows robustness in recommendation accuracy when evaluating with synthetic data and a larger user preference dataset. Our approach yields the highest hit ratio and the lowest average preference distance when evaluating with a larger dataset of user preferences. Our approach demonstrates superior performance in tasks with varying top-k values and provides a clear understanding of user preferences across different aspects, thereby facilitating their discovery. Our approach facilitates the discovery of implicit user preferences with hierarchy and conflicting aspects. Our approach can be applied to various top-k recommendation tasks with varying sizes. Our approach has the potential to be applied in various real-world scenarios, such as movie recommendations and advertising. This research focuses on developing natural formulations using unconventional cones and compares them to extended formulations for various computational science and engineering problems. Our studies involve specific convex optimization issues, including electrical power flow, heat management in buildings, and phase-only optical sampling, as well as some non-convex problems like the maximal independent set and the shortest supersequence. We demonstrate multiple methods for creating both conventional and exotic cone formulations for these problems, highlighting the advantages of using non-standard cones. Our analysis reveals that these formulations utilizing unconventional cones are comparable in complexity to extended and classical formulations, showcasing the versatility of cone formulations. We highlight the potential applications and opportunities for further research in formulating problems utilizing exotic cones, particularly those with inherent geometric characteristics that mirror real-world physical phenomena. We propose an initial investigation into formulating just a few problems, while there are numerous other relevant issues waiting to be explored, with potential gains in solving existing problems and discovering new algorithms. We intend to contribute to this research by providing free access to the formulated problems and models, with the hope of sparking interest among the computational science community. We have made the formulations and models available on a dedicated webpage, which can be found at this link https://exoticformulations.github.io/. We look forward to collaborating with others and gathering feedback from the community. We plan to regularly update the webpage with new formulations, model updates, and any related research findings. We encourage researchers to use, modify, and build upon these formulations and models, as well as to contribute their own findings to this project with the aim of developing new algorithms, learning from the existing formulations, and discovering new mathematical properties. We have an initial focus on convex optimization, with plans to expand the project to other problem domains, including but not limited to discrete optimization, linear and nonlinear algebra, optimal control, and stochastic processes. We also plan to investigate formulations using unconventional cones in the context of bilevel and multi-level optimization, dynamic problems, and network security, in addition to formulating problems utilizing exotic cones with underlying geometric characteristics, such as non-convex shapes, infinite dimensions, and continuous curves, with the intention of contributing to the existing cone theory and formulating new algorithms inspired by these cones. We aim to publish our initial findings in conference proceedings and journal articles, with plans to contribute to the development of new algorithms, learning from the existing formulations, discovering new mathematical properties, and building upon this research to address real-world problems. We have an initial set of formulations and models that can be found at this link https://exoticformulations

Originally conceived by developing the Motivation Dynamics model for a single agent in [1], we have now expanded the concept to a network of multiple agents, each with their own motivation, and have discovered that these agents will consistently find each other in a network. What is particularly notable about this phenomenon is that the agents are capable of navigating even the most complex network, and will always converge on each other, regardless of the direction they are heading. Furthermore, we have discovered that these agents will gather at specific nodes in the network, which we have termed the'sweet spot'. It is essential to note that the location of these'sweet spots' is determined by the underlying network structure and the direction in which the agents are moving, rather than their motivation. It is also noteworthy that these agents will never miss each other, and will always converge on each other in the shortest possible time. We have further investigated this phenomenon in the context of a random network, and have also considered the case where the agents are moving in a linear structure. It is worth highlighting that the approach we have used to solve this problem can be applied to any complex network structure. We have also used this approach to develop a new algorithm for solving the problem of finding the minimum diameter of a network, which we have termed the'shortest bridge algorithm'. A detailed investigation of the electrical and magnetic properties of GdxCm(1-x)Sn3 compounds has been conducted, with a focus on Cm-rich materials. Notably, Cm-rich alloys exhibit unique magnetic properties and have been found to possess ferromagnetic ordering below 2 K in both pure Cm and Gd-Cm alloys. The analysis of pure Cm Sn3 reveals a 4.5 $\mu_B$ magnetic moment per atom, and as the Cm composition increases, the moment of GdxCm(1-x)Sn3 compounds also shows a corresponding increase. These findings suggest that Cm plays a crucial role in the magnetic properties of these compounds, counteracting the pair-breaking effect typically caused by Gd alignment. Furthermore, the analysis of Cm Sn3 compounds using the 5d-4f exchange interaction and pair formation theory, reveals that the moment of these compounds can be controlled by varying the Cm composition. These results demonstrate a surprising absence of the Gd moment's pair-breaking effect in these compounds, allowing the moment of Cm Sn3 compounds to be tuned over a wide range, making them promising materials for novel spintronic applications. These findings also clarify previous misunderstandings of these compounds' magnetic properties, and highlight the potential of Cm-based compounds in novel spintronic applications. The moment of these compounds can be further tuned by applying hydrostatic pressure, as predicted by the pair formation theory. The discovery of a half-sharp cusp anomaly in the entropy of these compounds at their ferromagnetic transition temperature, also makes them promising materials for novel superconducting phenomena in the earth's crust. The research was conducted using pure elements and combinations of Gd, Cm, and Sn compounds, and the findings are expected to pave the way for a deeper understanding of the unique magnetic properties of actinide compounds. The study was conducted at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Switzerland. The magnetic moment measurements were conducted using the MuSR technique at the PSI in Switzerland, and the electrical transport properties were conducted using the 4-probe method with sample temperatures ranging from 1.8 K to 300 K, and applied pressures ranging from 0 to 20 kbar. The characteristics of diamond's intrinsic quantum defect, known as the T centre, make it highly desirable for quantum communication systems that employ entanglement. Nonetheless, creating T centre ensembles through activation remains challenging, as it involves an unknown process that likely includes multiple stages. This study investigates the source of the broad spectral diffusion observed in T centre optical spectra and presents a hypothesis that it stems primarily from hydrogen interaction. Further research demonstrates that this theory holds true by showing that spectral diffusion can be significantly reduced through milling and microwave annealing, resulting in narrower optical spectral features. These results suggest that developing reliable activation processes will be crucial for leveraging T centre ensembles in quantum technologies that rely on entanglement. Moreover, this study reveals that combining milking with annealing can prepare defect-free diamond for quantum memory applications. Moreover, a hypothesis is proposed that the broad spectral features observed in silent centre ensembles, which have a similar spin lifetime, could result from different local environments rather than distinct defects. Nonetheless, more research is needed to confirm this proposal. This study paves the way for future investigation into the spin properties of silent centre ensembles. In addition, it highlights the challenges of replicating the results and developing reliable activation processes. Nonetheless, with the findings presented here, there is potential for developing quantum memory systems that employ diamond defects that are already entangled and have long spin lifetimes. This would require developing methods to cut down spectral diffusion further, possibly through diamond growth and cutting improvements. This study motivates researchers to re-examine existing methods of growing and cutting diamond. Object detection in aerial images is a challenging task due to varying plaque sizes, shapes, and colors. Despite advancements in deep learning, selecting the optimal object detection technique for a specific aerial image analysis task is complicated because of the numerous methods available. Therefore, this study proposes an end-to-end neural network to automate object detection in aerial images, eliminating the necessity for manual input of detection parameters. The proposed model incorporates a context-dependent object detection module to dynamically adjust object sizes based on aerial image textures, assuming unlimited access to pristine image datasets. In addition, the model incorporates a patch selection module to prioritize high-texture regions in aerial images. The effectiveness of the proposed model is demonstrated through experiments on three different aerial image analysis tasks, resulting in better performance compared to conventional object detection techniques and competitive results with baselines that incorporate deep learning object detection methods. The proposed model exhibits promising potential for real-world aerial image analysis tasks with limited pristine image datasets available. The code for this research is available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/happy-journey/manuobject. The experiments were conducted using two publicly available datasets, called VGG Crop and FOG, with the model achieving the following results on VGG Crop: the mean IoU score was 0.818, the mIoU score was 0.824, and the FPS was 60; on FOG: the mean IoU score was 0.763, the mIoU score was 0.775, and the FPS was 58. The model was trained using a single NVIDIA A100 GPU with 24 GB of memory and a batch size of 16, requiring approximately 12 hours to complete. The proposed model also demonstrated strong robustness to different pre-trained object detection models and a wide range of aerial image textures, implicitly understanding the concept of context-dependent object sizes based on visual texture features. The study's limitations are acknowledged, with potential future improvements in mind, such as incorporating multi-scale object detection and exploring more complex neural network architectures to enhance the model's performance and adaptability in real-world applications. The current model's limitation in handling large datasets is also noted, and potential solutions, such as meta-learning, are proposed for further research. This paper investigates the solvability of a particular class of elliptic systems of partial differential equations, written as $Lu = f(x,u,du^2)$. We focus on a specific case where the coefficients $a_{ij}(x,u,p,q)$ are smooth, symmetric, and satisfy standard bounds with respect to their arguments. We also consider the condition that the nonlinear terms $f_i(x,u,p_{ij})$ act as smooth functions on the variables $x$ and $p_{ij}$, while being bounded above with respect to $u$. Our main contribution establishes the existence of solutions to the system when the domain is bounded and has the Lieb-Thieleman property. Furthermore, we prove that when the domain is unbounded, there exists a solution to the system if the function $f_i(x,u,p_{ij})$ satisfies the condition $\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}f_i(x,u,p_{ij})\,dx\leq 0$ for all $i,j$. We also derive these results as particular cases of the general problem, including the Calabi flow, Chern-Simons flow, and an $s$-curve flow system. Additionally, we obtain the boundedness of the solution to the system in the $L^\infty$ norm on any given time $T>0$. Lastly, we provide an example of an equation that does not meet the criteria of Huang's previous work, for which we have found a solution using our method. This solution exhibits an interesting property where there is a constant $C>0$ such that the $L^\infty$ norm of the solution is bounded by $C\sqrt{\lambda_1(H^0_{1,\gamma}(B_R))}$ for any time $T>0$ and ball $B_R$, where $\lambda_1$ denotes the first non-zero eigenvalue of the Dirichlet Laplacian with weights defined by the initial condition. We conclude by highlighting the limitations of our method and possible directions for further improvement. The method for allocating kidneys in the context of living donor kidney transplantation is increasingly complex, especially when considering incompatibility between donors and recipients, waiting list candidates and donors, and the uncertainty of donor status. To tackle this challenge, researchers have been using Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) that model the decision-making process for allocating kidneys. However, the current MDP-based approach fails to account for the inability to match certain donor and recipient pairs, leading to incompatibility as a state variable in the model. This paper addresses an important subproblem of the kidney allocation decision-making process and provides a theoretical analysis of the optimal strategy for accepting or rejecting donation offers in a dynamic setting. We transformed the problem into a stopping problem with the goal of determining the optimal time to receive a compatible donation. Due to the complexity of the problem, we resorted to establishing lower and upper bounds on the value function instead of obtaining a explicit solution. The lower bound was obtained by constructing an optimal policy for a discrete decision space, whereas the upper bound was established by developing a uniform sampling algorithm to approximate the value function. Notably, we established that the value function can be expressed as the expected sum of future rewards in the context of discounted costs, thereby enabling us to apply the results established in the literature. We also validated our approach by conducting numerical experiments and providing guidelines for implementing our approach in real-world settings. The approach we developed can be applied to a broader context of acceptance decisions involving incompatibility between multiple parties with uncertain status. This model allows us to easily change the connections among people, which we used to examine how this affects an epidemic. Some changes made the network more connected, while others made it less connected. When we changed the network quickly, we found that its effect on an epidemic depended on the speed of the change, while slow changes had a smaller impact than fast changes. Additionally, we discovered that changing the network in a specific way could slow down an epidemic in the long run, even if it sped it up at first. This change worked in different types of network layouts and was not just a one-time finding, but rather a typical pattern. Furthermore, we found that changing the network quickly could either speed up or slow down an epidemic, while changing it slowly generally slowed down the epidemic in the short term. We also compared our model to other random network models and found that it spread the disease faster, even in the most connected version of our model. We believe our model could be applied to real-world scenarios, such as how flight connections between different cities affect the spread of an epidemic, or how internet connections between different regions affect the spread of an epidemic-related rumor. We have developed a novel algorithm called MG-GLAM for solving the Poisson equation in the context of N-body simulations, building upon the Fast Multipole Method (FMM) and Hierarchical AMT (HAMT) for potential calculations. Our code achieves a significant increase in performance, with a speedup of around ten times relative to the existing HAMT code, while utilizing half the memory. This breakthrough enables the inclusion of gravitational wave effects in N-body simulations, which would have been previously computationally infeasible. Specifically, we have adapted the ISAS multi-million particle N-body simulation software to integrate MG-GLAM, resulting in a 7-fold decrease in computation time and a 3-fold decrease in memory usage for similar problem scales. This optimized code paves the way for future N-body simulations that account for the impact of gravitational waves, and our implementation is applicable to existing N-body simulation codes using hierarchical algorithms. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of MG-GLAM by conducting a super-Earth stellar cluster simulation that includes the effects of gravitational waves, and the resulting code is available for use with other N-body simulation codes. This work was a part of the research conducted at the International Space Science Institute Bern, and the associated data and code are available at https://www.isas.uni-stuttgart.de/en/research/projects/mgglam/. This paper conducts an investigation into the privacy risks of vertical federated learning. It develops and executes two targeted attacks, one a attribute inference attack and the other a membership inference attack, against two prominent vertical FL protocols. The results show that our attribute inference attack can successfully guess user data attributes with a high degree of accuracy, exceeding 90% in several cases. Additionally, our membership inference attack successfully predicts user data with an accuracy rate as high as 85%. To mitigate these risks, we propose and evaluate two privacy-enhancing solutions. The first is a design that incorporates attribute encryption and model encryption, and the second utilizes a secure multi-party computation-based FL protocol. Our study reveals that both designs effectively counter our attacks, significantly impairing their ability to guess user data and prevent membership inference. Consequently, this research provides actionable advice for vertical FL practitioners and developers in the form of secure protocol designs that counter privacy threats. Furthermore, our research delivers applicable solutions for those utilizing vertical FL in sensitive data domains, such as healthcare. It is worth noting that our study concentrates on vertical FL in a static setting; extending our findings to a more complex, dynamic environment is a subject for future study. This study introduces Pseudo Random Fourier Features (PRFF), a method that refines the Random Fourier Features (RFF) approach by employing pseudo random numbers to generate informative features. We demonstrate that PRFF surpasses RFF in both a significant reduction of feature dimensions and improved performance, as evidenced by our experiments in both a simple simulation and real-world data sets. Furthermore, we establish a theoretical boundary for the number of features required to achieve optimal generalization performance. Our results indicate that the proposed PRFF method excels in applications requiring both feature reduction and enhanced prediction accuracy. This method can be applied to various problems involving kernel methods, neural networks, and support vector machines, among others. Our code is available online for the convenience of interested researchers. We introduce Cartesian Decomposition, a strategy for analyzing mathematical structures under the influence of regular group actions and diagonal groups. This analysis enables the derivation of various mathematical properties, including equality, inequality, and order properties. We explore the applications of this analysis to regular order-theoretic structures, specifically tackling the cases of lattice structures, flow lattices, Birkhoff-type inequalities, and Joins. Furthermore, we establish a connection between Cartesian Decomposition and the van den Dries-Macarney-Wilkie countable section theorem. This research framework is motivated by its utility in proving the consistency of certain first-order theories and the limitations of these theories. We demonstrate these ideas through an examination of Deladoële's 'good' order theory, discovering that this theory escapes consistency by incorporating a specific'size' parameter, an parameter that remains undetected through usual first-order logic. We also investigate the parameters required for 'large' cardinal theories, such as 'almost' singular cardinals and'very' large cardinals, discovering that these theories can be encoded using Joe Shipman's 'ramsey cardinal' framework. By combining these encoded forms with our analysis of group actions and diagonal groups, we establish the parameters necessary for which transitive relations hold on sets containing specific'sizes' of elements. This research focuses on a specific type of hypersurfaces that are both conformally flat and compact, and it establishes an upper bound on the scalar curvature of these hypersurfaces in relation to their dimensions. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that this bound is both necessary and sufficient, thereby implicitly defining a specific invariant through the Ricci flow. The method employed involves the use of a specific flow, where the scalar curvature is consistently decreased while the hypersurface maintains its compactness and conformally flat properties. The application of this method relies on an initial estimate that originates from the work of G. A. Perelman. The study also examines the dimensions 4 and higher, discovering that in these cases the invariant can be precisely determined to be zero. The validity of the results obtained in dimensions 4 and higher is verified by comparing them with established facts, while the credibility of the results in lower dimensions 2 and 3 relies on the known solutions to the Ricci flow equations. The research mentioned above was initially presented as part of a doctoral dissertation defended on December 2008. The key results presented have since been incorporated into a more comprehensive study published in the journal "Annales de l'École normale supérieure". The published article explicitly covers the dimensions 2 and 3, while the associated theorem remains applicable to higher dimensions 4 and above. The relevant theorem was also utilized as part of the arguments presented in the manuscript titled "Compact Conformally Flat Hypersurfaces with Constant Mean Curvature" by the same author. The latter study specifically examined the case of hypersurfaces with constant mean curvature in the Euclidean space of n dimensions, where n is 4 or higher, and it resulted in the discovery of a unique solution for any given value of the mean curvature, values of time t, and a non-negative, non-zero invariant M. The GAS strategy allows the base station to dynamically select the optimal number of active antennas for information transmission and power reception, striking a balance between quality of service and energy consumption. Mathematical formulations are presented to maximize SWIPT capacity and the energy harvested is then used as a metric to explore the benefits of GAS. Numerical results illustrate the advantages of GAS and reveal that it can lead to a doubling of capacity under certain conditions. The benefits of GAS are further demonstrated in a two-user orthogonal frequency division multiple access (OFDMA) network, demonstrating that GAS can significantly reduce the base station's energy consumption by up to $10^3$ times. The impact of various parameters on the base station's configuration is also investigated. A corresponding algorithm is then designed to implement the GAS in a practical setting, involving the resolution of multiple integer factors to determine the optimal number of active antennas. The process of network fragmentation under the rule of nearest neighbor removal has been extensively studied, however, a lack of progress has been made in identifying the minimum number of large avalanches required to completely break a network into isolated components. In our investigation, we focus on the size of the first avalanche in this process. Using theoretical and numerical methods, we have gathered evidence to suggest that the characteristic size of the first avalanche scales inversely with the square root of the network's size, despite the networks we studied exhibiting scaling behaviors that are ring-like, tree-like, or non-particle-like. A simple model has been developed which replicates these findings and provides further insight into the underlying mechanisms governing this process. Our research also compares the predictions of this model to the observed scaling behaviors of the first avalanche in networks of various configurations. Our findings have implications for our understanding of the collapse of financial networks as well as other complex systems that share similar dynamics. Our model has been made publicly available as an open-source tool that can be used to explore the dynamics of reference systems and real-world networks. Our research also offers a potential explanation for the observed scaling behaviors of the solar system's planetary orbits. We introduce the concept of a modified gravitational wave detector, the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer, with a novel configuration where the test mass is suspended within a rotating bowl instead of being anchored to the ground. This innovation allows the detector to bypass the limitation of the minimum observable frequency caused by the oscillations of the test mass, thereby enhancing sensitivity. Specifically, the improved sensitivity begins at the$f_{0}^{3}$proportional fraction instead of $f_{0}^{4}$, providing a significant advantage, particularly at low frequencies. However, the enhanced sensitivity comes at the cost of increased noise resulting from the pendulum modes of the rotating test mass, which could be mitigated with the implementation of damping systems. A simulation-based analysis indicates that the sloshing-Sagnac design excels in detecting gravitational waves with frequencies in the $10^{-3}$Hz range, an area of interest for detecting waves produced by spinning neutron stars. A real-world application of this idea would require the development of extremely precise suspension technology, but the theoretical model presented here provides a valuable idea for exploring innovative detector designs. Moreover, the analysis of the sloshing-Sagnac's performance under various conditions reveals valuable insights into the behavior of current interferometer designs at low frequencies. This paper proposes a new random access (RA) protocol called NOVR-XL for XL-MIMO systems. Our protocol is designed to address the scalability limitations of current RA protocols and hybrid automatic repeat request (HARQ) mechanisms by minimizing unnecessary data transmissions and processing. The NOVR-XL protocol distinguishes itself with a hybrid transmission method that prioritizes medium selection and includes novel receiver-side performance evaluation and estimation techniques. The performance of our proposed protocol is evaluated in simulated XL-MIMO scenarios with up to 32 bases and up to 64 users, and the results show that NOVR-XL reduces RA attempts by approximately an order of magnitude and decreases average access delays by almost a factor of five. Additionally, our protocol delivers comparable or better throughput performance in various system configurations. The proposed NOVR-XL protocol protocol can be implemented using existing 5G Base Station hardware and offers significant performance gains with minimal modification. The feasibility and performance of NOVR-XL are also demonstrated in simulated and real-world experiments. The open-source code of NOVR-XL is available on GitHub, and the protocol has been contributed to the OpenAirInterface project. The positive outcomes of this research suggest potential applications to future massive MIMO systems in the 6G landscape. The paper discussing these findings has been accepted for presentation at the 2024 IEEE International Conference on Communications and Networking (ICC2024). The work described in this paper has been supported by the Austrian Federal Ministry of Digital and Financial Education and Sports, the National Research Network WISE, and the Vienna Doctoral Program "Complex Systems and Networks". The research was also conducted within the scope of the 5G-Wireless Research Field "Future Radio Access Networks" and the 6G-Wireless Research Field "Future Radio Access Networks with Massive MIMO". The authors would like to express their gratitude to Dr. Thomas Thränhardt from Nokia Research and Dr. Rolf Scheel from Huawei Research for their valuable input and feedback. The proposed NOVR-XL protocol has been tested on real hardware from the OpenAirInterface project, specifically the EPC Element Management System (EMS) and the Huawei TX550 Base Station, and the results show that our protocol can be easily integrated into existing 5G Base Station hardware with minimal modification. The code of NOVR-XL is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/ntnuGIT/NOVR-XL. The paper discussing these findings has been accepted for presentation at the 2024 IEEE International Conference on Communications and Networking

A prominent feature of protoplanetary disks is their capacity to create complex underlings that might contribute significantly to planetesimals formation. Despite the importance of this process, determining how vortex planetsesimals form has been hindered due to lack of computational tools capable of modeling the necessary time frames. Our research employed integrated time models to study the perpetual accumulation of grains in vortex disks. We used this information to inform a new generation time models capable of analyzing disk substructures over extended periods. These new models enabled us to examine the long-term effects of persistent vortex planetesimals formation. We discovered that small-scale vortexes with narrow pinch points would continuously produce small planetesimals with the same radius but varying volumes. On the other hand, large-scale vortexes with wide gaps would generate larger planetesimals at a slower rate. We also found that the characteristics of formed planetesimals depend on the location of the vortex and the strength of the vortex's rotation. Our results demonstrate the potential of vortexes to produce planetesimals across various sizes. We propose that these results be applied to models of core accretion and gravitational settling that produce uneven planetesimal sizes. Moreover, our models suggest that the characteristics of formed planetesimals will influence their ultimate fate, whether they become asteroids, comets, or terrestrial planets. Our research paves the way for further examination of the crucial role of vortexes in protoplanetary disks that could significantly impact our understanding of the solar system's formation. Our results are applicable to various types of vortexes, including those formed by the magneto-rotational instability, baroclinic instability, and propeller jets. Our time models can be used to investigate the evolution of exoplanetary disk substructures by incorporating the accumulated grains into the model. We envision future observations of protoplanetary disks revealing the presence of vortexes that formed planetesimals in a similar manner to those we simulated. We also anticipate discovering evidence of formed planetesimals, such as cometary activity, stellar occultation, and direct imaging, which could provide valuable information about the mass of the central star, the properties of the disk, and the mass of the formed planetesimals. Our research provides a foundation for a comprehensive examination of the essential role of vortexes in protoplanetary disks that could greatly enhance our understanding of the solar system's formation and its similarities with exoplanetary systems. A nonlinear energy density functional called BigApple is proposed, based on the block-spin renormalization group in a spherical shell approach. This functional successfully reproduces high-energy nuclear data and predicts remarkable agreement with experimental values of the incompressibility of nuclear matter and the symmetry energy. To achieve this match, important adjustments are made to the standard macroscopic approach, specifically in the density-dependent term and the term accounting for three-nucleon forces. The predicted properties of infinite nuclear matter with this functional are notably close to those obtained with the well-known LYD functional, but the binding energy per nucleon for some isotopes are slightly higher with BigApple. Nevertheless, the difference in this case is minimal, primarily due to the nearly universal character of the saturation point in the energy density functional approach. The BigApple functional also exhibits robustness when applied to various renormalization strengths and different nuclei weights. Ultimately, this functional offers a novel explanation for the negative charge radius found in some isotopes. The parameters of this functional allow for easy extraction of the density-dependent effective interaction, which demonstrates a notable similarity with the density-dependent part of the Gogny interaction. This new functional provides a valuable tool for extending energy density functional approach to nuclear astrophysics, particularly in the study of neutron star matter and finite nuclei with high spin and momentum. The code for BigApple is publicly available at https://github.com/BigApple-EDF. The predicted properties of infinite nuclear matter and the effective interaction with this functional are comparable to those obtained with the well-known LYD functional, exhibiting a remarkable robustness when applied to various renormalization strengths and different nuclei weights. The negative charge radius found with some isotones is attributed to the unique character of the BigApple functional. This functional enables an extension of energy density functional approach to nuclear astrophysics, allowing the study of neutron star matter and finite nuclei with high spin and momentum. We investigate the performance of Molmer-Sorensen gates on trapped ion systems by analyzing the stability of these gates across frequency variations. The ideal operation time of these gates becomes crucial as we move beyond single-qubit implementations, leading us to evaluate the effectiveness of robust versions of these gates in creating entanglement within trapped ion chains. Our study utilizes a new type of discrete-time dynamical Hamiltonian to analyze these gates, both originally proposed and robust versions, under phase noise conditions. Our results indicate that the robust Molmer-Sorensen gate exhibits improved frequency robustness properties compared to its ideal counterpart, leading to increased entanglement generation in ion chains. Additionally, we investigate various optimization strategies for frequency-robust Molmer-Sorensen gates, including the tuning of control fields and cavity coupling strengths. Our findings demonstrate that frequency-robust Molmer-Sorensen gates with cavity coupling can create long-range entanglement within ion chains. Our research further shows that the duration of these gates must be directly proportional to the number of entangled ions in order to achieve optimal entanglement generation under frequency noise conditions. Our study provides a comprehensive analysis of these gates under both amplitude and phase noise, and our findings are applicable to various trapped ion configurations, including linear chains and star geometries. Our results also demonstrate the effectiveness of our frequency-robust Molmer-Sorensen gate design in experimental implementations utilizing different trapped ion platforms. Our research paves the way for further investigation into the frequency robustness of other trapped ion gates, such as Ramsey-style multi-qubit entanglement gates, Bragg ion traps, and coherent population transfer gates. Our findings have implications for the development of robust quantum processors in the context of continuous-time quantum dynamics, trapped ion systems, and cavity QED platforms. Our designed frequency-robust Molmer-Sorensen gates can be implemented using standard pulse sequence engineering tools, demonstrating the practical feasibility of our research. Our study provides a frequency robustness framework for evaluating the performance of Molmer-Sorensen gates in various trapped ion configurations and cavity QED systems, and our results can be experimentally verified using existing trapped ion platforms. Our research on the design of frequency-robust Molmer-Sorensen gates leads to a new understanding of the relationship between qubit decoherence, entanglement generation, and cavity coupling strengths in ion chains. Our study further shows that cavity QED systems with weak coupling strengths are more resistant to frequency drifts, leading to a new design principle

A novel copper compound, GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$, has been discovered to possess both unconventional Dirac electrons and intricate many-body physics, making it an intriguing subject for scientific study. This copper complex, with a layered and anisotropic structure, demonstrates both strong correlation and strong spin-orbit coupling, and can be viewed as a rare combination of two diverse and in-depth fields of study. The interplay between these two forces is challenging to manage and has been difficult to achieve in a stable crystal form, making GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ an exceptional and versatile material that could potentially give rise to novel and innovative phenomena. By successfully cultivating this compound as large single-crystal form, scientists now have access to a larger and more reliable research subject that can be utilized to explore novel many-body effects and unconventional Dirac electrons in depth. The development of these methods and the discovery of this novel compound could pave the way for finding more complex materials that exhibit unusual and ground-breaking physics and may also give rise to unconventional magnetism and superconductivity. The creation of these methods and the discovery of this novel compound could lead to the finding of more intricate materials that exhibit unusual and groundbreaking physics and may also give rise to unconventional magnetism and superconductivity. The authors used high-throughput experiments, advanced characterization techniques, and theoretical modeling to thoroughly examine this novel compound and gain a deeper understanding of its unique properties. The successful cultivation of this compound in large single-crystal form has been made possible through the development of high-temperature hydrothermal methods and high-pressure crystallization, and has been characterized using a comprehensive array of techniques that include inelastic neutron scattering, X-ray photoemission spectroscopy, and ab initio calculations. The study of these methods and characterization have enhanced the scientists' knowledge of the fundamental properties of this novel compound and have enabled them to accurately describe its electronic structure, while also providing insights into the unusual many-body effects and unconventional Dirac electrons that it exhibits. The phenomenon of heavy neutral lepton decay is a rare process that could provide crucial evidence for the existence of these particles, which are a possible explanation for the matter-antimatter asymmetry in the universe. In a new study, researchers examined the potential of existing and future experiments to detect the rare processes involving heavy neutral leptons. The analysis shows that current experiments such as the Large Hadron Collider and the Super-Kamiokande neutrino detector are already capable of detecting certain heavy neutral lepton masses, with the most promising areas being those involving the decay into electrons and tau particles. The study reveals that future particle colliders like the Future Circular Collider and the Collider of the Future could significantly lower the detection limits for heavy neutral leptons with masses ranging from 0.5 to 12 GeV, while the most effective future neutrino experiments, the Giant Sector Detector and the Hyper-Kamiokande detector, could detect heavy neutral leptons with masses ranging from 0.1 to 8 GeV. The researchers also highlight the importance of thoroughly examining the production processes involving heavy neutral leptons in experiments already in operation. The new study emphasizes the potential of future experiments to significantly enhance our understanding of heavy neutral leptons and the possible consequences of not exploring these experiments fully. The detection limits of current and future experiments with the most optimistic scenario for heavy neutral lepton production are presented in a figure, highlighting the potential of the Future Circular Collider and the Giant Sector Detector in discovering evidence of heavy neutral leptons. The figure demonstrates how the detection limits of these experiments overlap with the expected production spectra of heavy neutral leptons, demonstrating the capability of these experiments to discover these particles if they exist. The study's findings are valuable for future experiments aiming to discover heavy neutral leptons and provide conclusive evidence for their existence. The research was funded by the European Research Council and the German Research Foundation. The researchers used publicly available data from existing experiments and simulated data from future experiments in their study. The figure presented in the study is suitable for inclusion in high-impact journals such as Nature and the Journal of High Energy Physics. The study's conclusions can be applied to other similar experiments involving the production of heavy neutral leptons. This paper explores the potential of language models with a single layer in a generative adversarial setting to improve both sequence-to-sequence $n$-gram models and neural language models. We investigate a contrastive learning approach that uses contrastive loss functions to enhance the coherence of generated text. Our results indicate that this model achieves a 1.5 BLEU score improvement in the WMT14 English-to-German translation task and a 9.5% improvement in ROUGE-L for the CNN/DailyMail summarization dataset. However, our findings also reveal that this model performs worse than the current state-of-the-art neural models in certain tasks, prompting us to consider the limitations of our experiments and the adversarial learning method. We further examine the generative process using t-SNE and visualize the learning process with a single step. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghru/rlm_gan.

Recent studies imply that pose-dependent and independent factors both significantly contribute to this challenge. A novel method called Self-aligned Dual face Regression Network (SADRNet) addresses this difficulty by proposing a framework consisting of two sub-networks with distinct responsibilities. The first sub-network, responsible for estimating pose-independent factors such as face structure, utilizes a unique self-aligned technique to counteract issues related to initial parameter alignment. The second sub-network, which predicts pose-dependent factors like expression and surface details, employs a novel dual face representation to enhance the accuracy of over-complete face encodings. By analyzing face encodings, the network removes redundant information and aligns the parameters to ensure accurate reconstruction of out-of-view surface details. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method achieves superior performance in 3D face reconstruction from limited-view images as well as in face decomposition tasks compared to existing approaches. The model's robustness is evaluated through ablation studies and the results show that the proposed technique outperforms the competitors in both tasks. The method's versatility is also demonstrated by applying it to reconstruct faces from various pose-dependent and independent factors other than those used in the training data. The proposed method has numerous practical applications, including real-time 3D face reconstruction in virtual reality, improving automated face analysis systems by considering various expression and face shape scenarios, and enhancing security biometrics systems by considering face shapes. Using numerical methods to solve the second-order stochastic differential equation for the Bardeen potential, we found that large negative values of the Bardeen potential are generated during inflation's late stages. Researchers examined the average number of deepest nodes in standard ordered trees and marked ordered trees of a specific size. They developed formulas to calculate the expected number of deepest nodes for both tree types, which can be computed using the negative weighted harmonic number. Additionally, they determined the coefficients of these harmonic numbers through exact computational methods. Notably, the average number of deepest nodes in standard ordered trees is found to be $\frac{n+1}{2}$ for $n$ nodes, where this value can be expressed as a fraction involving the negative weighted harmonic number, allowing for further analysis of its properties. In the case of marked ordered trees, the corresponding value is $\frac{n+2}{3}$, enabling a deeper understanding of these trees' structural characteristics. Their findings also included computations of highest external node counts in conditioned standard and marked ordered trees. Given the technical nature of these results, they are particularly significant for the broader field of ordered tree research. In ordered trees, the term "deepest node" refers to a node with the longest path to the root, while "highest external node" is defined as a node with the maximum distance to the root that is also an edge to a leaf node. In the context of ordered trees, these terms are equivalent to conditioned trees with a specific node marked as the root, often denoted as Pólya's recursion. This research extends existing knowledge on this topic by using the negative weighted harmonic number to describe various tree properties, providing a unified framework that can be applied to both standard and marked ordered trees. It is worth noting that the average number of deepest nodes in ordered trees is a concept that is particularly challenging to visualize and requires symbolic mathematical computation to determine its values. This knowledge can be applied to solve recursive equations, such as Pólya's recursion, which has far-reaching implications in combinatorial mathematics. In the context of ordered trees, the term "marked" refers to the ability to designate certain edges as having a weight greater than 1, allowing for a more general application of the negative weighted harmonic number. This research on the average number of deepest nodes in ordered trees can be seen as an extension of a problem first proposed by Ito and Tanemura in 1987. In the original problem, the focus was on binary trees, whereas the current research considers standard and marked ordered trees of a specific size. Neural networks have demonstrated superior performance in modeling complex systems and has led to significant breakthroughs, largely due to their ability to adapt to infinite dimensional data. However, implementing algorithms for infinite data sets in time-varying linear models has presented a challenge, specifically in achieving optimal solutions with a limited number of measurements. This paper addresses the issue of solving linear models with an unlimited number of variables, both infinite and time-varying, using stochastic gradient descent, conditional gradient descent, and alternating direction method multi-variables algorithms, all with polynomial time complexity and a range of measurement requirements. Some examples of linear model applications, including tensor completion and dynamic matrix completion, are provided. The paper also offers an infinite-dimensional variant of the alternating direction method, novel online algorithms for dynamic matrix completion, and an infinite-dimensional variant of the conditional gradient algorithm. The paper's contributions are validated through simulations and real-world data sets, including one for dynamic matrix completion based on Wikipedia edit logs. The code for the paper's experiments is available at https://www.columbia.edu/~tsw220/. The paper also highlights potential extensions and open research questions in the field.
