As the frequency and severity of extreme weather events increase, storing energy and managing risks becomes increasingly vital in low-carbon electricity systems. In a new model, we examine the coordinated management of multiple storage resources with different risk-tolerance levels through a game-theoretic approach, assuming each storage operator prioritizes maximizing their expected profit. Our results show that, in the presence of price fluctuations and renewable energy variability, the storage operators with higher risk aversion will charge higher prices for their services and be more selective about the projects they participate in, and will typically lose out in negotiations with more adventurous operators who are willing to take on more risk. Our study further reveals that risk-averse storage resources will often fail to fully utilize their capacity, and that this unused capacity can delay the deployment of new storage projects and drive out existing ones, with negative consequences for the community, especially when combined with rising electricity prices and reduced renewable energy integration. Our research demonstrates that regulatory policies aimed at incentivizing storage projects must take risk aversion into account and offer discounted licenses to storage projects that are willing to serve urgent needs, such as during peak demand or when renewable energy is abundant, in order to make storage a more viable option for the community. Our data-driven analysis based on historical electricity price data in Australia, the UK, and the US, along with renewable energy forecasts in Australia and the US, shows the potential benefits of our approach in these regions. Our research provides a framework for policymakers to assess the impacts of storage risk aversion in their own local contexts and find tailored solutions, with potential applications in other energy systems beyond power generation, such as heating or transport networks. Our findings also highlight the value of risk-aware storage in addressing the challenges posed by intermittent renewable energy sources, with implications for the design of electricity markets and policy support schemes, with potential gains including reduced renewable energy integration delays, decreased electricity prices, and more storage capacity deployed. Our research offers a risk-aware storage management approach that can be applied to current energy systems with potential benefits, and with the potential to be highly relevant to future low-carbon energy systems with high shares of renewable energy sources, such as solar and wind power. Our study further reveals that risk-averse storage resources will often fail to fully utilize their capacity, and that this unused capacity can delay the deployment of new storage projects and drive out existing ones, with negative consequences for the community, especially when combined with rising electricity prices and reduced renewable energy integration. Using numerical simulations, this study recreates an Earth-like atmosphere on Mars and observes the emergence of a persistent storm on the planet's equator. These simulations were conducted over a 10-day period using a cloud-resolving model and resulted in a stable circulation pattern similar to those seen on present-day Mars, including the polar ice caps and massive dust storms. Notably, a mid-latitude storm developed on the equator and persisted for an extended period, exhibiting characteristics analogous to those observed on Earth, including the formation of a low-pressure eye and spiraling winds. Notably, this storm was surrounded by a vast ring of rising air that produced extensive precipitation, reminiscent of the circulation patterns seen in Earth's baroclinic storms. Another observed phenomenon on Mars was the gradual cooling of the polar caps, leading to the formation of polar ice caps similar to those found on present-day Mars. Furthermore, this simulation revealed the presence of frozen carbon dioxide in the mid-latitudes, trapped between two circulation patterns, and suggested that the Martian surface could have had liquid water in the past, given the presence of precipitation and a water cycle driven by the baroclinic storm. Observations from NASA's Mars Global Surveyor and Orbiter have validated the simulation results, including the presence of polar ice caps, extensive precipitation, and evidence of past liquid water. This simulation provides a plausible explanation for the features observed on present-day Mars and offers insights into the mechanisms that govern the planet's climate and geography. Furthermore, this study demonstrates that Mars was capable of supporting liquid water and presents a plausible scenario for its disappearance, with implications for the search for life on the planet. This simulation has been made publicly available as part of the Mars Science Laboratory's Pre-Landing Preparation Environment. Calculations demonstrate that by adjusting the position of the donor atom, researchers can either prevent or facilitate coupling between qubits, allowing for the construction of both coherent two-qubit logic gates, such as the CZ gate, and noisy one-qubit logic gates, such as the X gate. Reconstructed top quark events are identified based on a multivariate technique analyzing kinematic properties of decay particles, and the analysis yields 7.7 thousand such events. The measured cross section for top quark pairs is found to be 8.62 plus or minus 0.24 (statistical) plus or minus 0.15 (systematic) plus or minus 0.15 (theoretical) times ten billion barrels per steradian squared. This result agrees with predictions from quantum chromodynamics and, with improved precision, surpasses earlier findings. Ongoing research aimed at further refining the analysis incorporates advanced reconstruction methods and more comprehensive event data sets. The study highlights the significance of CDF data in a new area known as top quark phase-space studies. The associated papers explore specific aspects of this study, including improved reconstruction techniques and cross-section calculations for single top quarks and certain rare decay channels. The methods developed here will underpin upcoming experiments at the Large Hadron Collider. The analysis of top quark pairs encompasses approximately one-third of the total CDF data set, or 20 terabytes of data. The study of top quarks has far-reaching implications, as they decay into bottom quarks at a rate of approximately 85%, offering opportunities to investigate rare decay processes and sub-processes, including those involving W bosons, Higgs bosons, and rare decay channels involving photons, W bosons, and Z bosons. Precise and efficient SPARQL query processing relies heavily on accurate cardinality estimates, which can be challenging to obtain, especially when database details are lacking. Existing approaches primarily focus on using static metadata and graph structure properties, neglecting the potential benefits of instance data in enhancing cardinality estimates. In our research, we propose an innovative framework, capable of incorporating instance data to enhance cardinality estimates, even in the absence of full database contents. In our framework, we introduce a method to estimate instance-based cardinalities for simple ALICE queries by analyzing the structure of endpoint descriptions and instance data, leveraging the 4store database schema. Furthermore, we develop an algorithm to approximate the number of results returned by an endpoint for a given SPARQL query, utilizing the estimated cardinalities of relevant instance datasets. Our experiments, using real-world instance datasets and diverse metadata sources, demonstrate that our approach can provide accurate estimates of result sets even with limited database information. In our evaluation, we discovered that our approach compares favourably to conventional estimate methods, demonstrating the value of instance data in SPARQL query cardinality estimation. Our proposed framework and the associated algorithms have been made available online as open-source software on GitHub. In our research, we also contribute a new dataset to the community, comprising various metadata sources along with corresponding instance datasets and result sets from endpoint queries, available for download from the REWERSE data repository and as supplementary data on our project website. In addition, we have conducted and documented our experiments, including the relevant instance datasets and metadata sources used. This work delves into the computational challenges of privacy loss in differently private machine learning, as the interconnectivity of data points in graph structures complicates existing privacy loss calculations. Our explorations into this issue are motivated by the growing usage of graph-based representations in machine learning, where standard privacy calculations can lead to inaccurate results. To address this problem, we develop two novel methods for computing privacy loss in two distinct scenarios: first, in the case where training data consists of graphs with connected structures, we establish an upper and lower bound on privacy loss; second, we create an algorithm to determine the maximum privacy loss in a more complex, disconnected graph-based training dataset. Our empirical evaluations using real-world datasets demonstrate the practical applications and accuracy of these innovations in the context of neural network learning tasks. Furthermore, we establish theoretical limits on privacy loss in relation to graph topology and provide researchers with a set of guidelines for overcoming the challenges of privacy loss computation in more complex graph structures. Our work and associated code are available online at https://github.com/Qianhewu/SparseNE.

We investigate the statistical properties of letter sequences in independent and identically distributed texts, investigating both unconditioned and conditioned cases with external field. Unconditioned, we show the existence of a tail exponent for the renewal process, which is equivalent to a specific growth rate of words. This in turn affects the likelihood of letter sequences occurring, with a resulting weighted random walk exhibiting a quenched large deviation principle with a non-uniform weight. In the conditioned case, weighted random walk also adheres to a quenched LDP, with a specific variance determining the scaling of the deviation. Both findings are connected to weighted random walk's asymptotic behavior and its connection to first passage percolation on a binary tree. Our methods combine analytical and numerical approaches, including an explicit formula for the tail exponent derived from the weighted random walk's DVH function's asymptotic behavior. Furthermore, we numerically determine the tail exponent for English text, finding it to be approximately 0.24, and compare it with results obtained through numerical data of weighted random walk on a binary tree with an uniformly distributed start node, finding both methods to be consistently applicable. We also examine the validity of our LDP condition by verifying the summability of weighted edge probabilities, which holds true for English text. Our research was motivated by an investigation of the root-causality of letter sequences in independent and identically distributed texts, which we suspect is connected to the weighted random walk's asymptotic behavior on a binary tree, providing theoretical foundations for these phenomena. These findings have potential applications in fields like linguistics and coding theory. We used the Nagumo condition to validate our LDP, the Kac-Walker condition to verify the weighted random walk's asymptotic behavior, and the Cram\'er condition to validate our weighted random walk's DVH function's asymptotic behavior. Our research also involved numerical data obtained from the FAIRPLAY corpus of English text. Recent advances in relativistic heavy-ion beams have enabled the study of 64Ni through the measurement of its various excited states following the collision of Ni with Ca at a relativistic energy. By determining the energies of its excited states, researchers gained insight into the evolution of energy across the N=40 subshell gap and the influence of the monopole interaction within the 64Ni nucleus. Data showed that gamma rays emitted by the 2+1 and 0+2 states of 64Ni decay at rates 1.5 times slower than predicted by a standard nuclear model, leading scientists to explore alternative theories that account for delayed gamma emission, similar to observations in neighboring nuclei. Furthermore, studies of gamma ray spectra revealed that energy was distributed unevenly among the neutrons within 64Ni's inner shell, providing a foundation for future research into the importance of the monopole interaction in stopping power and heavy-ion fusion reactions. Additionally, researchers discovered a unique phenomenon called particle-rigid flow, accompanied by a significant shift in gamma ray energies, which may occur when nuclei interact through electromagnetic forces. Expert analysis suggests that the majority of 64Ni's excited states were reached through two-step processes, starting with the collision of Ni with Ti at a lower energy, followed by gamma decay. By reconstructing the gamma ray histories of 64Ni's excited states, scientists were able to map the energies of its collective states, delve into the characteristics of gamma ray fluctuations, and lay the groundwork for a deeper understanding of gamma ray fluctuations in general. Ultimately, this research paved the way for studying small groups of nucleons within heavy, relativistically accelerated nuclei. A TeV-scale muon collider, with an energy range between 1-100 TeV, is highly versatile and can be easily converted into different configurations, making it an attractive option for a future particle physics facility. In this research, we examine the potential of a TeV-scale muon collider, focusing on the production of heavy particles such as electroweak vector bosons, heavy quarks, and third-generation leptoquarks. We also explore the possible experiments with this collider, including conventional processes that can aid in background reduction and new phenomena like explicit neutrino mass generation and its associated effects. Furthermore, we investigate the expected performance for benchmark scenarios and standard model processes at such a collider. We then discuss possible beam energy and luminosity options, as well as the potential for a muon collider to serve multiple purposes, such as simultaneous operation of a collider and a neutrino oscillation experiment. We also examine the technical challenges and potential paths to addressing them. We propose a tiered approach for developing a TeV-scale muon collider, beginning with a lower-energy version as a stepping stone, and explore the physics potential of this facility in depth. We also outline possible locations for such a facility and the required infrastructure. We then discuss the expected costs and potential funding opportunities. We conclude by examining the long-term prospects for a muon collider and its potential to lead to breakthroughs in the field of particle physics. We provide comprehensive appendices detailing the detector requirements, relevant physics processes, and relevant experiments. We also outline the existing research and key references in the field. We demonstrate the versatility of a TeV-scale muon collider, showing that it can be easily converted into different configurations, and we discuss the potential for a muon collider to serve multiple purposes, such as a collider, a neutrino oscillation experiment, and a lepton flavor violation experiment. A proposed sampling method, rCASPR, is introduced for the purpose of minimizing the point-spread function (PSF) in fan-beam CT without the need for a full-detector array. The rCASPR method selectively acquires data from a subset of detectors, tailored to the geometry of the actual scanner, with the aim of replicating original data with the fewest possible detectors. This method is compared to traditional linear sampling, resulting in a rCASPR-sampled data set that exhibits a 42% reduction in PSF and improved image contrast in a low-contrast object. The efficacy of rCASPR is demonstrated across various scanner geometries and contrast objects. A crucial finding indicates that the optimal rCASPR sampling pattern remains relatively stable, filling about 52% of the available detectors, with the caveat that it is essential to account for the specific detector layout to avoid oversampling. The proposed rCASPR method showcases promise for the development of under-sampled low-dose protocols in clinical settings. The code used for producing the results is available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/SEEMOO/rCASPR. The proposed method is an initial step towards the creation of adaptive sampling patterns tailored to specific noise-reduction techniques, with possible variations such as re-projection onto the actual scanner geometry following acquisition. The rCASPR method can be used in a variety of applications beyond CT, including SPECT, PET, and radiography. The code provided allows users to modify the sampler according to their specific needs. The proposed method leverages the CASPR algorithm, a non-local means-based image reconstruction method that utilizes the gradient descent optimization method to solve the regularized problem. The CASPR algorithm was initially introduced in the following paper: H. Kudo, et al., "CSPR: A Variational Approach to Compressed Sensing Problem with a Non-Local Regularizer," IEEE Trans. The paired-permutation test, also known as the paired-randomization test, is a statistical method used to analyze differences between two groups. This test involves calculating a test statistic from paired observations, then determining the probability of obtaining a result as extreme or more extreme due to random chance. The standard approach to achieving this probability involves employing Monte Carlo approximation methods. However, these methods can be time-consuming, particularly when conducting large-scale data analyses. In response to this limitation, we have developed a more efficient algorithm for an exact version of the paired-permutation test. The new exact algorithm leverages the efficient computation of a specific permutation test statistic, which originates from the work of Good (1952), and modifies it to accommodate two-sample comparisons. The new algorithm delivers significant performance improvements while maintaining the accuracy of the results. In particular, it delivers the same output as the Monte Carlo approximation with approximately ten times better computational performance. In addition to its applicability to large-scale data analyses, the new exact algorithm also offers more precise results than the Monte Carlo approximation, especially when dealing with small sample sizes. The paired-permutation test is an increasingly popular statistical method used in various applications, including the comparison of continuous outcome measures in randomized controlled trials. In the context of these trials, we have employed the new exact algorithm to conduct a test of the difference between two groups, as well as a test of the difference between treatment and control groups for each pair of observations. In particular, we have utilized this approach in a trial involving 160 participants in each group. The trial data were artificially constructed to determine the computational performance of the new exact algorithm. In this example, the algorithm required approximately 37 seconds when employing the Monte Carlo approximation method, whereas it took around 370 seconds for the exact algorithm on a single CPU. In contrast, employing the new exact algorithm led to a completion of the trial analysis within 13 days, whereas it took approximately 13 months when utilizing the Monte Carlo approximation method on a single CPU. In addition to the large-scale data analysis, we have also investigated the performance of the new exact algorithm through the simulation of different statistical scenarios. In these simulations, the performance of the algorithm was evaluated based on its ability to yield the correct test result while considering various factors such as the sample size, the distribution of the data, and the magnitude of the difference between the groups. In particular, we have found that the new exact algorithm delivers accurate results even in the presence of small sample sizes, often considered challenging for the paired-permutation test. The shipping industry is known for its strong competition and diverse players, but historically, a small number of large companies dominated global markets through cartels that fixed prices and divided territories. These traditional shipping cartels began dissolving around the mid-20th century as anti-trust regulations tightened and new entrants emerged, leading to a surge in freight rates and a collapse in shipping volumes in the 1960s, with similar patterns observed in the 1980s and 1990s. This study explores the recent decline of shipping cartels in the containerized market, drawing on newly collected data from 1960 to 2011 for four major shipping routes. The findings reveal that the absence of cartels led to increased shipping volumes and higher freight rates in the short run, but in the long run, prices returned to their initial levels as companies competed more fiercely. The study also discovers that the collapse of cartels accelerated in the 1990s and 2000s, primarily due to tighter anti-trust enforcement in Asia, but not in Europe or South America. Furthermore, it is observed that the dissolution of cartels resulted in lower freight rates and increased shipping volumes in the medium term, with the effects more pronounced in the 2000s. The study concludes that shipping cartels exert significant influence over shipping markets, with policy interventions and changes in industry dynamics affecting their persistence. The findings also highlight the limitations of existing empirical research on shipping markets due to reliance on incomplete and inaccurate data. The study recommends collecting more comprehensive historical data on shipping industries and their practices. The findings of this study are relevant to industry players, policymakers, and financial institutions that invest in the shipping industry, with implications for the ongoing consolidation in the sector. The study suggests that the shipping industry will continue to undergo significant changes in the future, with consolidation driven by differences in carrier profitability and changes in carrier alliances. The study also highlights the risk of anti-trust enforcement action in emerging markets with weak regulations, with the Chinese shipping market a prime example due to its large share of global shipping volumes and relatively lenient anti-trust regulations. The study recommends that Chinese shipping companies expand through acquisitions in weakly regulated markets rather than consolidating in strongly regulated markets. The findings of this research provide a historical context for the future of the shipping industry, with the study's data extending to 2011 but necessary extensions to the data period needed to understand the industry's developments in the 2010s. We establish that every loom space is associated with a specific type of triangulation, which we call a filtrating triangulation. This type of triangulation satisfies the condition that the vertices of the triangulation are divided into distinct layers, with no edges connecting vertices across different layers. This result has significant topological implications, allowing us to derive insights into the properties of loom spaces. Furthermore, we discover that the homotopy type of loom spaces can be determined by the homotopy types of their associated filtrating triangulations. Building upon this finding, we establish that the homotopy type of loom spaces is invariant under the condition that their associated filtrating triangulations have the same homotopy type for any sequence of changes to the vertices. Additionally, we discover that the homotopy type of loom spaces remains unchanged when the loom space changes in a specific way that is analogous to knotting/unknotting behavior. Lastly, we develop a method to decide whether a loom space with a specific property is knotted or unknotted by examining its associated filtrating triangulation. All of these discoveries were made possible by our initial discovery that every loom space can be converted into a sequence of changes to the vertices of its associated filtrating triangulation. We believe this research opens up new avenues for exploring the topological properties of loom spaces. We also introduce the concept of a loom space's knotting degree, which provides a measure of how complex its knotted state is, and we discuss the possibilities of applying this research to various real-world applications, including biology and materials science. We hope our findings will be useful in these fields and provide a foundation for future research. Our research demonstrates a promising application of deep learning in finance, with results that could be enhanced through the incorporation of more advanced techniques and more comprehensive data sets. We employ a novel "pre-non-relativistic" parametrization to smoothly connect the fundamental expressions of general relativity and its non-relativistic counterpart, enabling an analytical expansion of gravitational effects in the context of a second-order perturbation theory. By introducing a small parameter $\epsilon$, we can express general relativistic quantities using $\epsilon$-powered terms, and this expansion proves useful in calculating gravitational influences in multi-electron atoms. Our approach allows us to accurately determine the non-relativistic limit's fine structure corrections and other relativistic effects, which are crucial for achieving high precision in atomic energy level measurements. In our study, we focus on first-order (leading) and second-order (fine structure) effects resulting from the interaction between electrons and the gravitational field, as well as the field's direct impact on atomic energy levels. Our calculations involve evaluating various multi-electron atomic integrals that describe the distribution of electrons in atoms, and we employ numerical methods to calculate these integrals while assuming a static atomic configuration. Our research demonstrates that the discrepancies between experimental and calculated values of energy levels in atoms, when measured to a high precision, primarily arise from the interaction between the atomic electrons and the gravitational field, rather than other relativistic effects. Our findings also show that the energy differences between the ground states of atoms, measured to a high precision, cannot be accounted for by the conventional definition of the fine structure constant. We propose a modified version of the fine structure constant, denoted as $\alpha_G$, which takes into account the interaction between the electrons and the gravitational field, and could be crucial for achieving a precision of 10 orders of magnitude in atomic energy level measurements. We estimate the value of $\alpha_G$ to be approximately $4.3 \times 10^{-45}$, and believe it is essential for accurately measuring energy levels in atoms to a high precision. Our approach and resulting value of $\alpha_G$ are applicable not only to atoms but also to molecules and their ions. We acknowledge the limited scope of our research, which does not encompass particles at very high energies or those in cosmological contexts. We anticipate that our work could be significant in the development of gravitational constants in systems with low energies and large dimensions. We have conducted an in-depth examination of our methodology's reliability by implementing various techniques to validate our results, and our findings suggest that our approach is free from any ambiguities. We investigated the drag experienced by a cylindrical intruder moving through granular beds at various speeds, both superficial and subcritical, in a two-dimensional configuration. Our study reveals the presence of two distinct drag components: a constant drag associated with subcritical flow and a velocity-dependent drag evident in supercritical flow. The preponderant drag component shifted from the velocity-dependent to the constant component at a critical velocity, which decreased with the size of the intruder. Our findings further indicate that the drag experienced by the intruder is the sum of the constant drag and a velocity-dependent drag proportional to the square of the difference between the approach velocity and the intruder velocity. We also observed the same drag profiles in experiments using a fluid similar to water, albeit with a greater influence of the intruder's size in this case. Our results can be explained by the physics of shock formation around the intruder and highlight the importance of considering the intruder's size in a manner that reflects its impact on the surrounding environment. In the context of our experiments, the constant drag component can be interpreted as the drag associated with shock formation in granular beds, while the velocity-dependent drag component is linked to the presence of turbulent flows around the intruder. Our study paves the way for exploring similar phenomena in three-dimensional setups and extends our understanding of drag experienced by obstacles in fluid and granular dynamics. We also propose a universal drag coefficient based on the geometry of the intruder that holds true for both fluid and granular environments. Our research provides valuable insights for numerical models aiming to simulate the motion of objects in complex fluids and granular beds. Our experimental data are available for the benefit of the scientific community. Our investigation uncovered a striking parallel between the transverse momentum-dependent variations of PbProton triangular flow $v_{3p}$ and PbPair elliptic flow $v_{2p}$, exhibiting similar scalings with transverse momentum. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that the ratios of $v_{3p}/v_{2p}$ at 40 GeV are nearly invariant with respect to particle identification, albeit exhibiting a minor increase of approximately 10% as one moves from midrapidity to forward rapidity. The observed convergence of $v_{3p}/v_{2p}$ ratios from proton and antiproton data to those obtained using the PbPair signal is noteworthy. The measured values agree well with the expectations of iEBE-VISHNU v2 and v3 predictions, with the exception of a slight underprediction of $v_{3p}/v_{2p}$ ratios at forward rapidity. The success of iEBE-VISHNU in replicating our results encourages the continuation of event-by-event hydrodynamic simulations. The discovered similarity between $v_{3p}$ and $v_{2p}$ may be understood through the influence of initial state fluctuations or other mechanisms affecting triangular and elliptic flow. The minor dependence of $v_{3p}/v_{2p}$ ratios on transverse momentum or particle identification suggests that the underlying dynamics are relatively robust, laying the groundwork for future studies aiming to understand the underlying physics of these similarities. The robustness of these findings across different rapidity ranges allays concerns about potential contamination from forward emissions resulting from the PbProton scattering process. The detailed analysis of our results is consistent with our initial hypothesis that there exists a direct connection between triangular and elliptic flow in PbProton and PbPair collisions at the LHC. The discovered similarities also raise important implications for future experiments aiming to identify potential signals in rare processes like triangular flow. The event-by-event hydrodynamic simulations, coupled with initial condition generators like iEBE, will undoubtedly play a vital role in furthering our understanding of these phenomena. This research investigates rare decay events in B mesons, specifically the rare occurrences of B^0_s decaying into mu+ mu- and B^0 decaying into mu+ mu-. Accurate measurements of these rare processes are crucial for revealing potential new phenomena resulting from the influence of heavy elements on the fundamental theory of particle physics. Our study utilizes two significant datasets collected at the LEP collider by the ALEPH experiment, with an accumulated energy of 3.0 TeV in the first dataset and 3.0 to 5.5 TeV in the second, spanning the period between 1990 and 2000. We employed sophisticated detection methods to identify decay events, combining data from different sources and accounting for potential false counts. The observed frequencies of these rare events were then compared to predicted values based on the fundamental theory of particle physics, revealing that the actual occurrences of B^0_s and B^0 mesons decaying into mu+ mu- are substantially lower than expected, with the results being: the frequency of B^0_s events occurring within the 1 to 14 GeV energy range is 1.54 times the predicted value, with an energy range of 1.04 to 1.06 times the expected value for the B^0 events within the 10 to 57 GeV energy range; the frequency of B^0 events occurring within the 10 to 57 GeV energy range is 1.06 times the predicted value, with an energy range of 1.04 to 1.06 times the expected value for the B^0 events within the 10 to 57 GeV energy range. We also discovered that the energy ranges of the two B^0 events are slightly different from the predicted values based on the fundamental theory of particle physics, but we cannot rule out uncertainty associated with our method of detection. We estimated the branching fractions of these rare events as the following: the branching fraction of B^0_s events occurring within the 1 to 14 GeV energy range is 8.6 x 10^-5, with an energy range of 6.8 x 10^-5 to 9.8 x 10^-5 for the B^0 events within the 10 to 57 GeV energy range; the branching fraction of B^0 events occurring within the 10 to 57 GeV energy range is 6.8 x 10^-5 to 9.8 x 10^-5. The Fast Generalized Minimum Residual (FGMRES) method has become a premier Krylov subspace method for solving large linear systems due to its efficiency and convergence properties. However, the standard FGMRES iteration sometimes experiences issues with stability, particularly when dealing with ill-conditioned matrices. To address this problem, the anonymous authors proposed an anonymous strategy based on matrix preconditioning in an anonymous year. Building upon their work, we introduce a new variation of the FGMRES method that leverages an inverse operator as a preconditioner and achieves better convergence results. Theoretical analysis has confirmed that this new method reduces the number of iterations required compared to the standard FGMRES. To further enhance the method's performance, we also introduced a new variation of the FGMRES iteration that uses the converged residual from the previous iteration as the initial residual. The proposed method can be applied to a wide range of applications, including the Helmholtz equation, the Helmholtz equation in the presence of scattering, the time-dependent heat equation, the Helmholtz equation with discontinuous coefficients, and a nonlinear Helmholtz equation. The numerical experiments conducted across different scenarios demonstrated the proposed method's effectiveness in obtaining accurate solutions. The code developed for the numerical experiments is available online. The research presented in this paper was financially supported by the National Science Foundation. Accurate organ modeling through registration is crucial for enhancing surgical outcomes, but it becomes increasingly challenging in real-world surgeries due to the presence of noisy intraoperative data. This study introduces a novel non-rigid registration method that can handle various types of data irregularities, including those commonly found in laparoscopic visions, for the purpose of modeling major abdominal organs. The proposed algorithm, based on a geometric formulation using Euclidean distance, is designed to be computationally efficient and robust in processing noisy data. The method's performance is evaluated through simulations and ex-vivo data testing. The results show that our algorithm effectively models the liver and spleen with high accuracy, even in scenarios with substantial data noise. Furthermore, our framework has the potential for integration with haptic feedback technology to enhance surgical experiences. Estimating optical flow is a fundamental and intricate problem, and recent self-supervised methods have achieved remarkable results. However, flow estimation still struggles with occlusions. In order to enhance robustness to this common real-world phenomenon, this study introduces a novel self-supervised optical flow estimation framework called SmoothConnect. Initially, the model learns to predict forward flow utilizing a standard time-contrastive objective, and then employs another contrastive loss to calculate the reverse flow. These two contrastive objectives are designed to create correspondence between a point and its surrounding spatial neighborhood, effectively linking dispersed parts of an image. The model further leverages the smoothness property of optical flow by integrating a voxelized connectivity graph, thereby enhancing connectivity between distant points and areas hidden by occlusions. In order to evaluate the proposed method and existing state-of-the-art self-supervised flow estimation techniques, a new occlusion annotation dataset is constructed and tested on clean datasets, yielding superior results. Moreover, SmoothConnect is compared to state-of-the-art methods on the MPII Flow and KITTI 2015 datasets, demonstrating its performance. The code of the proposed method is publicly available at: https://github.com/zhengyun113/SmoothConnect. The newly constructed occlusion dataset is accessible at: https://github.com/zhengyun113/OcclusionFlow. The developed model is an initial step towards creating self-supervised optical flow estimation techniques that are more robust to occlusions, and there is considerable potential for improvement. The evaluation dataset and code will be continuously updated based on feedback from the community. The design of the proposed model does not incur a significant computational cost, and the training of the model takes approximately 12 days on a single NVIDIA A100-48G GPU. The trained model achieves the following results: an error of 5.43 on the MPII Flow dataset and an error of 4.75 on the KITTI 2015 dataset. Researchers have successfully developed memristor-based neural networks with a single-layer architecture, but a comprehensive analysis of their functionality requires further investigation. This study develops a fundamental 2-tier neural network and proves that it operates in accordance with standard perceptron principles, thus validating the memristor-based 2-tier network by associating it with known data sets. A single-example classification algorithm and a majority-voting scheme were both tested and yielded accurate results. A 2-tier network was also found to exhibit tunable learning capabilities and its memristor implementation was verified using a simulation of a real-world circuit. In addition to this, a 2-tier network was found to demonstrate excellent classification performance on MNIST, Reuter, and NUS3D data sets, surpassing the performance of traditional ANNs while consuming significantly less power. In the area of image classification, a 2-tier network was found to achieve memorable results, with a 96.75% accuracy rate on the MNIST data set, and a 93.57% accuracy rate on the NUS3D data set, both being the highest rates reported to date. In the case of a larger 50-class Reuter data set, a 2-tier network attained a 93.13% accuracy rate, which is the highest reported rate to date, achieving this with just a 20-fold training and without employing deep learning techniques, thus validating the robustness and effectiveness of this simple yet efficient classification model. A 2-tier network was also found to demonstrate a linear scaling of learning and a significant reduction in power consumption of up to 18 times when implemented using a memristor-based circuit, making it an extremely attractive solution for real-world, real-time classification applications. A strong magnetic field is found to significantly influence the state of matter composed of quarks, particularly one that is spin polarized, and may lead to the formation of quark matter with unusual properties. In a study, the equation of state for this type of matter under a magnetic field was examined in detail. It revealed that for a sufficiently strong field, quark matter may become overdense and potentially explain certain astronomical phenomena. Furthermore, strange quark matter may be created at high temperatures and densities, and its ability to sustain itself through degenerate electron captures was investigated. In addition, a model was used to estimate the maximum density of strange quark matter in various scenarios. It was discovered that a magnetic field can cause strange quark matter to become extremely dense, with densities that could be comparable to neutron star densities, and even lead to the formation of quark stars rather than neutron stars. Numerical solutions to the Dirac equation for a single quark in a magnetic field were also obtained. Lastly, a hypothesis proposing that quark matter with the highest density may have spin polarization was tested by calculating the density of strange quark matter as a function of spin polarization. It was found that even a moderately polarized quark matter density could be extremely high, reaching densities that may be associated with the missing mass problem. It was also discovered that adding strange quarks may not increase the density of quark matter as expected, and that a maximum density exists before quark matter becomes too dense, which was found to be linked to spin polarization. It was concluded that spin polarization may be a crucial factor in determining the equation of state for quark matter and could provide an explanation for certain astronomical phenomena that may be related to quark matter, such as supernova SN 1987A and gamma-ray bursts. It was also suggested that quark matter with the highest density may have spin polarization and associated densities that could be associated with the missing mass problem, quark stars, and certain extreme astronomical events. It was noted that the study's findings depend heavily on a specific model and that different models may lead to different results. It was also pointed out that the study assumes that the magnetic field has a significant impact on quark matter but acknowledges that this assumption may not be accurate in all scenarios. It was further mentioned that the study's limitations include not considering interactions between quarks and other particles that may also contribute to the equation of state, and not accounting for fluctuations in density and temperature that may influence the state of quark matter. An even-2-factorable cubic graph is defined as a cubic graph whose edges can be divided into two disjoint matchings, subject to certain conditions, and we have discovered that constructing 1-factorizations or 2-factorizations from them doesn't necessarily result in all possible 2-factorizations of the graph. Our research delves into even-2-factorable cubic graphs and we have multiple results: a cubic graph is considered even-2-factorable if a specific orientation of its edges satisfies certain conditions; another definition of even-2-factorable cubic graphs utilizes the number of matchings needed to cover its edges; also, we have an algorithm that generates all 2-factorizations of a cubic graph by first determining all 1-factorizations and modifying some of them, as well as identifying specific classes of even-2-factorable cubic graphs that include all graph enantiomers, torus graphs, and certain wedge-sums of graphs. System call filtering is crucial for preventing malicious system calls in applications, although implementing it can be complicated, especially for programs written in interpreted languages that leverage native libraries via foreign function interfaces. To address this issue, we present Timeloops, a Linux-based isolation mechanism that intercepts native system calls for programs in interpreted languages. Timeloops utilizes Dynamic Linker magic to redirect system calls and employs eBPF to filter system calls with native performance. Our initial implementation includes two variants: Timeloops-Dev, which targets Python applications via ctypes, and Timeloops-Prod, designed to work with PHP/FPM. Our testing shows that both variants exceed native system call speeds and successfully block malicious system calls. Furthermore, we outline possible enhancements, including support for additional languages and more sophisticated system call filtering. Our findings demonstrate that system call filtering is feasible with native performance, even for programs in interpreted languages, and provides a foundation for additional security features and deeper system call analysis. A key issue in FWI arises when using time-domain wavefields, as the gradient norm often increases rapidly and eventually becomes unbounded due to the growing oscillations, making it difficult to apply convergence theory and resulting in a difficult optimization problem. We investigate the possibility of applying frequency-filtered source waveforms to mitigate this frequency mode mixing and examine the impact on the gradient norm in both time and frequency domains through the application of filters before computing the data misfit. We analyze the impact of different filter types, including those based on recorded data and the background model, on the estimated gradient, and consider the effects of different parameterization methods, such as elemental and model-conditional methods. We also investigate methods to constrain the model update by combining the filtered gradient with the elemental gradient computed from the time-domain wavefields. We test our approach on synthetic data sets involving the Marmousier model with point sources and a 3D mesh, and observe that pre-filtering the source waveforms can significantly reduce the mode mixing and the resulting unbounded gradient norm, especially when using the frequency-filter method, which is found to be the most effective approach, although elemental conditional method also produces satisfactory results. We further examine the performance of filtered source waveforms in the acquisition geometry test, where we remove the filtered source locations from the data set, and successfully recover the true model with the filtered gradient only. We conclude that applying frequency-filtered source waveforms can mitigate mode mixing and the resulting unbounded gradient norm, and that this approach is valuable for the application in real data sets. We also emphasize the potential challenge associated with the parameterization method in the filtered source method, and recommend further research on this issue. We believe our approach provides a promising solution for the challenging source wavefield mode mixing issue in time-domain FWI, and our results encourage the further exploration of this approach with real data sets. We also propose the frequency-filtered source waveform approach as a useful tool for interpreting the mode mixing phenomenon with wavefield simulations, and for examining the robustness of the gradient norm with different parameterization methods. Understanding how vocabulary changes over time to reflect a concept's evolving characteristics is crucial for tracking linguistic and societal developments. Variations in contextual variance, a statistical property of word distributions, can contribute to the perceived shifts in language meaning. To separate genuine semantic evolution from changes in contextual variance, we must distinguish between intrinsic and extrinsic factors affecting language. Intrinsically, this distinction is comparable to differentiating a symbol's inherent meaning from its usage in a particular context. To achieve this, we propose a context-dependent model where the representation of a word is explained by both its intrinsic semantics and extrinsic factors influencing contextual variance. To illustrate the significance of this distinction, we analyzed the semantic shift hypothesis related to the word "youth", finding that changes in contextual variance primarily accounted for its perceived semantic evolution over time. To further validate our proposed model, we conducted additional experiments on a broader set of words ("obedience", "honesty", and "luck") and the descriptors associated with famous people in the PG-13 movie dataset, both showing similar results and demonstrating the robustness of our approach. We also explored the relationship between contextual variance and several extrinsic factors, including part-of-speech patterns, syntactic dependencies, and temporal variations. Furthermore, we employed our proposed model to track the semantic evolution of the word "youth" incorporating these extrinsic factors, revealing that the model's performance is comparable to the baseline established by Kuperman (2018) and the features alone. Nonetheless, our approach is not without limitations, as our proposed model assumes that the intrinsic semantics of a word remains relatively stable over time, an assumption that may not hold true for words with complex or nuanced meanings, as demonstrated by the example of the word "youth". To overcome this limitation, we suggest future research directions, such as analyzing the intrinsic semantics of words with complex meanings and tracking the semantic evolution of descriptive attributes associated with famous people in the dataset of movie titles. This research paves the way for a deeper understanding of the relationship between language, society, and semantics, and the dynamics that underlie the interplay between context, variance, and meaning. A sensing matrix with reduced mutual coherence can lead to superior reconstruction performance, which has driven research into methods for minimizing coherence. However, these optimizations are generally computationally intensive. The paper presents a novel, efficient algorithm to generate a compressed sensing matrix with optimized mutual coherence for real-time applications, specifically targeting image processing tasks. The proposed scheme utilizes a pseudo-random matrix as the initial input and applies a modified Giraud algorithm to achieve streamlined mutual coherence reduction. The algorithm's performance is evaluated in various compressed sensing scenarios, including Gaussian and Bernoulli matrices, and notable improvements in the Laplace norm of the Gram matrix are observed with only a limited increase in encoding complexity. The proposed method demonstrates notable reconstruction performance gains, which are measurable in the mean squared error (MSE) metric. The paper also showcases the scheme's versatility by adapting it to a non-uniform compressed sensing setup, which exhibits promising results. The algorithm's efficiency, combined with its performance enhancements, make it suitable for a wide range of real-time compressed sensing applications. Let $\Sigma$ be a compact surface without boundary, of positive Euler characteristic, and denote by $\mathrm{Diff}_0(\Sigma)$ the group of diffeomorphisms of $\Sigma$ that are isotopic to the identity. We investigate actions of a subgroup $G$ of $\mathrm{Diff}_0(\Sigma)$ on the interior of $\Sigma$, which we denote by $\mathrm{Diff}_0^*(\Sigma)$. When this action is transitive and the orbit space is precompact, we show that $G$ has a finite-dimensional manifold of orbits in $\mathrm{Diff}_0^*(\Sigma)$, realizable as a submanifold of the space $\mathrm{Diff}_0^*(\Sigma)$ with a specific smooth structure. Conversely, we establish that any action of $G$ on the interior of $\Sigma$ with a certain property, which is equivalent to a specific condition on the first cohomology group of $G$, arises from an action on a manifold of orbits in $\mathrm{Diff}_0^*(\Sigma)$. Finally, we examine relationships between these actions and those described by Gueritaux on surfaces with boundary and by Franks-Weiss on three-dimensional manifolds. Our results also provide a solution to Hilson's problem, extending works by Hilson, Gueritaux, Franks-Weiss, and Baragiola. Given two finite sets of complex numbers, not including rational numbers, we investigate the computational feasibility of determining if there exists a rational function that is continuous across the plane that connects these two sets. A rational function is characterized by the formula f(z) = A(z)/B(z), where A and B are polynomial equations with coefficients from the set of rational numbers. We can determine if a rational function is continuous for any given set of complex numbers using a computational procedure known as the Identity Theorem, which relies on evaluating the function at the elements of the given set and solving a system of linear equations. However, this method requires an infinite number of computations, rendering it an essentially impossible task. To circumvent this limitation, we consider a more practical solution that involves connecting the given sets with rays and evaluating the function along these lines by solving a sequence of linear equations. We demonstrate that this approach belongs to the computational complexity class NP intersect coNP, which is equivalent to NP according to the 1971 Cohen-Shelah proof. We also examine instances of connected sets for which this approach has a linear as well as a quadratic complexity variant, both belonging to the NP class. Furthermore, we show that deciding the continuity of a single rational function across a specified line segment is essentially impossible by establishing a connection with the computational intractability of solving systems of linear equations and the non-emptiness problem for context-free languages. We conclude by highlighting the relatedness of our findings to prior work on the complexity of the Hilbert's Nullstellensatz problem.

A pervasive issue in processing complex time series involves systems that evolve on multiple scales and exhibit multiple stable states, complicating traditional machine learning methods.  A new approach is proposed, utilizing a spiking neuromorphic reservoir computer that efficiently handles Kolmogorov-Landau type time series and switches between different attractors by incorporating a multiscalar encoder and a phase reset function.  This approach successfully replicates multiple coexisting dynamics, outperforming a comparable conventional computer by 10 orders of magnitude in terms of training data.  Furthermore, this novel reservoir computer, in the form of a 1,024-neuron TrueNorth chip, is capable of real-time, unsupervised classification of nonlinear phenomena observed in a complex system, with a significant reduction in required data.  The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through applications to a multiscalar Koch curve and the coexistence of rotating and stationary states in the Taylor-Couette system. We develop a reachability analysis method for a class of dynamic systems with feedback control, based on the concept of causal interpretations. This approach utilizes sequential numerical computation to calculate the reachable state sets within a given time frame. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by applying it to a specific aircraft pitch system. Furthermore, we compare its performance to existing methods utilizing nonlinear optimization and feedback linearization. The proposed approach is shown to be superior in terms of both the accuracy and computation time required to determine reachable states. The study also highlights the potential uses of this method in assessing system reliability and developing feedback control strategies. The research and test results are supported by numerical data. A curious aspect of human perception involves the difficulty in categorizing certain visual stimuli as being animate or inanimate, leading some images to be perceived as both non-animate and animal-like. Prior research has attempted to explain this animacy spectrum, but a comprehensive framework has yet to be established. We propose a dual-path model, separating the spectrum into two distinct components: visual categorizability and agency. Our framework showcases the distinct contributions of these components to the animacy continuum, demonstrated through a series of controlled experiments using a crowd sourcing platform. Our findings validate the two-path model and reveal its practical applications, including the creation of highly believable deer-like images through a generative model. Furthermore, our framework extends the understanding of the animacy spectrum to more complex and realistic representations, paving the way for enhanced photorealistic generation. Our research and approach are relevant to various fields, including computer vision, graphics, and the study of human perception. This research develops a formal logic known as quantum relational Hoare logic with the ability to numerically examine the connection between a program's input and output in relation to specific quantitative properties, expanding previous variants by incorporating relational Hoare logic with quantities. We have confirmed that our logic is equivalent to its underlying hypothesis, namely the quantitative variant of relational Hoare logic with monads, as well as establishing the soundness and completeness of our logic through proof. Further, our findings have been tested on notable examples, including recursive functions and quantum programs. A real-world application of our framework involves verifying the correctness of a quantum algorithm for approximate nearest neighbours, known as the quantum cosine similarity estimator. This application was initially proposed by [Cai et al, arXiv:2005.10492, arXiv:2011.13169]. We have also demonstrated the ease with which our framework can be adapted to accommodate variations of this algorithm, demonstrating the versatility of our approach. DeepSet achieves a new record in the accurate simulation of protein-ligand interactions, reducing the required computational data by 35 times, surpassing the previous deep learning-based model "AlphaLigand". Literature-based analysis reveals that AlphaLigand's limitations stem from its reliance on hand-crafted features and inadequate utilization of advanced deep learning techniques. This research develops a multiscale model to simulate the thermomechanical properties of polymers as they undergo crystallization caused by stretching. By incorporating the effects of material structure at two scales, it provides a framework for understanding the intricate relationships between material microstructure, mechanical forces, temperature, and the resulting crystalline patterns. A unique feature of this model lies in its use of the Cahn-Hillard equation, a mathematical equation established in material science, to describe the formation of crystalline regions within the material. Furthermore, it accounts for the heat generated and dissipated within the material as it crystallizes. Numerical simulations of this model were conducted and the results compared with experimental data obtained from physical simulations of stretching polydomain elastomer crystals. These comparisons validated the proposed model and revealed its capability in predicting the distribution of crystalline regions and the resulting heat within the material. Additionally, this model predicts the occurrence of unique crystalline patterns, referred to as armchair shapes, which have been observed in experimental data but remained unexplained until now. The proposed model offers a valuable tool for predicting the thermomechanical properties of polymers and other crystalline materials by providing insights into the intricate relationships between material structure, mechanical forces, temperature, and the resulting crystalline patterns. This innovation enables the voltage at which a nanowire transitions to superconductivity to be altered in a controlled manner, thereby compensating any fluctuations in the nanowire's properties. Utilizing a silicon capacitor near the nanowire results in the capacitive coupling of its electric properties, which in turn allows the nanowire's critical voltage to be adjusted in response to the applied voltage. Furthermore, the system's stability can be maintained with minimal fluctuations in the capacitance. Unlike conventional approaches, DVS-Net predicts videos in the ego-reference frame instead of the target view, yielding higher accuracy in novel view synthesis. This beam splitter can successfully control vortices of any order, with simulation results confirming its effectiveness. We investigate how a restriction on the Lipschitz constant of a neural network's activations function influences its optimization, leveraging a variety of $p$-norms. Our analysis shows that this limitation can be expressed as a regularizer, enabling a unified view of existing approaches that employ weight decay and the margin-based regularization method. Furthermore, we establish that this regularizer diminishes in proportion to the $2p$-norm of the network's weights, leading to a hypothesis on the suitable choice of $p$ that minimizes overparameterization. Empirical evaluation through multiple datasets and networks confirms our findings, revealing that $p=2$ often results in the most accurate predictions with the fewest parameters. Our work provides a theoretical foundation for various regularization techniques and practical guidance on hyperparameter selection in neural network optimization. The accuracy of WiFi-based positioning systems can be enhanced by estimating the distance between geospatial WiFi fingerprints. This distance estimation challenge has hindered the development of self-learning mapping technologies, including those utilizing neural networks. Our research introduces KRD, a novel kernel-based method that leverages reinforcement learning to estimate these distances. The development of future particle accelerators might rely on energy recovery linacs (ERLs).  These machines use a small number of acceleration stages to reduce electrical power requirements and emissions.  A multi-pass ERL design, in particular, could provide high beam energies while maintaining compact structures.  However, beam-RF interactions pose a challenge, particularly if multiple pulse modulation is employed, as it requires a more complex phase management, potentially leading to a higher threshold current and unnecessary power losses.  This research focuses on mode-locking, another potential issue, which could arise from interacting beams and RF fields, potentially limiting modulation efficiency and leading to unexpected effects, such as beam loss, RF breakdown, or unexpected emission of radiation.  We investigated how different filling patterns influence these problems and possible solutions were found, including changing beam energy, adjusting phase management, and modifying the configuration of RF cavities.  Our studies suggest that careful selection of filling patterns can prevent mode-locking, delaying its onset until higher currents are reached, and demonstrate that current limits are primarily related to beam-RF interactions rather than radiation emission.  We propose that improved designs incorporating multi-pass ERLs could meet the requirements of future particle and radiation experiments with the same level of efficiency but significantly reduced emissions.  Our proposed concept is applicable to future particle and radiation experiments that require high beam energies, such as the Lattice Electron-Positron Collider (LEP), the Future Circular Electron-Positron Collider (FCC), and the International Linear Collider (ILC).  Our research was conducted as part of the FCC project, but our findings are relevant to other circular colliders and linear lepton colliders with high beam energies.  Our results also provide a framework for optimizing the efficiency and reducing emissions of other particle accelerators that employ energy recovery techniques.  Our studies were performed using the FCC main linac as an example, but our findings are applicable to other energy recovery linacs. The model of polymer brushes is a fundamental model describing long polymer chains ending at points that are fixed in space, and it has significant applications in various fields such as biotechnology, materials science and biology. In this study, we examine the free energy associated with stretching polymers in curved surfaces by applying the parastochastic flow method. As a result, we derive a free energy equation for stretching polymers in curved surfaces. Furthermore, we obtain specific equations for the free energy associated with stretching polymers in spherical and cylindrical surfaces. Our research demonstrates that the free energy equation can be expressed in terms of a $|\nabla \phi|^2$ term, where $\phi$ represents the local density of polymers. Our study also reveals that the average end-to-end distance of polymers is directly proportional to the surface curvature. Our results for spherical and cylindrical surfaces match previous research findings. Our work paves the way for further research on polymer brushes in complex surfaces. Our approach based on the parastochastic flow method provides a new perspective on the free energy associated with stretching polymers in curved surfaces. Our equations for spherical and cylindrical surfaces can be used as benchmarks for other numerical methods. A graph G is described as having a specific "truncated metric dimension" value, denoted as τ (k), which represents the smallest integer t, where for any pair of nodes u and v in G, the geodesic distance between u and v is capped at t, and this results in u and v being distinguishable. In other words, if u and v can be told apart with a distance limit of k, then u and v are at a distance less than k. This concept leads to a characterization of τ (k) in terms of the parameter k and the metric dimension of a graph G, especially in the cases of graphs without loops and without double edges and those with loops and without double edges. Additionally, we investigate the relationships between τ (k) and the concepts of upper metric dimension, dominant metric dimension, and half metric dimension. Finally, we provide algorithms for calculating the truncated metric dimension for specific types of graphs, including trees, power trees, regular trees, and cycles. Moreover, we establish lower and upper bounds for τ (k) in the mentioned graph structures, with the exception of power trees for which only an upper bound exists. A noteworthy finding reveals that the difference between the upper and lower bounds of τ (k) increases proportionally to the square root of k. We also investigate the relationship between the truncated metric dimension and the number of nodes in these graph types, which can serve as guidelines for constructing graphs with desired properties. Our research on the truncated metric dimension also extends to its application in a problem related to the capability of a distributed system to identify its nodes based on message exchange distance thresholds. This enables us to derive performance indicators for a specific distributed system in a circular environment, denoted as WSN Circle-Pro, which can determine its own structure after execution. Our data also includes the lowest possible distance threshold k_min, the corresponding metric dimension m_min, the number of nodes n_max, and the corresponding distance threshold k_max in the graph types we examined. Our research provides a foundation for further study on the truncated metric dimension in graphs. Active galactic nuclei (AGNs) vary significantly, making long-term monitoring and in-depth analysis crucial. However, conventional techniques can be ineffective for decades-long observations, leading to significant losses in data utility. We introduce a novel method, DeepForest, that employs a deep learning algorithm, specifically a deep neural network, to analyze long-duration AGN data without manual intervention and accurately identify patterns of variability. This approach enables researchers to leverage full datasets, uncover hidden trends and anomalies, and compare them to established variability indicators. By applying DeepForest to UGC 12140, we discovered unusual, decade-long fluctuations that could be related to its inner bulge characteristics. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of machine learning in AGN variability analysis and provides a foundation for further investigation into the unique characteristics of UGC 12140. We also outline potential future research, such as applying this method to other AGNs and exploring more variability indicators. Additionally, we make the code and data available for the community to use. We plan to extend our research by using DeepForest to analyze larger datasets and more complex galaxy populations. We have made the code and data for this study publicly available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/AstroTOM/UGC12140_analysis. We look forward to collaborating with the community to advance our understanding of UGC 12140 and the variability of AGNs in general. We have submitted this study as a pre-print to the astro-ph journal, and it awaits peer review before official publication. We expect the final version to be published in the journal soon. We have also presented the findings of this research at conferences, including the annual meeting of the Astronomical Society of Australia, and it has been recognized with an award. We are open to feedback, suggestions, and proposals for new projects related to this research. This research investigates the computational challenges and fair valuation approaches for several prominent decision-making applications, including matching, network, and market problems. The discovery of small binary asteroids relies heavily on wide field surveys, which provide positional data for several asteroids. However, most asteroids appear as single points in space, making it challenging to confirm their binary nature. A new method has been developed that analyzes the point spread function of images from these surveys using tools like the Moffat function and the Gaussian function for ground-based and space-based observations, respectively. These analyses help determine the apparent sizes of asteroids and their shapes, which are crucial for identifying binary asteroids. Applying this technique to pre-existing data sets, a re-examination was conducted of suspect binary asteroids found in the Palermo Asteroid Survey and Pan-STARRS, and the results show that while some of these asteroids have irregular shapes, none of them have the characteristics expected of binary asteroids. A new criterion is proposed for identifying binary asteroids based on their elliptical shapes and the uncertainty of their positions, and it is necessary to observe these asteroids in close orbit using high-resolution telescopes to confirm their binary nature. A study of the astrometry of 20 suspect binary asteroids found in the survey data showed that while shape and size can remain the same over time, there are instances where the orbits decay quickly and these asteroids become active comets. Therefore, close observations are necessary for a comprehensive understanding of these small binary asteroids that are on the verge of breaking apart and becoming active comets. A comprehensive study was also conducted of the asteroid 2013 DA14, which had a close call with Earth in 2013, and its orbital decay was simulated using various initial conditions, and the results show that while some asteroids with decay periods of over a year were not found, there are many small asteroids with decay periods of weeks to months that were not observed despite being in close proximity to Earth. Our in-depth analysis of three distinctively "shallown" knotted protein structures reveals a common "channeled" folding pattern, contrasting with the more complex pathways predicted for "deeply" knotted proteins. The absence of intermediate states in the folding sequences of these three proteins is noteworthy. Our study used molecular dynamics simulations to recreate two possible scenarios: one from scratch and one starting from an initially random, fully unfolded state. The simulation results for the three "shallown" knotted proteins align with our predictions, showing that the folding process involves a direct, single-chain pathway with no need for chain threading interactions typical of "deeply" knotted proteins. In contrast, the simulated folding of a "deeply" knotted protein, protein GdtC, yielded a different outcome, with our simulations indicating a more complex folding pathway that includes intermediate states and chain threading interactions. Our study provides a initial look at the folding patterns of knotted proteins and highlights the need for further research into the folding mechanisms of all knotted proteins. Our simulations are consistent with the recently proposed model that protein folding is largely determined by the protein sequence itself, with the knotted proteins we studied serving as intriguing examples. Our simulations were performed using the GROMACS software version 2018.6, with the AMBER ff99SB-ILDN force field. We explore a variation of an irrationality condition that applies to a specific type of symplectic form, which we call Steplike Irrationality. This condition enables us to demonstrate the existence of a wide range of notch mappings on a certain class of closed manifolds with specific symplectic properties, including those without any closed trajectories. Furthermore, we establish that this class of manifolds, which include those without any closed trajectories, are topologically distinct from Fomenko's "Dollars bills" ($\mathbb{CP}^2$ and $S^2 \tilde{\times} S^2$) when $H_1(M) = \mathbb{Z}$, providing an alternative proof of a result previously obtained by Matsumoto. We also demonstrate that our Steplike Irrationality condition can be applied to a subset of fillable manifolds without any closed trajectories and show that these manifolds are topologically equivalent to $\mathbb{CP}^2$ or $S^2 \tilde{\times} S^2$ when $H_1(M) = \mathbb{Z}$. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between our condition and Gromov's filling inequalities to discover a range of integers for which there are symplectic fillable manifolds without any closed trajectories. Moreover, we establish that our Steplike Irrationality condition cannot be applied to Eskin-Ulcigrai's example or to many other closed manifolds with rational flows. We also provide a new example of a closed manifold with a rational symplectic form that is not fillable, thus answering an open question posed by Gaydt Kostiantynov. Single-layer graphene on copper grew with 50-150 nm thick epitaxial films of AlN, GaN, or AlGaN developing into distinct, temperature-dependent micrometer-scale domains.  High-resolution transmission electron microscopy revealed that at lower temperatures, the materials formed cubic aluminum nitride in their center and wurtzite GaN at their edges, while higher temperatures resulted in cubic aluminum nitride around the edges and wurtzite GaN in the center.  This unique phenomenon was not observed in multi-layer graphene.  Furthermore, higher growth temperatures led to increased wurtzite GaN formation and greater distances between its domains.  This research demonstrated the intricate dynamics of graphene and material interactions, offering insights into reliable large-scale synthesis of epitaxial materials.  A proposed mechanism involving temperature-dependent surface free energy was suggested to explain the observed results.  This study's findings provide a foundation for understanding and controlling the formation of heterogeneous epitaxial domains at the nanoscale.  The demonstrated technology and underlying physics have far-reaching applications in materials science, nanotechnology, and device manufacturing. We evaluate two variants of S2M sampling in single and multi-grained settings and find it outperforms synthetic data methods and simple uniform sampling. It is demonstrated that the concept of weak naturality adapts to adjunctions and, in turn, these adjunctions are found to be mediated by the coequalizers of the monads resulting from combinatorial transformations. Furthermore, this paper establishes a connection between the property of weak naturality and the universal property of colimits. The utility of these concepts is illustrated through applications to the categories of presheaves and functors. Additionally, this work explores the theoretical framework of universal weak naturality, encompassing the instances of universal weak naturality that arise from the categories of presheaves and functors. The results presented in this paper are tailored to categories equipped with a monadic structure. The case studies provided involve categories rooted in topology, logic, and algebra, serving as empirical evidence for the theoretical framework established. The technical aspects of this research are underpinned by the principles of category theory, leveraging the mathematical framework to enhance the understanding of theoretical concepts and categorize the intuitive experiences of practicing researchers. The categories of presheaves and functors are found to embody the property of universal weak naturality, whereas the categories of sets and functions are considered the most basic instance of weak naturality. The distinction between the concepts of adjoint functors and monads and the related categories of Eilenberg-MacLane, along with the combinatorial transformations of categories, are also explored in this research. The categories studied in this work are structured by monads, serving as a framework that encompasses both algebraic and geometric contexts.
