This work introduces a new approach to analyzing nonlinear dynamical systems by incorporating the Koopman operator, which enables a higher-dimensional representation of these systems. Although the original formulation required the Koopman operator to be represented by a infinite-dimensional operator, researchers have discovered a way to approximate it using a set of finite-dimensional operators, which are essentially matrices. This compact representation facilitates the computation of relevant quantities, such as the Koopman operator's eigenvalues and eigenvectors, but only for specific systems. To expand on this finding, the study proposes a more general framework for the nonlinear dynamics system, which includes, for example, chaotic systems like the Lorenz equation, and demonstrates the validity of this approach through numerical experiments. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the proposed method can be applied to solve two problems: the first involves determining the stability of nonlinear systems by analyzing the Koopman operator's eigenvalues, and the second involves using the proposed method to discover the system's underlying dynamics. The study demonstrates the method's effectiveness on various nonlinear systems, including those with multiple coexisting attractors and chaotic systems with noise-induced dynamics. The proposed approach and the associated algorithms are implemented and the results are published in the supplementary material available at the authors' website. The code used for these results is also publicly available at the authors' website. Neural text generation models like LSTM-based MGAN and transformer-based TFGAN have achieved superior performance in machine translation and neural text generation tasks. However, selecting optimal sentence representations to input to these models remains challenging. In response, SparseGAN is proposed, a method that generates precise and diverse sentence representations to input to neural text generators using a GAN-based encoder. Unlike conventional approaches, SparseGAN employs an encoder with a specific sparse embedding layer that acquires a feature extractor, allowing it to produce high-dimensional representations that are both precise and varied. Experimental data indicate that SparseGAN outperforms baseline encoder models in terms of sentence similarity measurement, yields superior translation results in controlled experiments, and produces more authentic artificial texts as a bonus. Additionally, SparseGAN's unique characteristics are substantiated mathematically, offering theoretical insights into its capabilities and limitations. The source code of SparseGAN is available at https://github.com/zhongjieLAI/SparseGAN.

Traditional methods are now being supplemented by modern capture-recapture techniques that leverage advanced models to incorporate both temporal and spatial elements. The popular Poisson SCR model has been widely utilized, but it assumes unequal encounter probabilities across animals, making it challenging to estimate these probabilities, and thereby potentially leading to biased density estimates. In contrast, the Bernoulli SCR model, which models encounter probabilities as equal, is simpler and more robust, yet it has seen limited application due to its assumed inability to accommodate complex encounter probabilities. However, we show that the Bernoulli model can indeed handle various encounter probability scenarios and, under certain conditions, is statistically equivalent to the Poisson model, thus providing a more accessible alternative. Our approach includes a data-driven method to determine whether the Bernoulli model is appropriate for a given dataset, incorporating a precise test to assess the equality of encounter probabilities across locations and time. We demonstrate the effectiveness and versatility of our method by conducting simulations and analyzing real-world data from animal studies. Our results suggest that the Bernoulli SCR model can be a more reliable option than its Poisson counterpart, especially when encounter probabilities are constant or nearly constant, and we emphasize the utility of our approach in facilitating the selection of suitable SCR models based on empirical data. Our findings reveal that, in multilayer networks, nodes with the ability to change others' preferences tend to destabilize cultures, whereas those that are only influenced by others stabilize existing states. Our research also uncovers the mechanisms through which changes in node preferences interfere with cultural dynamics and provides a simplified approach to assessing the stability of states within multilayer networks. Our results serve as a foundation for further exploration of more complex multilayer systems and networks comprising multiple interactions. Building on the concepts of differential modules and differential operators, this work develops the theoretical framework for a new type of differential modules termed relative differential modules. These modules are defined as the pullback of differential modules along a mapping of rings, and this process creates a connection between their operator coefficients. In particular, this connection can be described as the action of another operator on the first set of operators. A specific case of these relative differential modules is then explored, resulting in what the authors call the relative differential modules with respect to an operator, which in turn leads to the concept of semi-free differential modules. These last modules are utilized in deriving an algebraic definition for the exterior derivative on free graded commutative algebras. The paper also delves into the applicability of these relative differential modules to the theory of rational homotopy types. The authors successfully reexamine the construction of a rational homotopy type for R.R. Moore, establishing the isomorphism between the homotopy types' rational homotopy groups and the modules' homology groups. The document also clarifies the relationship between the exterior derivative's nilpotency and the compositeness property. The exterior derivative's compositeness property is demonstrated through the application of relative differential modules to the Baues-Dietmeyer-Ganter-Wiskin construction. If we consider a variant of these root systems that includes the maximal root as part of the system, we can establish a correspondence between them and the root systems of type D and A, respectively. This correspondence involves reflecting one of the variant systems' roots across a specific hyperplane defined by its highest root. This process results in a root system that comprises the original variant system's roots, minus the maximal root. This new root system is called the "holey" variant of its original counterpart. A direct relationship between the root systems of types D and A can also be established by repeating the process described above, now using the root system of type D to create the variant of A, and then using this variant of A to create the variant of D. We introduce a novel randomized distributed algorithm designed to estimate the size of a specific type of network - specifically, networks composed of interconnected clusters - with an overall time complexity of $O(\log n)$ and a space complexity of $O(1)$. This algorithm surpasses the previous time complexity record of $O(\log^2 n)$ for estimating network size, achieved through cooperation between nodes. Our algorithm leverages a unique cooperative approach, enabling clusters to estimate the total number of nodes with over $10^{9}$ digits in $O(\log n)$ rounds, where each node only requires a constant amount of memory. Our solution also offers an improved cooperative approach for calculating network diameter in $O(\log^2 n)$ rounds with $O(1)$ memory per node. Our research relies on recent cooperative depth-first search innovations and applies cluster-based network division. The proposed algorithm serves as an essential component for various data collection and query tasks in large networks. Our experiments using both simulated and real-world data demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of our algorithm. Our algorithmic achievement has been accepted as the best paper in the ACM Symposium on Parallel Algorithms and Architectures (SPAA) 2022. Our algorithmic solution has been open-sourced and is available on GitHub. Our research has been financially supported by the National Science Foundation under grant number CNS-1932646. Our team also acknowledges the support of the Research Experience for Undergraduates (REU) program funded by the National Science Foundation under grant number CNS-1952416 as well as the University of California Research Initiative and Collaboration (UCRIC) program. Our algorithm has been tested using the RW8020 dataset of large-scale wireless sensor networks. Our team also experimented with a smaller dataset of 100 nodes, which is available upon request. Our algorithm has the potential for applications in various real-world scenarios, such as estimating the number of animals in wildlife populations based on acoustic data. Our research team is currently exploring such applications with wildlife biologists. Our algorithm can be adapted for use in Internet-of-Things (IoT) networks and has implications for the theory of random walks on groups. The results show that our non-parametric strategies match the accuracy of parametric methods, which requires knowledge of the system's parameters, obtained through numerical analysis. Furthermore, we establish conditions for the convergence of our estimation algorithms and provide explicit formulas for our main method. This allows us to gain insights into the required observation intensity, the impact of system parameters, and the accuracy of our estimates. Our studies demonstrate that our methods successfully estimate queue lengths with the accuracy of parametric methods, which can be computationally costly to obtain, especially in large networks. Our work paves the way for further investigation of this queueing system, enabling analysis of critical performance metrics, such as system throughput and agent utility, which are obtained by solving convex optimization problems involving the estimated queue lengths. Our findings also highlight the robustness of our non-parametric methods, demonstrating the feasibility of estimating queue lengths in complex systems with changing configurations, without the need for continuous system parameter updates. We introduce a novel solution to the Hamiltonian constraint in the context of 3+1 dimensional gravity, where the conformal factor is resolved through a nonlinear elliptic equation following an initial guess. This approach bypasses the conventional strategy of first solving the Hamiltonian constraint for the conformal factor and then determining the shift vector. The nonlinearity of the elliptic equation allows for a greater degree of freedom in the choice of conformal factor solutions. This scheme has been effectively put into practice in numerical simulations of complex systems, including general relativity coupled with a scalar field and electromagnetism. The implementation involves both analytical and numerical methods to solve the nonlinear elliptic equation for the conformal factor. This approach has been successfully applied to resolving the Hamiltonian constraint in simple analytical examples and more complex numerical configurations arising from initial value problems. The resulting solutions for the conformal factor have been found to compare favourably with those obtained using the conventional approach, as measured by the Carminati-Huisken quasi-spherical embedding method. This new scheme also offers promise for its potential in reducing grid size requirements in numerical simulations. The present formulation can be readily extended to the inclusion of matter fields, however issues with long-term stability in the evolution of the spacetime metric have been encountered and will require further resolution. This novel solution to the Hamiltonian constraint is currently being employed in ongoing research aimed at solving the initial value problem for the Einstein-Klein-Gordon system of equations. A theoretical model has been developed to describe the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskites, specifically in nickelantiperovskites, by utilizing a phenomenological approach to study thermal and electric field influences on magnetization. This model leads to the creation of a nonequilibrium antiferromagnetic state and predicts the anomalous Nernst effect can be both positive and negative, differing based on the direction of the current flow. Furthermore, calculations indicate that the anomalous Nernst coefficient in nickelantiperovskites can be up to 100 times larger than its ferromagnetic counterpart, and this anomaly originates from the unique antiferromagnetic spin arrangement and the small size of the Nernst effect coefficient in its equilbrium state. This model also demonstrates that the anomalous Nernst effect can be influenced by both electric field and temperature, and the magnitude of this effect is directly related to the magnitude of the electric field and temperature. Moreover, calculations reveal that the anomalous Nernst effect can be enhanced by point defects, an observation consistent with experimental findings involving nickelantiperovskites. The predicted values for the anomalous Nernst effect coefficient in nickelantiperovskites match the measured values, solidifying the theoretical model and providing a clear understanding of the anomalous Nernst effect in this specific material. The origins of the anomalous Nernst effect in nickelantiperovskites have been fully elucidated through this research, highlighting the unique properties of this material and the essential role that electric field, temperature, and spin arrangement play in this phenomenon. The significance of this research extends beyond nickelantiperovskites, shedding light on the universal mechanisms governing the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic materials. The study also emphasizes the potential applications of these materials in thermoelectric technology. The theoretical model developed in this research can be further utilized to explore the anomalous Nernst effect in other antiferromagnetic materials and phase change memory materials. The research has important implications for the development of new materials and the understanding of anomalous Nernst effect in solid state physics. A novel self-sensing concrete composite incorporating recycled aggregate includes a unique method of defect identification. Traditionally, machine learning algorithms are used for this purpose, although they require extensive training data and sophisticated computational tools. An alternative approach utilizes a genetic algorithm to enhance the self-sensing capabilities of the composite, thereby reducing costs and environmental impacts associated with recycling methods. The proposed algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated by minimizing cost functions in two scenarios of loading conditions, resulting in improved accuracy of damage detection. Furthermore, the optimal solution is compared with results obtained from a particle swarm optimization algorithm and machine learning algorithms using neural networks and support vector machines. The genetic algorithm is found to be the most efficient option among the compared methods. The proposed approach provides a feasible and environmentally friendly solution for the production of concrete composites with self-sensing capabilities, and the study offers valuable insights for its further development. The findings are applicable to various concrete composite types and can be utilized as a framework for innovative technological solutions. We introduce a mathematical model that extends the Lotka-Volterra predator-prey system by incorporating different levels of intelligence into its equations. This enables us to examine the impact of problem-solving ability on species coexistence and extinction. Our analysis focuses on a simplified scenario where one species has perfect intelligence and the other faces recurrent extinction events. Our mathematical investigations leverage a novel approach that combines the method of upper and lower solutions with a source solution technique. This allows us to derive explicit conditions for the species with intelligence to drive the other species to extinction. We also investigate a second scenario where both species have access to limited problem-solving abilities. This extends the previous results and provides us with the conditions under which the species with intelligence can exploit this ability to maintain coexistence with the other species. Our study demonstrates the novel applications of the method of upper and lower solutions in addressing a specific problem, as well as the distinctive outcomes it yields in comparison to the conventional stability analysis. Furthermore, our research highlights the distinct features of our findings, which are informed by our deliberate simplification of the intelligent species' problem-solving ability in a highly selective scenario. Our work paves the way for the exploration of more intricate intelligent species' problem-solving strategies and associated outcomes. Our results are further illustrated through numerical simulations that are presented in the subsequent figures. Our approach provides a unique blend of analytical and numerical investigations that are interconnected and interdependent. In addition to the scientific knowledge we gain from this study, our approach also offers a teaching resource for graduate students who are studying nonlinear differential equations and the method of upper and lower solutions, as well as those exploring the dynamics of species interactions. Our work concludes with the potential applications and extensions of our research, as well as some final remarks. Accurate brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) rely on effective decoding methods. High-resolution electrocortical signals, particularly ECoG, have shown superior performance compared to lower-resolution EEG signals. However, the precision of these recordings is hindered by hardware limitations, prompting researchers to explore compressed sensing for efficient decoding. This study utilizes sparse regression, a precise technique, to compare the predictive power of ECoG and EEG signals in predicting walking functions following stroke. Our results reveal that ECoG signals indeed outperform EEG signals in predictive accuracy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a compressed sense-based approach can effectively recover the precise solution obtained through l1-norm regularization, thereby providing a potential solution for real-world applications. Our work has implications for the development of effective BCIs in predicting post-stroke outcomes and informs future studies on the utilization of compressed sensing for reduced recording hardware. This research can be extended to predict other walking functions by substituting relevant data, and our code is available online for public use.

A new neural network structure called DECENNT is proposed to represent complex dynamic graphs, which outperforms existing methods in modeling various graph dynamics, according to a comprehensive set of metrics. DECENNT successfully captures the evolving connections between nodes, enabling it to make predictions in tasks like link prediction and classify nodes in changing graph scenarios. The model's capabilities are demonstrated across six different datasets, showing improved performance compared to state-of-the-art approaches,, including GraphSAGE, GCN, and ATTENTIVE. DECENNT is also compared to conventional embedding techniques, surpassing them significantly. The code for the model has been openly shared on GitHub, showcasing potential applications in dynamic social network analysis. The design of DECENNT facilitates an intuitive understanding of its workings through a visualizer, which can be accessed online. The research on DECENNT has the potential to contribute to better comprehension of evolving social connections and community structures, also offering practical utility in real-world scenarios, such as recommendation systems, traffic flow management, and epidemiology. Analyzing the movements of various entities, whether living or not, is a universal human tendency, and people often differentiate between these movements based on their perceived intentionality. While researching the behavior of microorganisms such as bacteria and their movement through surfaces, scientists can mistakenly attribute motives to these non-intelligent entities due to their inherent tendency to attribute human-like qualities to living things. To rectify this error in interpretation, researchers must employ a more objective analysis of these movements, focusing solely on observed facts rather than assumptions of intentionality. To demonstrate this necessity, this study explores the unintentional movement of bacteria across surfaces using a simulation called the sub-surface flow model, and it highlights the distinction between intentional and unintentional movements with the help of a statistical tool called mutual information analysis. By employing this method, a clearer understanding of the relationship between surface characteristics and the movement of bacteria can be obtained. Furthermore, this study illustrates the applicability of this approach to a broader context of analyzing the movements of non-biological objects. It also paves the way for extending this research to the movements of living beings with simple nervous systems, such as nematode worms, by incorporating the element of motivation. To accomplish this, new simulations and more advanced statistical tools will be necessary. In conclusion, this study offers a unique method for analyzing the movements of non-biological objects and provides the framework for extending this analysis to biological entities with simple nervous systems. It utilizes the sub-surface flow model as an example, but it presents a broader and more versatile approach that can be adapted to various other scenarios involving the study of movements. In the MSSM, the search for heavy Higgs bosons, particularly $A^0$ and $H^0$, is a priority, especially given their potential to address electroweak symmetry breaking puzzles. Calculating squark contributions to $A^0$ and $H^0$ production through top-quark and bottom-quark virtual processes is the focus of this work, with an emphasis on the RGE improvement for low-energy hadron collisions. Our research utilizes the Phase Space Optimization method to prioritize relevant squark phases, demonstrating significant effects on the production cross-section, particularly when considering $pp\to A^0 b\bar b$ and $pp\to H^0 b\bar b$. Specifically, we find that in the regime of $\tan\beta\gtrsim 10$, the $\text{Next-to}-\text{Leading}$ Order (NLO) squark contribution to $A^0$ production can reach up to $10\text{ fb}$ at the LHC with $\sqrt{s}=14\text{ TeV}$ and $\mathcal{L}=300\text{ pb}^{-1}$. Additionally, we propose an optimized analysis for $A^0\to $\tau^+\tau^-$ with a cut on the pseudo-rapidity of the tau leptons, which we estimate to reach up to $5.7\text{ ab}^{-1}$ at the High-Luminosity LHC. We emphasize that incorporating squark effects is crucial for comprehensively understanding the processes involved in heavy Higgs boson production at hadron colliders, and we encourage experimental and theoretical researchers to combine forces in this area of study. Contextual linear bandits with linear contexts can be solved using linear Thompson sampling (LTS), which yields a near-optimal regret of order $d^{1/3} \sqrt{T}$ in $d$-dimensional space after $T$ time steps. However, the bit requirement for communicating policies in practice is a significant issue. Our research indicates that LTS policies necessitate $\Omega(dT)$ bits to be transmitted, implying a cubic relationship with the number of time steps. In contrast, a context-independent linear policy can be defined using only $d$ bits, prompting us to investigate shorter communication strategies. Our main finding shows that contextual linear bandits' bit requirement can be reduced to $\tilde{O}(d^{5/3}\sqrt{T})$ using LTS and a specific linear learning algorithm, demonstrating a square root savings in bit requirement relative to the absolute need, while remaining within the optimal regret range of $O(d^{1/3} \sqrt{T})$. For efficient policy learning using approximate dynamic programming techniques, it is possible to create value function estimates that require minimal data. However, the effectiveness of these methods relies on utilizing a large amount of test data. This research investigates the limitations of these methods when the available data is limited, focusing on the consequences for policy evaluation and learning. Experiments with both positive and negative results reveal that, in certain cases, value function estimates can be overly aggressive and lead to poor policy improvement. A new approach is proposed, involving a regularization-based method to constrain the value function estimates and ensuring they are more conservative. This regularization parameter is determined through cross-validation, allowing the model to balance accuracy and caution. Experimentation demonstrates the superiority of this new approach over existing methods, highlighting its potential for policy evaluation and learning in situations with limited data. Experimental code and models are available online. This research paves the way for further exploration of the regularized approach, suggesting potential enhancements, such as utilizing neural networks and exploring other regularization techniques, to enhance policy learning when data is scarce. This work is part of the author's PhD thesis, contributed to their understanding of policy learning with limited data, an area they plan to continue investigating in their future research. Our research examined the transverse momentum distributions of charged hadrons, pions, kaons, and protons as well as the elliptic flow of these particles in two types of collisions: those with central collisions and those with collisions that occurred on one side (near or far-side). Our data comes from high-energy collisions at the LHC using ALICE detectors. We compared our findings to theoretical predictions from iEBE-VISHNU, AMPT, and MCMC models. Our results showed that charged hadrons, pions, kaons, and protons exhibit similar momentum distributions, fulfilling the expectation of quantum chromodynamics. These distributions were also consistent with current generators, also fulfilling expectations. However, the proton-to-pion ratios of these particles exhibited slight discrepancies from predicted values, particularly in the medium-mass range. We also found that collisions on one side exhibit the same behavior as central collisions, with the same momentum distributions and elliptic flow patterns. Our data for charged hadrons, pions, kaons, and protons also show that the most central collisions exhibit the highest particle production and lowest elliptic flow, while the most outside collisions exhibit the opposite behavior. Our research also demonstrated that even the most outside collisions follow the same momentum distributions as the most central collisions, exhibiting little deviation. Our findings also compared favorably with current generators and models, with the exception of the medium-mass range proton-to-pion ratios. Our results are significant because they mark the first time that charged hadron and pion proton-to-pion ratios have been measured in collisions on one side of the detector, and the first time that charged hadron and pion momentum distributions have been compared in collisions with outside events. Our data also demonstrate the capability of the ALICE detector in these areas. Our research is also the first to provide comprehensive data on the properties of final-state interactions in collisions on one side of the detector, and the first to compare data from these collisions with predictions from current generators and models. We investigate a large-scale wireless network consisting of many transmitters and receivers that share a common frequency band. Each transmitter and receiver is equipped with a limited range sensor to detect each other's distance, which allows them to set independent transmission power levels. We developed a simple, efficient algorithm called binary power control that reduces the performance loss caused by power control. In a random network with an infinite number of nodes, we found that this algorithm results in a 1 dB decrease in signal strength compared to optimal power control, which is the baseline for comparison. We also found that this decrease occurs quickly, within the first few meters of range, and levels off as the distance increases. In addition, we found that this algorithm performs best, requiring the smallest number of power level changes, in networks with medium-sized areas, and we were able to derive mathematical equations that predict its performance in networks with infinite areas. We also tested this algorithm in realistic network scenarios with fixed locations and various obstacle layouts and found that it performs significantly better than the baseline optimal power control, which is a complex problem that often requires a long time to solve, in some cases taking several hours to solve for just one configuration, whereas our algorithm takes only a few seconds. We also found that this algorithm is highly robust and its performance varies very little in different network configurations. We believe that this algorithm has great potential for use in real-world applications of wireless networks with power control, such as public Wi-Fi networks, cellular networks, and other similar systems. We also hope that this research will help inspire new algorithms that are at least this good, if not better. We present a formula that expresses 7 raised to the power of n as a difference of two positive integers a and b, which can also be represented in a different order with the opposite sign. We achieve this in two distinct ways depending on whether n is an even number or an odd number. For even n, the expression takes the form $a-b$ and for odd n, the expression takes the form $b-a$. We further establish additional mathematical representations for the same value of $7^n$ using our initial formula. Additionally, we demonstrate the applicability of these representations to provide solutions to two distinct problems. We first show how they can be utilized to prove the existence of two positive integers a and b for which the sum or difference is equal to a given number k, which is an odd power of 7. We then employ these representations to find the largest positive integer less than a given number N that can be expressed as $7^n$ for some positive integer n. We conclude by proposing these representations as potential components in the solution to other problems involving powers of 7. We also offer a brief discussion on how these representations can be used to find the largest number below a given N that is of the form $7^n$ for some positive integer n. We then propose an alternative approach which enables us to find this number for any given number N, and demonstrate this approach by finding the largest number below 2020 that can be expressed as $7^n$ for some positive integer n. We determine this number to be 1790, which is equal to $7^{8}$, and provide the line of reasoning that led to this result. We also examine the same problem for powers of 11, and find the largest number below 2025 that can be expressed as $11^n$ for some positive integer n to be 2130, which is equal to $11^{10}$, and demonstrate this result using a similar approach. This research focuses on a robotic hopping model that navigates a vertically vibrating, flexible surface. Because the robotic legs' footfalls create significant disturbances on this sensitive terrain, tracking desired trajectories is extremely challenging. A feedforward and feedback control strategy is devised to mitigate the deleterious effects of the ground's vibrations and the robotic hopping mechanism's inherent instability, thereby enhancing the robotic hopping performance. The proposed controller is implemented in a simulated environment with a multibody robotic hopping model that incorporates differential drive legs, as well as in a hardware setup utilizing a single-legged hopping robot. The results indicate that this control approach succeeds in reducing ground reaction forces, enhancing stability and allowing the robot to hop at various speeds and heights in sync with desired trajectories. Moreover, the feedback controller is found to be robust in addressing model uncertainties. The findings of this research have the potential to contribute to the development of control methods for hopping robots moving on soft ground, as well as to the creation of testing frameworks for future lunar and mars missions. The proposed control strategy and simulation tools can be adapted for similar applications involving jumping robots and quads on flexible terrain. Quantum annealing's effectiveness relies on its ability to navigate complex energy landscapes, and understanding the annealing gap's dynamics can significantly optimize protocols. We investigate the annealing gap's behavior during quantum annealing, focusing on a near-degenerate Ising ring with variable coupling strengths. Through simultaneous measurements of energy and number of qubit errors, we found the annealing gap's width is directly proportional to the average number of qubit errors. Additionally, we observed the gap's width fluctuating unpredictably throughout the annealing process, and these fluctuations are more pronounced in scenarios with larger annealing gaps. A QPU's errors can either hinder or help the annealer, depending on the stage of annealing and qubit placement. Our findings suggest incorporating error correction into quantum annealing protocols, particularly towards the beginning and end of the process, and our research demonstrates the importance of accurate QPU characterization prior to quantum annealing simulations. We propose a simple, scalable protocol with potential applications in classical-quantum hybrid systems. A key component in evaluating the metrological capabilities of quantum systems is the analysis of number variance, particularly in coherent, coherent-like states.
Researchers have discovered that an increase in state variance corresponds to a rise in precision achieved in parameter estimation.
A theoretical investigation into the number variance of a compass state reveals an interesting relationship with a specific damping parameter, which exhibits a minimum variance at a particular value of this parameter.
Conversely, a state with minimum variance may not necessarily represent optimal parameter estimation; other factors like mean value also contribute significantly.
Through numerical simulations, a distinct optimal point in damping parameter estimation is identified for both average and variance measurements of the compass state. 
Ultimately, this study demonstrates that there exists an optimal damping value in quantum system measurement that minimizes the variance of the compass state, thereby potentially enhancing parameter estimation in metrological applications. 
Additionally, a comparative analysis between compass and coherent states reveals varying levels of resilience to decoherence. 
Both states exhibit distinct behavior in relation to number variance, with the compass state displaying a more pronounced minimum variance at a specific damping parameter. 
Notably, the optimal damping parameter corresponds to a maximum average value in the compass state, whereas this is not the case for coherent states. 
A crucial finding in this research is the minimal impact of initial condition preparation over time as both states evolve in a environment with continuous measurement. 
Conversely, the environment's influence cannot be disregarded as both states demonstrate an identical trend of decreasing precision in parameter estimation over time. 
All simulations were conducted using the QuTiP library in Python. 
The research concludes by highlighting the limited utility of coherent states in damping-environment scenarios and the potential of compass states in quantum metrology, despite the unavoidable deterioration of precision over time. 
All relevant code has been made available online for the benefit of the scientific community. 
Future work is proposed, focusing on the generation of non-classical correlations in two-level systems and, ultimately, the development of quantum clocks based on compass states, which could, in turn, enhance our understanding of continuous measurement effects on precision. 
All simulations were executed on standard desktop computers but could be efficiently transferred to supercomputing platforms if necessary. 
The research hypothesizes that access to high-performance computing could reveal new findings, particularly in the analysis of random variance sequences over extended periods. 
All necessary code has been deposited into relevant repositories on GitHub, in line with FAIR guidelines, ensuring the results can be reproduced by the scientific community. 
All researchers are invited to contribute to the project

High-precision astrometric measurements reveal a significant parallax shift for stars located close to the Sun's path, where ecliptic latitude is concerned. To better understand this phenomenon, researchers divided a sample of 1.44 million stars from the Tycho-2 catalogue into four groups based on their ecliptic latitudes, and then compared the parallaxes using a Bayesian approach. The results showed that the phenomenon is more pronounced for smaller parallaxes and may be influenced by a systematic error. Furthermore, a relationship between the shift and a star's position on the sky was discovered, which could be attributed to a temporary position shift rather than a true distance change. This interpretation is supported by the fact that the phenomenon is more evident for faster-moving stars with shorter orbital periods. The method developed in this study can be applied to future high-precision astrometric datasets, and has implications for the understanding of the Milky Way's structure. This study presents a novel method for generating theoretical vibration spectra for a specific class of molecular ions, focusing on cations with one oxygen atom and a limited number of atoms in total. Researchers typically employ equilibrium geometries derived from experimental data to create such models; however, this approach poses difficulties for several reasons. Firstly, determining equilibrium geometries through experiments is often complicated and may require additional data. Additionally, many essential variables, including electron density distributions and bond lengths, are not fully captured by these geometries. To address these limitations, this work proposes a new approach that leverages theoretical predictions from ab initio methods, specifically DFT-based results. The resulting spectra reveal distinct patterns that correlate with the molecular structure, allowing for the prediction of spectrum trends for unknown molecules based on theoretical models. This research demonstrates a promising pathway for developing full spectral models of small molecular ions and identifies potential applications in identifying unknown molecules and investigating reaction pathways. The proposed method demonstrates versatility in modeling various molecular ions and provides a foundation for extending this work to larger molecules and more complex anions. Distributed learning models, where multiple agents contribute their local data to perform
a task, are subject to communication limitations when sharing information. This issue
prevents the exchange of continuous-valued data, hindering the efficiency of
machine learning. To address this problem, the random walk approach was proposed,
enabling agents to send discrete, symbolic information to each other, thereby
reducing data exchange costs. This technique enables agents to exchange
categorical, instead of continuous, data with each other, thus cutting down the
data exchange costs. To facilitate cooperation, a protocol was devised based on
a random walk on a graph, where agents exchange symbolic information with each
other, with the aim of converging to a shared outcome. Although this approach
has the potential to enhance collaboration, its limitations arise when tasks cannot
be represented by a fixed number of categories, hindering its scalability. To
address this limitation, a new approach was developed, allowing agents to exchange
continuous-valued data while minimizing communication by utilizing the random walk
approach. This novel method, known as the Federated Learning Walk (FLW), combines
the benefits of random walk cooperation with the efficiency of federated learning,
enabling the sharing of continuous data while reducing communication costs. As a
proof of concept, FLW was applied to solve a linear regression problem, and the
results showed that it outperforms traditional federated learning methods by
providing more accurate predictions with significantly reduced communication costs. 
Additionally, FLW excels in comparison to non-federeated learning models on
non-linear tasks, such as multiclass classification, due to its ability to exchange 
continuous data. The code for FLW has been made publicly available on GitHub,

The concept of weak convergence for function estimate parameters, which arises in various applications and models, has been examined in a theoretical probability context. This work specifically considers the case of Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods and Markov thin chain Monte Carlo (MTCMC) algorithms generating samples based on target density functions. The study focuses on estimating functions of parameters, denoted as $\psi(\theta)$, where the relationship between the original estimate $\theta^n$ and the generated samples is explored. Under regularity conditions and the ergodic theorem applied to the mean of the generated samples, the weak convergence of $\psi(\theta^n)$ is proven for both MCMC and MTCMC algorithms. The investigation also delves into the strong properties of the estimated functions $\psi(\theta^n)$, the law of large numbers, and the asymptotic normality of $\psi(\theta^n)$ for both MCMC and MTCMC. The results are demonstrated to hold under weaker moment conditions, utilizing the ergodic theorem for Markov chains. A numerical example and a real-world application are provided to illustrate the methods discussed. This research contributes to the understanding of estimating functions of parameters in statistical models and provides theoretical foundations for various MCMC and MTCMC algorithms. The veriT proof system has undergone significant developments since its debut at the PxTP workshop in 2009, with improvements made to address issues identified during proof checking tool evaluations. Initially, veriT's ability to provide proofs was marked by uncertainty, but evidence presented here demonstrates the certainty of this capability. Furthermore, the current version of veriT can generate proofs for a vast majority of instances where counterexamples exist, covering numerous benchmarks from various sources and different problem-solving scenarios with both SAT and SMT solvers. The research reveals key factors contributing to this advancement, including an enhancement to the default configuration, a critical fix for a particular instance, and technological upgrades to veriT itself. The findings also reveal instances that are difficult for veriT in its proof-generating capability, shedding light on potential limitations of the system. Ultimately, this research paves the way for a more precise understanding of veriT's behavior and its ongoing development. The implementation details and various benchmarks are now available for the sake of reproducibility. The associated zip file contains, among other things, the source code for veriT as well as the benchmark datasets used in this research, which were utilized in the CPS 2023 evaluation of proof checkers. The evaluation results themselves are also included. Using transfer learning from a linguistically distant source language can improve a speech recognition system's performance in a target language that is difficult to work with, as seen with certain Asian languages. However, the benefits of transfer learning are limited to specific source and target language pairs and don't generalize to other pairs of languages with the same level of distance. Our research proposes a new training method that utilizes a more universally useful "bridge" language as the source for transfer learning, leveraging the known benefits of cross-language training. We tested this approach using Japanese as the target and a range of source languages including German, French, and Spanish, and found that it consistently performs better than speech recognition systems trained without transfer learning and some systems trained with direct transfer learning from the distant source languages. Moreover, our experiments demonstrated that selecting the most suitable "bridge" language is crucial and that we can induce a similar positive effect on the system's performance by training the system on the transcriptions of public speech datasets in the target language, without using the actual data. Our proposed approach is easy to implement, requires minimal additional data, and can be an effective solution for speech recognition systems that struggle with certain Asian languages. System performance was evaluated using the NIST CTMC scoring method and the results show that our proposed approach can achieve a 9.1% absolute reduction in word error rate (WER) compared to systems trained without transfer learning. Our proposed method has the potential for further improvement by integrating it with other successful speech recognition systems techniques such as i-vector/XYT-based approaches. Our research code is available online at the GitHub repository https://github.com/Shu87/Speech-Recognition-with-Bridge-Languages. Our future work will concentrate on exploring more suitable "bridge" languages and integrating this proposed method with i-vector/XYT-based approaches to create a more advanced bridge language speech recognition system. Our future plan is also aimed at applying this proposed approach to speech recognition systems in certain Asian languages that have limited research resources. Our proposed approach has the potential to revolutionize speech recognition systems in certain Asian languages with limited research resources by providing a cost-effective solution that requires minimal additional data. Our research contributes to a crucial open problem in speech recognition research, specifically dealing with languages that are difficult to work with and has been challenging researchers worldwide for a long time. We develop a novel algorithm, SPGP-SARSA, which leverages sparse grid methods and Monte Carlo tree search, and employs policy evaluation to enhance the framework for policy improvement. This algorithm enhances the efficiency of policy evaluation, a critical component underlying value iteration. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SPGP-SARSA in a complex underwater navigation task and observe significant improvements in both policy evaluation and the corresponding optimal policy. Our results show that SPGP-SARSA yields superior outcomes in comparison to benchmark algorithms across various problem sizes. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the algorithm excels in problems featuring high dimensionality and uncertainty, and we validate the statistical significance of these findings. Our code is available at https://github.com/akshayteri/SPGP-SARSA. This research paves the way for further optimization of the algorithm and explores the potential applications of SPGP-SARSA in more intricate tasks involving multiple agents and noisy data. Our findings highlight the potential of the proposed method in tackling various challenging underwater tasks, such as navigating schools of fish and managing underwater sensors. Our work also highlights the promising outlook for the algorithm in the realm of continuous action spaces and non-linear systems. Our research framework is composed of two primary components, an explorer and a learner, which we have made available for use with existing policy iteration frameworks, alongside our custom implementation of policy iteration. In this study, we develop a method to obtain solutions for relativistic stellar models composed of two fluids, with specific applications to neutron stars, by modifying known single-fluid solutions. We demonstrate that for a static, spherically symmetric star with two fluids, an energy-momentum tensor component can be transformed into a perfect fluid form, allowing us to reconstruct the star's interior geometry. We then utilize this approach to modify two types of well-established solutions: (1) an isothermal relativistic stellar solution with a superfluid neutron star, and (2) a relativistic stellar solution with a neutral fluid and a Proca field. We then map these modified solutions onto mass-radius planes. Additionally, we re-examine the binding energy estimates for these two-fluid stars. Lastly, we propose possible future research directions involving the incorporation of additional fluid components, such as kaon fluids, within these models. This study proposes a novel method for adapting generative editing components (GEC) by leveraging unedited images. Our approach trains a generative model on an image dataset with corresponding editing targets and released GEC codes. We achieve this using a multi-task framework with shared encoders, which enables code adaptation without pretraining the GEC network. Our method excels in tasks like generating new edited images and adapting new GEC codes, surpassing state-of-the-art baselines in various evaluation metrics. Specifically, our approach outperforms traditional multi-task transfer learning methods in L1 distance and Frechet inception distance (FID) scores by significant margins of 19 and 15, respectively. Our approach and implementations are now publicly available, showcasing promising potential for GEC without the need for expensive pretraining. Code resources can be accessed at https://github.com/yangzw/peca.

In the context of scheduling tasks for multiple agents with conflicting interests, we investigate a specific problem where one agent has an initial advantage due to higher priority tasks. We aim to devise fair task scheduling strategies for two types of agents: one with high priority and one with low priority. The former can choose between two tasks with different durations, while the latter has a fixed task with a longer duration. We develop two algorithms to ensure fairness: the first assigns tasks based on priority and duration, while the second assigns tasks based on priority, duration, and a random draw. We establish theoretical upper bounds on the maximum time the high-priority agent can save in both cases. Additionally, we provide simulated data illustrating the efficacy of these algorithms in limiting the high-priority agent's time savings. Furthermore, we examine the optimal cut-and-choose algorithm and demonstrate that both our algorithms yield fair schedules with greater efficiency than the optimal algorithm, as measured by the maximum time the high-priority agent can save. We also discuss possible extensions to our work, including incorporating additional agents and tasks with varying durations. We stress that our task scheduling model can be applied to various real-world scenarios, including traffic light control, sports scheduling, and resource allocation, among others. We make the code for our simulations publicly available to facilitate replication and future research. We hope our findings and approach can guide practitioners and researchers in similar contexts faced with conflicting priorities and limited resources. We propose the Round-Robin mechanism as a fair allocation strategy for a specific multi-agent problem with conflicting interests, comparing it to the cut-and-choose algorithm and deriving similar (1-2e^-n) n^2 upper bounds on the maximum time the high-priority agent can save in both cases, where n represents the number of tasks. We examine possible applications of this approach to traffic light control, sports scheduling, and resource allocation, and make the code for our simulations publicly available. UGC 8839, a spiral galaxy, exhibits an unusually sparse core and lacks a prominent central bulge in images taken by the Hubble Space Telescope's Wide Field Camera 3. A comprehensive analysis of its young star populations, including HII regions, open clusters, and massive star masses, has been conducted. Contrary to previous observations in nearby spiral galaxies, the majority of the HII regions in UGC 8839 are located within the outer radii, accounting for 53% of the total observed in its disk. This unusual distribution might be attributed to a central stellar mass deficit caused by tidal interactions or a massive black hole. Additionally, the discovery of an unusually long central stellar bar segment, approximately 40kpc in length, distinguishes UGC 8839 from other spiral galaxies. Furthermore, a massive globular cluster, with an estimated 10 to the power of 5.5 solar masses, was found on its outskirts. The unique characteristics of UGC 8839 provide valuable insights into its intricate past, suggesting it may have undergone interactions with a massive spiral galaxy similar to the Milky Way. Such encounters have been infrequent in past observations and simulations of nearby galaxies. The research on UGC 8839 highlights the significance of in-depth examinations of spiral galaxy cores and the need to consider the effects of tidal interactions, central mass deficits, and massive black holes on their development. The Hubble data used in this study have been enhanced with new observations and advanced modeling techniques. The resulting enhanced images reveal previously unseen features in UGC 8839, its neighboring galaxy UGC 8840, and the background galaxy QSO 1634-243. A recent complete 0+ lattice QCD simulation, involving the simulation of quark masses ranging from nearly zero to those currently observed, has led to a comprehensive understanding of the behavior of pions. The resulting data set, comprising approximately 500,000 configurations, forms the basis for our analysis. We have calculated various pion properties, including their masses, decay constants, elastic form factors, and correlation functions, using lattice sizes of 4.75 fm in each dimension. Our study has allowed for the correction of quark mass truncation errors in two ways. Firstly, we employed the built-in quenching of light quarks in the lattice simulation by varying quark masses. Secondly, we corrected for the lattice spacing error by calculating the decay constant of the vacuum gluon field, known as the topological mass, which we found to be minimal (~10^-3 GeV). Our findings confirm that quark mass ratios influence pion elastic form factors, with our lattice analysis indicating that even at currently observed quark masses, quark mass ratios remain significant. We have developed several important scaling relations governing the behavior of pions and their properties in the real world. Our research demonstrates the necessity of considering quark mass ratios when interpreting experimental data and highlights the value of future simulations with variable quark masses. We have tested our scaling relations using two different methods and the resulting predictions for the mass and decay constant of the pion are accurate to within 0.5%. Our study suggests that future lattice simulations with variable quark masses are crucial for a deeper understanding of hadron physics in the real world. Our lattice data set has been made publicly available for the benefit of the scientific community. Offline learning for multi-agent systems is crucial for developing agents that can adapt to novel situations and colleagues. Current offline methods typically focus on discovering general representations or policies, which can be applied broadly, often without considering the specifics of individual agents. To address this limitation, we introduce the Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) framework, allowing agents to distinguish between shared and individualized knowledge and trajectory data. By doing so, agents can prioritize learning shared tasks and strategies while also acquiring unique insights relevant to their individual experiences. We evaluate the SIT framework through offline multi-agent reinforcement learning experiments and the results show that it facilitates more efficient learning of shared tasks and more effective exploration of individual trajectories. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the SIT model is capable of adapting to varying levels of data noise and successfully distinguishes between shared and individualized knowledge in open-world scenarios. Our approach and associated code are available online. We anticipate the SIT framework will serve as a foundational contribution to offline learning for multi-agent systems and similar settings characterized by co-evolving agents and diverse knowledge sources. We encourage future researchers to build upon our work and explore applications of the SIT model in these dynamic environments. We choose the term Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) as a working title for the approach presented in this paper. This transformer generates entanglement in two qudts based on their properties, specifically correlation and steering, while also exhibiting nonlocal behavior. We developed an applicable measure for both average and scenario-based single-particle entangments, which we utilized to investigate the composition of single-particle entanglement, as well as its correspondence to two-particle entanglement, correlation, and quantum steering. Additionally, we explored the resilience of these measures under decoherence caused by a Markovian noise source. Our study demonstrates that despite its limitations, single-particle entanglement still holds significant value and can serve as an essential resource in various quantum technologies. V392 Persei, a known binary system, underwent an extraordinary brightening in 2018 that is believed to be attributed to a nova eruption.  Follow-up observations were conducted to study this phenomenon further.  Data collected from photometric and spectroscopic observations reveal that V392 Persei returned to its pre-eruptive state within about two years.  During this period, the binary system's orbital period remained constant at 0.79457 days.  Observations of spectral lines before the eruption indicate that the approaching star is absorbing more light than the receding star, suggesting that the binary system is not spinning quickly and the new star is not massive, with a mass likely below one and a half solar masses.  Additionally, no evidence was found for the presence of a white dwarf spin pulse, which is a characteristic feature of some novae, and the absence of certain spectral lines also suggest a low mass white dwarf.  Based on pre-eruptive mass estimates, the team calculates that the nova carried off about 1.5 solar masses during the eruption, primarily in the form of fast moving particles, with about one solar mass retained in the binary system.  Furthermore, evidence was found for a massive accretion disk on the white dwarf with a temperature of about 10 kilokelvins, and an orbital period of about 3.9 days, which is much shorter than the binary system's minimum period, indicating that the binary system is in the stage of rapid decay known as the "common envelope phase". We are investigating the possible presence of Population III binary remnants in the universe observed today and their potential influence on electromagnetic and neutrino waves. These remnants, resulting from the merger of two primordial stars, could be identified through the detection of heavy elements, such as gold, uranium, and thorium, released in supernovae explosions. We evaluated the likelihood of finding these remnants in the universe observed today. They could exist at high redshifts, z = 20-30, where the peak of their formation occurs at z = 5-7 with a merger rate density of approximately 1 per year inverse gigaparsec cubed. This rate could lead to the detection of heavy elements, specifically gold, in the gas surrounding quasars through spectroscopic observations with a sensitivity of 10^-17. We also considered possible signals from these remnants in the background neutrino and electromagnetic radiation, particularly in the high-energy gamma-ray band. For the most optimistic case, where the most massive stars are considered, we found that the most promising current or future observations are the X-ray satellite eROSITA, the Spectral Energy Distribution Machine (SEDAM), the extended Gas Imaging Spectrometer (EGIS) on board the Solar-C, and the next-generation neutrino detectors, with detection probabilities of 10-30% for the most sensitive ones. We also examined the constraints that future observations will place on the formation of Population III stars and the properties of these remnants. We propose a new standard model of binary III remnants that includes both neutron stars and black holes with initial masses between 4-60 M\odot, and masses of the primary star ranging from 60 to 500 M\odot, and the secondary star ranging from 4 to 100 M\odot. This model could explain the abundance of gold and other heavy elements, however more realistic simulations of star mergers are necessary to confirm this hypothesis. We have made the code used in this research public so that others can utilize it for their own studies. We demonstrate that employing a physical gauge, such as the Feynman or Landau gauge, avoids this issue and yields a more plausible formulation of the Weak Gravity Conjecture. Furthermore, using these gauges allows us to derive a more suitable "self-binding energy" expression that agrees with previous literature obtaining no binding energy in anti-de Sitter space. We have explored multiple approaches to validate our findings, including analyzing the "self-binding energy" through a double-extremality hierarchy and direct computation using a double-hierarchy perturbation theory. We have also examined scenarios with matter content beyond a single scalar field. We propose that our findings provide a critical framework for examining the Weak Gravity Conjecture in anti-de Sitter space, particularly in the context of extremal black holes and Spinning Branes. We have further established that our results are consistent with the "swimming against the tide" principle proposed by P. Draper and A. G. Cohen. We have also discovered that the appropriate gauge significantly affects the formulation of the Weak Gravity Conjecture in spaces with a cosmological constant, an aspect we believe deserves greater scrutiny in the broader context of AdS gravity and its relation to the concept of bound states of gravitons. This paper presents findings from the Cassini spacecraft regarding the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex on Saturn. Contrary to the strong and well-defined south polar vortex on Saturn's during its summer, the vortex in the north pole appears much weaker. The formation of the north polar vortex on Saturn occurred in the fall, which is earlier than expected based on polar oscillations, and it has persisted to the present day. The weaker vortex in the north pole is associated with a unique feature - a prominent polar stratospheric wave three times larger than the one observed on Saturn. This large wave may be responsible for the weaker vortex by providing an additional source of heat that contributed to the break down of the polar temperature gradient. The Cassini observations also reveal the weaker vortex in the north pole is surrounded by a massive polar circulation that is similar to the one found in the south pole but developed much earlier. This stronger circulation in the north pole may be a result of the weaker vortex and the larger polar wave. The research on the north polar vortex on Saturn provides valuable insights into the planet's polar atmosphere dynamics. The weaker vortex in the north pole may indicate a phase shift in the planet's polar oscillations that could be influenced by its axial precession. The presence of the larger polar wave in the north pole may be linked to the position of the planet's satellites, particularly Jupiter and its gravitational influence. The study on the north polar vortex on Saturn is crucial for better understanding the complex interactions within the planet's upper atmosphere. The research will be valuable for modeling the atmosphere on Saturn and similar gas giant planets. The findings from this study highlight the necessity for continued observation of the south pole on Saturn and the north pole on Jupiter with advanced spacecraft to enhance the understanding of the formation and evolution of the polar features on these planets. The research on the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex on Saturn concludes by emphasizing the significance of the findings from the Cassini mission, which demonstrate the dynamics of the planet's upper atmosphere are more complex and varied than previously believed. We also show that our method can be applied to the 1D Schrödinger equation with beam profile boundary conditions, which are more general than Dirichlet boundary conditions. Moreover, we improve previous research by extending the range of certain positive constants and demonstrating that these constants can be optimized to suit specific boundary conditions. This research paper introduces the concept of a symplectic double vector bundle, which is equivalent to a type of symmetric $k$-fold vector bundle. A symplectic double vector bundle is created by combining two vector bundles over the same base, with the fibers of one vector bundle acting on the fibers of the other via a symplectic double bracket. We demonstrate that this construction results in a symmetric $k$-fold vector bundle and use this relationship to identify the differential geometric properties of symplectic double vector bundles. Furthermore, we apply this equivalence to the subject of connections on symmetric $k$-fold vector bundles. Given the connection on the underlying bundle, we define a flat connection on the symmetric $k$-fold vector bundle and demonstrate that this is equivalent to a certain type of connection on the original double vector bundle, known as a twisted connection. Finally, we examine the associated bundles derived from the symmetric $k$-fold vector bundles and double vector bundles under these constructions. The development of x-ray phase retrieval methods has significantly enhanced x-ray scattering experiments by enabling the accurate reconstruction of energy spectra. However, existing approaches face limitations when dealing with noisy data, leading to incomplete or inaccurate determination of unknowns. In response to these challenges, a novel algorithm has been created that leverages the complex amplitude information from a single x-ray image to estimate the energy spectrum with an order of magnitude faster processing time compared to state-of-the-art methods. This new technique, based on a unique factorization technique, successfully reconstructs energy spectra with enhanced accuracy in just a few iterations, without requiring any initial guess. The algorithm's performance has been consistently demonstrated across various scenarios, including simulations and real-world data experiments, and exhibits particular resilience to noisy data. The code associated with this work can be utilized to explore the algorithm's capabilities and facilitate further research in this area. The proposed method shows considerable potential for addressing various inverse problems encountered in x-ray imaging experiments. This paper introduces DiscSense, a comprehensive, openly available dataset consisting of 5,000 English sentences with annotated semantic relations, making it the largest dataset of its kind to date. Each sentence is labeled with a primary semantic relation, and in many cases, a secondary relation is also annotated. What sets DiscSense apart from other datasets is the explicit labeling of discourse markers within the sentences. This is particularly significant because there is a lack of standardized approaches for identifying and categorizing discourse markers and semantic relations in existing work. Current state-of-the-art approaches are limited by relying on hand-crafted features and models that are not easily adaptable to various languages. In response to these limitations, we present a novel approach for automatically identifying discourse markers and semantic relations in English text. This method leverages pre-trained language models and deep learning techniques, and we validate our approach through extensive experiments using the DiscSense dataset. Our results demonstrate that this approach is highly effective, yielding performance gains over existing methods for both discourse marker classification and semantic relation prediction. We also explore the robustness of our approach by conducting ablation studies and evaluating our method on other publicly available datasets. Our code is publicly accessible on GitHub at the following URL: https://github.com/zhong-jian/DiscSense. We also make the DiscSense dataset available on Hugging Face Datasets at the following URL: https://huggingface.co/datasets/wiki/discsense. Our research has far-reaching implications for the automatic identification of semantic relations in text, and we believe it will serve as a significant contribution to the discourse parsing and semantic role labeling communities. We also hope that our work will motivate the creation of larger, more complex datasets incorporating both discourse structures and semantic relations, as well as similar datasets in other languages. Our research demonstrates the efficacy of our approach on English text, and we are confident that our method can be adapted to accommodate such demands in the future. We investigate the geometric characteristics of a specific factorized objective function, which arises in matrix optimization under the assumption of restricted strong convexity and smoothness. We initially consider the context of the Euclidean space and later expand our analysis to the manifold $\mathcal{S}^{n_{1}} \times \cdots \times \mathcal{S}^{n_{k}}$ to establish conditions for the existence of geodesics on this manifold. We further explore the application of our findings to the problem of matrix mean estimation and the Euclidean sphere. Our results on the Euclidean sphere generalize previous work by Posa, Ramadani, and Vorderer, who only considered the case where the manifold has a large dimension compared to a fixed constant. We also establish the convergence rate of the iterative hard margin Perceptron algorithm using the Bregman divergence based on the factorized objective, which is related to our geodesic analysis. We demonstrate the efficacy of our dimension-free approach by obtaining the fastest known time complexity for matrix mean estimation using the Perceptron algorithm. We also provide a shorter proof of the convergence rate of the Perceptron algorithm in the case where the dimension is fixed. Our approach of using the Bregman geodesic provides an alternative proof of the convergence rate in the fixed dimension setting. We leverage our geodesic analysis to conduct a new dimension-free concentration inequality of the iterative hard margin Perceptron algorithm, which enhances and generalizes previous work by Crammer. This study investigates the co-evolutionary dynamics of genetic algorithms in a simple prisoner's dilemma context. Our investigation combines Hamming distance from optimal solutions and co-evolutionary learning dynamics to understand the underlying mechanisms. Our results reveal distinct differences in learning trajectories between individual and social learning methods. Interestingly, our findings show that the most fitting Nash Equilibrium (NE) is always located at the Hamming distance of 6 from the fittest individual in our simulation settings. Furthermore, our data indicate that the expected Hamming distance from NE varies significantly between individual and social learning scenarios. In the latter case, expected Hamming distance from NE remains relatively stable across generations, in contrast to the former case where it fluctuates extensively. Our research also compares the performance of different learning methods, combining the findings of previous studies with our own results. Our extended analysis includes an examination of the relationship between Hamming distance, cooperation, and algorithmic performance. Our empirical data demonstrate a positive correlation between Hamming distance and cooperation levels and a negative correlation with algorithmic performance. Additionally, our research delves into the genetic drift phenomenon observed in our co-evolutionary simulations. Our simulations demonstrate that social learning outperforms individual learning in both Hamming distance and algorithmic performance. Our research provides an empirical framework for understanding the co-evolutionary learning dynamics in genetic algorithms through the prisoner's dilemma game. Neural networks are susceptible to subtle errors caused by hardware malfunctions, leading to compromised performance and safety. While various methods exist to protect against intentional data corruption, our research focuses on an unrelated paradigm of data manipulation – range restriction – which can result from the leakage of floating point representation. We demonstrate that non-uniform range restriction methods can significantly impair neural networks and develop QuanGuard, a novel technique that enforces precise data ranges to prevent corruption. Our approach modifies QuanGuard to adapt to different floating point representations and validates the technique using real hardware. Our results show that QuanGuard efficiently mitigates the adverse effects of data corruption on neural networks in various floating point representations, including Intel Mac OS and Linux systems, as well as AWS and Google Cloud platforms. Furthermore, we observe that QuanGuard's benefits extend beyond safety guarantees, as it enhances the reliability of neural network-based systems in production environments. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub, contributing to the ongoing discussion on reliable artificial intelligence. We encourage further engagement and collaboration in this area.

We propose a novel, simple framework for learning to leverage high-resource language resources in NLP tasks, specifically name tagging and part-of-speech tagging. Traditional approaches utilizing transfer learning have been successful but require significant amounts of high-quality data to train the target model. Our method, which we call "Easy Knowledge Transfer," builds on the assumption that a linear transformation can be applied to a pre-trained model on a dissimilar task with a different paradigm, enabling knowledge transfer with just a small amount of target data. We tested this framework using the Conll 2003 dataset and discovered that it successfully integrates knowledge from a more complex task, achieving near-state-of-the-art performance. Moreover, our method demonstrated substantial gains in name tagging for three low-resource languages: Haitian Creole, Yiddish, and Malagasy, surpassing the current state of the art by 3.5-5.5% in F-score. Our approach was also compared to multi-task learning and our results showed that Easy Knowledge Transfer outperformed MTL by 1.5-2.5% in F-score. Our method is straightforward to implement, requires minimal hyperparameter tuning, and offers a significant boost in performance when there is limited target data. Our in-depth analysis involves examining final-state particles in various high-energy collisions, spanning from 39 AGe p+Pb, 13 TeV p+Pb, 13 TeV p+Pb at the LHC, 5.02 TeV Pb+Pb at the LHC, and ultimately 180 TeV Pb+Au at the Tevatron. We investigated several key particle ratios, including the ratio of protons to pions, the ratio of deuterons to protons, the ratio of helium-3 to deuterons, the ratio of particles to antiparticles, and the ratio of charged to neutral particles. Our study revealed a consistent pattern across all systems and energies studied, characterized by linear correlations between centralities (or transverse momenta) and collision systems. These observations are crucial for improving initial condition models, particularly hydrodynamic models used to study heavy-ion collisions. We also comment on the limitations of current data and the need for more detailed information on particle spectra. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the energy independence of our findings, demonstrating that the underlying dynamics of high-energy collisions are robust across different scales. To facilitate ongoing research, we have made our analysis publicly available on the HYDRO multicollision generator website. We encourage theorists and experimentalists to collaborate and leverage our findings to advance our understanding of high-energy strong interaction matter behavior. In recognition of the Tevatron's contributions, we also highlight the significance of the 180 TeV Pb+Au collision data set awaiting further study. In conclusion, our work paves the way for developing more precise initial condition models and informs future experiments, including the NICA and FCC-Hep experiments. In addition, our research emphasizes the necessity of thoroughly examining raw data, as illustrated by the 180 TeV Pb+Au collision analysis, and stresses the value of thorough investigations, as demonstrated by the p+Pb analysis, to minimize potential losses of existing data sets.
