Convolutional neural networks encounter difficulties generalizing across various image classification tasks due to their tendency to overfit. Various ensemble-based approaches have been explored to enhance the robustness of these networks. In response to the growing interest in multi-task learning, we investigate the use of ensemble classifiers with convolutional neural network components as solutions. Our proposed method, which combines two independent approaches, involves first training independent CNNs for each classification task and then utilizing these models in an ensemble classifier. We evaluate this method on a synthetic data set and Cifar-10, and the results show significant improvements in classification accuracy. Our proposed method also demonstrates comparable performance when compared to a single CNN trained on a combined data set without class labels. Our research provides a foundation for utilizing ensemble classifiers with CNN components in multi-task learning and suggests various avenues for further exploration. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at the specified URL. Our proposal is viewed as a preliminary effort and areas for future research are identified. We believe that ensemble classifiers with CNN components possess the ability to tackle more complex, real-world classification tasks, such as those involving self-driving cars, medical diagnosis, and facial recognition. We anticipate that our findings will be useful to the community and contribute to the advancement of ensemble learning and deep learning. Our work also reveals potential applications for our method in scenarios like parameter compression, robustness enhancement, and the discovery of intermediate features. We anticipate that our proposal will be valuable to researchers interested in these subjects as well. We intend to extend our research by a significant margin and our preliminary findings are presented here in an abbreviated manner with the goal of initiating constructive discussion. We wish to contribute to the understanding of ensemble classifiers and CNN components in deep learning and our work can be used as a starting point for further study. We engage in this research with the hope of making a meaningful contribution to the community and our findings are available for debate. A rotating Hele-Shaw cell with a water-filled upper chamber and a membrane separating it from a lower air-filled chamber was investigated. When the membrane was stressed, a stable, rotating liquid surface formed beneath the influence of a central rotating disk. Computer simulations revealed three possible membrane states: curved upwards, curved downwards, and flat, depending on the stress applied and the rotation speed. These simulations accounted for surface tension and fluid viscosity, and produced precise predictions for various experimental conditions. Experimental results matched simulations based on the membrane's stress and the surface tension of the water, and differences between simulation and experiment were attributed to minor imperfections in the membrane. A phenomenon known as the Kurabash effect was also simulated and observed in experiments, in which the membrane's state could suddenly change in response to changes in rotation speed or air pressure, due to a stability switch between two rotating liquid surface states. A dimensionless number, the Kurabash number, was introduced to explain and predict this behavior. Experimental results aligning with previous data showed that the water surface remained stable at rotation speeds below a certain threshold, and abruptly became unstable at speeds above that threshold, which was found to be directly proportional to the membrane's stress and the viscosity of the water, and was independent of the water's surface tension. A rotating Hele-Shaw cell with a liquid-filled lower chamber and an upper air-filled chamber was also investigated, and a similar phenomenon was observed, with a stable, rotating liquid surface forming above a central rotating disk, subject to the same laws of stress, viscosity, and surface tension. A simulation model was developed to predict the behavior of this system as well, by treating the rotating fluid as a solid, due to its high viscosity, and assuming a constant membrane stress, which was found to be a reliable approximation. Parameters for this model were found by matching simulation results with experimental data, and it accurately predicted experimental outcomes for a variety of conditions, including different membrane stresses, rotation speeds, and water viscosities, and provided precise predictions for water surface speeds and curvatures. The vibrational spectroscopy analysis of cyclopentadiene and benzene derivatives is compared to provide insight into the cosmic abundance ratio of these molecules in interstellar space. A previous study found the CCH bond mode's abundance ratio of cyclopentadiene's J=1-0 band to be 1.1 times greater than benzene's, with the CN derivative mode showing the opposite trend and a ratio of 0.79. High-resolution spectroscopy of these same modes in cometary plasmas revealed similar ratios of 1.0 and 0.76 for cyclopentadiene to benzene based on CCH and CN bond modes respectively. However, another analysis of these same spectra using the C--H and C--N bond modes yielded a ratio of 0.67, raising the possibility that these modes could provide a more accurate measure of these molecules' abundance ratios in space. If so, the revised ratios could help clarify the observed discrepancy with other methods of analysis. A survey of these modes in the Orion Nebula's central 0.5 parsecs revealed no cyclopentadiene and a benzene abundance 20 times greater than in the cometary plasmas. The ratio of these same modes in the Orion Nebula's outer regions, where the abundance of these molecules has not changed, is similar to their values in the laboratory, indicating that the chemistry of these molecules has not been altered since their formation. A ratio of these modes in a quasar's cometary plasmas' spectrum was calculated to be the same as those in the Orion Nebula. A linear fit of these ratios with the corresponding cosmic abundance ratios of these molecules yielded a for the weak interaction constant of 10^-45 based on cyclopentadiene's CCH mode and 2*10^-45 based on benzene's and CN derivative modes, both of which are consistent with each other and other measurements. A comparison of these modes in cometary plasmas to their values in the laboratory revealed a temperature of 590 K, a column density of 10^12 molecules per square meter, and a nitrogen-to-carbon ratio of 0.33. A search for these modes in the Orion Nebula's cometary plasmas' spectrum yielded a cyclopentadiene abundance 20 times greater than in the cometary plasmas and a benzene abundance that was the same as in the cometary plasmas. We propose a novel attention mechanism called look-ahead attention for our neural machine translation model, which we have found significantly improves translation quality when a specific constraint is applied. When combined with a long sequence length constraint, look-ahead attention enhances the performance of our model, we have found. Our approach to attention is motivated by the observation that existing attention mechanisms are based on dynamic pricing, where each node estimates the overall resources it should receive, without considering the impact of subsequent nodes. This guidance is unnecessary, as we have found, as our look-ahead attention mechanism shows. We prevent a node from considering the resources it should receive until all subsequent nodes have been taken into account, which we have found yields better results. Our look-ahead attention mechanism is straightforward and easy to implement. We have tested our approach on the WMT14 English-to-German translation task and the NIST Chinese-to-English translation task, obtaining better baseline performance for both tasks when sequence length constraints are applied. This method leverages a translational approach to transform grid computing into a utility computing model. We are presenting a platform called Grid-Utility-Computing-in-the-Cloud (GUCC), which facilitates on-demand computation services via a straightforward web interface. GUCC comprises a utility computing framework along with a grid computing environment, which includes multiple computation resources and data storage. The platform's key features include automated task scheduling, simple web-based application deployment, and the ability to provide computation services on a pay-per-use basis. Furthermore, GUCC employs an innovative pricing mechanism that charges users based on the computation resources utilized. We have tested the platform extensively and the results show that it excels in processing large datasets and executing multiple tasks in parallel. The GUCC platform has numerous practical applications, such as in big data processing, machine learning, and scientific research, which require significant computational powers. We have successfully demonstrated the efficacy of GUCC in processing real-world data sets originating from an industrial partner, leading to novel insights gained. We modified the model by assigning a variable viscosity coefficient that is directly proportional to the density of the universe and time. The proposed model meets the requirements of having a finite number of degrees of freedom in the early universe, while also successfully explaining the present-day observed density of the universe. The model's equations are expressed in a variable viscosity coefficient framework and the necessary conditions are derived for the proportionality constant. The validity of the model is assessed through the negative deceleration parameter phase and the compatibility with the Planck dataset. The predicted variable viscosity model exhibits the same growth rate of the perturbation scales as the $\Lambda$CDM model. The model's cosmological parameters are calculated through fitting the Planck dataset, resulting in a value of $68.43$ for the Hubble constant. A new algorithm called Multi-scale Factorized Hierarchical Sparse Singular Value Decomposition (MFSSA) is proposed, building on the singular value decomposition (SVD) framework by incorporating hierarchical sparse constraints to enable efficient computation. This algorithm excels in processing large-scale and complex data sets, requiring only minimal memory, making it suitable for analyzing extensive datasets, such as lengthy time series, extensive remote sensing images, and massive genomic data. Numerical experiments demonstrate MFSSA's performance, processing a 10 GB matrix in just 12 seconds on a regular desktop, and it outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods in various applications. Additionally, MFSSA yields comparable results to state-of-the-art methods in synthetic data and real-world examples, including analyzing Chinese temperature curves and a remote sensing image example. Furthermore, MFSSA has the potential for wide-ranging practical uses, including identifying patterns in Twitter streams, modeling complex genetic data, and analysing lengthy audio signals. The algorithm's efficiency and versatility make it a valuable tool for numerous real-world contexts, allowing users to explore their data sets, recover sparse components, and uncover hidden patterns, and the associated software is freely available for public use. Furthermore, the paper provides an in-depth mathematical explanation of the algorithm, along with theoretical analysis of its computational costs and memory requirements, and provides sample MATLAB codes for users to replicate the experiment results. Lastly, possible future enhancements to the algorithm are also discussed, such as adapting MFSSA to solve inverse problems and comparing the algorithm's performance on larger, more complex data sets. The paper on MFSSA contributes to the broader field of SVD algorithms and sparse representation methods, and the associated software is designed to be easily applicable to various real-world scenarios and genomic data sets. The code for MFSSA is publicly available on GitHub, along with example MATLAB codes that enable users to replicate the experiment results, including the evaluation of the algorithm on various applications, such as temperature curves and remote sensing images, and complex genetic data sets, and audio signals. The paper on MFSSA has the potential to be expanded, considering possible future enhancements to the algorithm, comparing the algorithm's performance on larger, more complex data sets, and applying the algorithm to various possible contexts, including Twitter streams, lengthy audio signals, and genomic data sets, and analyzing curves of different types, such as electricity consumption curves and temperature curves in different regions. The paper on MFSSA was published in the journal Mathematics, and the associated data is publicly available on GitHub, along with the code

This research considers a random walk with independent and identically distributed components that have a mean of zero. The study focuses on the asymptotic properties of the parameter 'b' as the number of steps increases without bound, and it examines the convergence of certain moments in relation to 'b'. The investigation reveals that the asymptotic value of 'b' determines the ultimate behavior of the moments in question. The paper also explores connections to existing research on polynomial decay and normal decay. Furthermore, it is shown that the conditions initially presented by Kesten and Stigum are necessary and sufficient for the convergence of the second moment. The study expands on previous work by Kolpnizki, extending his results to higher moments. The paper also provides additional research findings related to the moments of certain functions of the maximum of the random walk. The discovered relationships are then applied to achieve results initially obtained by Kolpnizki. The study uses results related to the moments of the maximum of the random walk to obtain asymptotic values, and it also uses the properties of the parameter 'b' to determine the asymptotic values of the moments in question. The findings of the research have been published in recent works of Birkner, Greven, and Vogl, and in the joint research of Birkner, Greven, and den Hollander. The presented results on the convergence of the moments also appear in the joint research of Kolpnizki and Schomburg, and in the work of Schomburg. The parameter 'b' is determined by the expected value of the p-th power of the maximum step in the random walk, and it serves as a key aspect in the study of the asymptotic properties of the random walk with zero-mean components. The research demonstrates that the condition of the normal decay of the moments leads to the asymptotic value of 'b' being equal to zero, whereas the polynomial decay condition results in the value of 'b' increasing in proportion to a specific power. The study explores the relationships between the parameter 'b' and the moments in question, and it establishes that the convergence of the r-th moment is directly linked to the condition 'r < b', whereas the convergence of the p-th moment is conditionally guaranteed when 'p > b' is satisfied. The research further delves into the properties of the parameter 'b' by establishing a lower bound for 'b' based on the variance of the random walk components, whereas an upper limit for 'b' is determined by the expected value of the p-th power

We investigate the rank of twists required for local gamma factors for specific supercuspidal representations in the special orthogonal group SO_{2n+1} and the symplectic group Sp_{2n}. Our findings reveal that a specific representation \sigma can be paired with \pi to obtain the gamma factor, which results in a twist of rank 0 for certain pairs (π, σ) and rank 1 for others. Furthermore, this allows us to establish an isomorphism between certain pairs of representations, extending the work initially developed by the third author for an earlier paper. Our analysis also includes an examination of the relationship between the Bessel function and the local gamma factor, leading to an interpretation of the rank of twists as the dimension of a certain subspace. Our initial goal was to provide the necessary groundwork for the investigation of Rankin--Cordy lifts of automorphic representations on the GL_{2n+1} space. In the process, we encountered several obstacles that hindered the achievement of this goal. In particular, we were unable to demonstrate the irreducibility of certain twists of supercuspidal representations in the special orthogonal group SO_{2n+1} and the symplectic group Sp_{2n}, which are essential components of such lifts. In the SO_{2n+1} case, this issue arises when n is an odd number greater than 1, while in the Sp_{2n} scenario, this problem occurs when n is an even number greater than 2. Moreover, another crucial aspect of Rankin--Cordy lifts involves the application of archimedean gamma factors, which are also explored in this research. Our study includes the derivation of these factors for a subset of pairs of automorphic representations. In addition, we have obtained the factors for pairs that are related to Shimura curves, and these results are comparable to the earlier findings obtained by Diaconu and Goldstein in their research on the subject. Our findings for the gamma factors in the Sp_{2n} case also include the contribution of the first two authors as well as L. Liu, whose contributions are yet to be published. Neural networks consisting of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and fully connected Neural Networks can be reinterpretated using Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs). This reinterpretation holds if the training data for these networks includes exact or approximate graph embeddings, which are necessary to achieve high performance. Our investigation confirms this relationship in multiple contexts, including the module networks used to identify handwritten numbers, the deep neural networks employed for face recognition, and the language models such as BERT and RoBERTc. Furthermore, we discovered that the graph structure underlying these networks can be used to enhance their reliability by reducing their complexity to a minimum required for task execution, without compromising their precision. This is accomplished by pruning the network graphs based on node importance, which can be accomplished without losing precision, according to our findings. Our research discovered that the most reliable versions of these networks correspond to tree-like graph structures, which we refer to as Convolutional Neural Networks with hierarchical structure, or CCNs. The development of artificial intelligence depends on the correct functioning of its underlying technology, which is threatened by the discovery of errors in logical code that ensure programs behave as intended, despite advancements in automated testing. To address this challenge, we are exploring a new methodology for verifying the correctness of logical code by comparing it against a more basic, safe version of the code, which serves as a kind of logical 'vaccine'. To accomplish this task, we are developing a new type of program called a 'logical sanitizer', capable of transforming any given logical code into an equivalent, safer version while maintaining its original functionality. Current sanctions, however, are limited in their ability to eliminate specific types of errors, such as 'inconsistent returns', which we will demonstrate using an example of a simple sanitizing program for Apache Kafka. Furthermore, we will showcase the feasibility of our approach by developing a basic sanitizer for Apache Kafka based on logical code guidelines established by Apache Kafka itself. Ultimately, our vision is to establish a framework of logical sanitizers for various technologies and datasets, which will collectively form the 'VeriTalk' verification framework, enabling an ease with which we can verify the correctness of our artificial intelligence systems by comparing them against a trusted reference standard. VeriTalk's potential applications extend beyond artificial intelligence to any system of instructions deemed crucial to society, including those for aircraft, finance, and healthcare. By exploring the intricacies of logical code verification, we aim to uncover its underlying challenges, opportunities, and possible solutions, as well as shed light on a related unexplored area known as 'correct program logic'. Moreover, we will delve into the possible implications of our framework on existing artificial intelligence testing methodologies, testing guidelines from leading technology companies, and the potential emergence of a new field of study called the'science of correct systems'. Lastly, we will outline the future directions of our research, including the development of formal methods for verifying the correctness of our sanitizer programs, the creation of a dataset for training machine learning models that can automatically detect errors in logical code, and the design of a user-friendly interface for verifying the correctness of artificial intelligence systems. By addressing the challenges of artificial intelligence testing, we hope to ensure the trustworthiness of our artificial intelligence systems and delve into the exciting possibilities of verifying the correctness of any system of instructions deemed crucial to society. To achieve this vision, we are willing to collaborate with leading technology companies, research institutions, and organizations that share our passion for verifying the correctness of systems and exploring the intricacies of logical code verification. This coreset reduces the problem's size while maintaining approximate clustering results and requires $O(\kappa^2 \cdot k \cdot d \cdot n)$ time to construct, where $n$ is the number of data points, $d$ is the dimensionality, and $\kappa$ is a measure of data points' magnitudes. Our approach leverages the ESTRIDGE bound, enabling us to construct a coreset with $O(k \cdot d \cdot n)$ size in $O(\kappa^2 \cdot k \cdot d \cdot n)$ time, which is more efficient than existing methods. Our algorithm LeMuC can be applied to solve the $k$-means clustering problem by approximately solving a smaller instance of the problem on a coreset derived from the original data. This coreset-enabled algorithm, LeMuC, achieves the fastest known time complexity of $O(k \cdot d \cdot n \cdot \kappa^2)$ for solving the $k$-means clustering problem via the well-known incremental mean-shift algorithm. Our results hold under a new condition, called the {\it bounded condition}, which provides a crucial improvement over the previously required condition of uniform data distribution. Our approach introduces a new one-pass algorithm, called the Distributed Embedding Algorithm (Dea), and demonstrates the effectiveness of this algorithm through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world data sets. In complex decision-making scenarios, the grid world is subdivided into higher-level states, some of which are interconnected by probabilistic transition rules, based on a novel path planning approach. This method has been tested in a pursuit-evasion game where one agent seeks to evade the others, and the available paths are limited, and the researchers aimed to determine how the grid subdivision affects the outcome by employing a range of state divisions and comparing the results to a random path selection approach. The study demonstrated that a strategically chosen state division can significantly enhance the evader's chances of success and, in some cases, ensure a win, whereas an randomly generated state division leads to despicable performance comparable to the random path selection method. Furthermore, the optimal state division was found to minimize the number of steps required to evade the pursuing agents, rather than maximizing the number of states reached, which the researchers proved analytically. The study's results have implications for various applications, including escape room design, robotics, and artificial intelligence, and demonstrate the benefits of a systematic approach to path planning in complex environments. The evaluation method employed in this research can be applied to a broad range of grid world scenarios, and the associated code has been made available openly for others to use and modify. The researchers propose several possible future work directions, including the extension of their novel path planning approach to grid worlds without limitations on horizontal movement, the investigation of optimal state divisions in worlds without obstacles, and the consideration of multiple evaders in pursuit-evasion games. The code and research data associated with this study are available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/yilunz/SmartMove. A new set of universal corrections to W and Z boson distribution functions has been discovered in high-energy proton-proton collisions. Collaborations between LHC experiments, specifically ATLAS and CMS, have led to these findings, which have been further confirmed by theoretical PDF updates from NNPDF and ABP fitting groups. These enhanced corrections were initially predicted to contribute approximately 1-2% to the inclusive production of W and Z bosons, however, they have a more substantial impact on certain kinematic distributions. Utilizing optimized PDF reweighting, researchers have implemented these improved FCFs, resulting in improved agreement between theoretical and experimental data for similar processes, including V+jet processes and Higgs boson production in the WW* and ZZ* channels. Additionally, these more accurate FCFs have been incorporated into Higgs boson cross-section calculations, which have been found to be in excellent agreement with experimental data, exceeding the 1% precision threshold required for accurate Higgs boson mass measurements. Furthermore, these enhanced FCFs have been made publicly available as part of the DYNNUM PDF set, which includes a range of processes crucial for Higgs boson and composite Higgs models. Evaluations have shown that these more accurate FCFs can significantly improve precision in Higgs boson mass measurements, with potential gains of up to 0.05 GeV in the current scenario, and much greater improvements in future colliders like the HL-LHC and future colliders. The enhanced FCFs and associated PDFs have been successfully validated through a range of consistency checks, including PDF and cross-section consistency, as well as comparisons with original processes. The research has implications for ongoing and future experiments, highlighting the significance of precise PDFs in achieving optimal performance, with the potential for further gains in the future. The developed approach has the flexibility to accommodate diverse scenarios and processes, demonstrating the potential for a similar framework to contribute to other particle physics initiatives. The enhanced FCFs and associated PDFs, dubbed DYNNUM, are accessible online, awaiting incorporation into official PDF sets used in the scientific community. The study has been conducted by a single author but the analysis suggests that a larger collaborative effort is necessary to thoroughly explore the findings and develop the framework further. The research has been supported by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada, with the computations conducted at the McMaster University research cluster and the theoretical calculations performed using various packages including HiggsCalc, VBF-NLO, and DYNNUMTools. Building on Godel's work, Rosser expanded upon this idea in 1936 and created a second incompleteness theorem for first-order logic, which concerned the consistency of a formal system. However, the validity of the second incompleteness theorem has been contested due to a mistake in Rosser's proof. Recently, Shahid also validated the second incompleteness theorem. Our research extends upon these findings and provides variations of the first and second incompleteness theorems for formal systems that are based on propositional logic. Additionally, we demonstrate how both the first and second incompleteness theorems can be applied to Peano arithmetic. Our proof of the first incompleteness theorem for Peano arithmetic has the added benefit of resulting in a specific arithmetical formula that expresses the undecidability of the system. Furthermore, our application of the second incompleteness theorem to Peano arithmetic yields a formula that defines the concept of the system's own consistency. Our approach to achieving these results involves using a specific type of formal system called the provability predicate for Peano arithmetic, which was initially developed by Godel himself. A key aspect of Hadamard's three circles theorem is its connection to certain analytic functions, and this concept has been expanded to higher dimensions. Previously established theorems in these dimensions lacked a specific connection to Riemann's boundary value problem. This study extends Hadamard's three circles theorem to the complex plane of any dimension, establishing a direct link to the solvability of Riemann's boundary value problem for monogenic functions in the respective dimension. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the solution to Riemann's problem is characterized by its norm, which is directly related to the area under the real part of the solution along a specific circle. The findings mentioned above are applicable to the complex plane of any dimension, except for the case of two dimensions where additional constraints apply. This study also explores connections to Dirichlet's problem in the complex plane of any dimension. The research discussed here is a natural extension of previous works on one-dimensional Hadamard's three circles theorem and Riemann's boundary value problem in the complex plane. The solutions to these problems have been found by utilizing the Cauchy-Transform and the Alexander-Pinch Runst Theorem, which were key components in extending the theorems to higher dimensions. The study at hand assumes a minimum background of basic concepts related to monogenic functions as well as the Cauchy-Transform and the Alexander-Pinch Runst Theorem. The most recent publication on this subject can be found in the book "The Cauchy Transform" by T. Whitcher. The findings presented have been accepted for publication in the conference proceedings subject to certain revisions that have been made in this study. This paper introduces a novel regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which we've termed WC-WGAN, to generate imaginary data samples from complex statistical models. Our proposed model, WC-WGAN, adds a regularized term to the standard WGAN loss function that encourages the discriminator to accurately identify samples from a specific posterior distribution. As a result, WC-WGAN is capable of producing posterior samples that are indistinguishable from actual data observations. We have successfully applied this model to generate synthetic versions of MRI scans and EHR entries with associated attributes. Furthermore, WC-WGAN outperforms existing methods in generating posterior samples when tested on both datasets. The code for our model is available online at this link: https://github.com/ghdeng/WC-WGAN. This work was fundamentally driven by the Wasserstein GAN framework proposed by Arjounin et al. We have also built upon the WC-WGAN model to create a conditional version that can generate synthetic data even when the target posterior distribution is not defined, which we've termed WC-WGAN-C. This new model extends WC-WGAN to the conditional setting, enabling the generation of specific attributes in complex datasets such as EHR entries. The code for WC-WGAN-C can be found at this link: https://github.com/ghdeng/WC-WGAN-C. Both models have the capability to generate synthetic data with complex structures, demonstrating strong potential in machine learning applications. This paper investigates fractional order linear systems with the property of invariance under linear transformations. We establish that a fractional order system can be modified to include linear subspaces within its reachable and observable sets by readjusting its initial conditions and input parameters. Specifically, we show that certain subspaces of a fractional order system can be targeted for state estimation and control. To facilitate this goal, we develop new mathematical expressions utilizing the Caputo fractional derivative, which enable the application of well-established linear algebra techniques. Our study provides a foundational framework for extending and adapting existing methods for linear systems to the realm of fractional order systems. In addition, we outline possible extensions and potential applications of this research. In particular, we discuss possible extensions to the Riemann-Liouville fractional derivative and the Caputo fractional derivative with different initial conditions, as well as potential uses in state estimation and control of fractional order systems. In this paper, we also correct and contribute to the existing literature on fractional order system invariance by addressing a significant error in a previous study. Observations of the millisecond pulsar PSR B1133+16, made possible by high
resolution full-polarization observations at 1.4 GHz with the NAO, revealed
57 individual scattering screens around the pulsar, located an average 20 kpc
from Earth.  The large distance of these screens is exceptional, as distances
this large are typically associated with the Galactic halo rather than the
pulsar's local environment.  A investigation into the origins of these screens
found that an alignment of screens with a particular electron density is linked
to a particular pulsar period, suggesting that the screens are embedded in a
halo component more closely related to the pulsar than to the surrounding
interstellar medium.  The average distance of these screens is consistent with
a halo population, but the presence of screens at such great distances requires
a re-examination of current scattering models, particularly for small scales. 
The discovery of these screens also leads to a better understanding of the
scattering properties of the halo component, particularly its reliance on the
pulsar's frequency rather than its period.  Future observations with the NAO
will be necessary to confirm these findings and investigate the halo component
further, although the method used here provides a promising pathway for this
type of investigation that can be applied to other pulsars.

The analysis of complex signals like speech often requires modeling their recurring patterns.  A new method called the cascaded recurrent neural network (CCRNN) is being proposed to replicate these cycles.  This innovation features a network of increasing complexity stages, starting from a basic recurrent neural network, and ends with a network similar to the one previously suggested by (Juang et al., 1994) that maps speech frequencies to their corresponding components.  Experimental results indicate that CCRNN yields superior outcomes in both speech frequency estimation and synthesis compared to the existing framework based on linear prediction.  Additionally, CCRNN demonstrates its potential in other tasks by achieving the lowest error rate to date in the TIDIT database used for identifying speech tones.  This technique's success can be attributed to its ability to be trained end-to-end, eliminating the need for separate training of its final network stage.  A critical limitation of CCRNN is its slower computation compared to other deep neural network models, requiring significant computational resources for real-time speech processing.  Nonetheless, this novel cascaded network structure is poised to influence the development of future recurrent neural network models, leading to a new benchmark for speech tone identification in the TIDIT database.  This research was conducted as part of a master's degree at the University of Science and Technology of Hanoi.  The underlying data and code are available for download.  Future work is suggested to be focusing on enhancing the efficiency of CCRNN to enable seamless speech processing in real-time environments.  This approach can be achieved by exploring alternative cascaded network designs, such as non-equivalent network stage cascades, to strike a balance between performance and computational requirements. VGG-Sound Source (VGG-SS) is a newly developed dataset that categorizes sound sources based on visual observations, differing from existing datasets that rely on object names or categories.  VGG-SS consists of 9,000 videos along with 8,000 audio clips extracted from them, and it covers 432 distinct sound sources with clear spatial origins in videos.  A baseline model utilizing ResNet-50 achieved an accuracy of 74.2% in identifying sound sources, which surpasses the performance of models utilizing other features like phase information or self-supervised learning.  VGG-SS outperforms the current state-of-the-art in sound source separation using visual cues and provides a more precise extraction method for spatial origins, paving the way for future research in this area.  The dataset and model codes have been made publicly available.  Experiments conducted also demonstrated the feasibility of using VGG-SS in real-world applications, including sound source isolation and a task called "cutting", as well as a comparison with models utilizing other features and learning methods commonly used in self-supervised learning.  Furthermore, an analysis was performed of possible sound source separation methods using visual cues, and the results showed that the VGG-SS model excelled in this area, setting a new benchmark.  The model's ability to determine the spatial origins of sounds with high accuracy also enabled the development of a method to improve the quality of sound source separation, and this improvement was noticeable in sounds with distant or soft source origins.  The model's limitations were found to primarily lie in the recognition of sound sources with complex spatial origins, and possible rectifications were proposed. A combinatorial approach is proposed to isolate the minimal set of degrees of freedom by utilizing the symmetry of the Poincaré group, and this method is demonstrated to yield a stable spectrum of the five linearized degrees of freedom in the gravitational field. The proposed combinatorial approach can be extended to accommodate the inclusion of a mass term in the linearized gravitino sector and yields identical results to those obtained utilizing the covariant derivative operator. We investigate quantum equilibrium states through Hamiltonian dynamics with a non-equilibrium drive. In the quantum setting, this investigation is carried out using Wigner functions, which allow us to study Hamiltonian dynamics across four categories, each defined by the sign of the Hamiltonian parameter: positive, negative, complex, and zero. Our analysis involves a driven Harper model and measures equilibrium state properties through the disorder parameter. These measures include the entropy per particle, the ratio of oscillation frequencies in the lattice, and the magnitude of these frequencies. Our results show that in the quantum setting, there is no distinction between positive and negative Hamiltonian parameters. Instead, we find that the Hamiltonian dynamics' sign affects the lattice's oscillation frequency ratio, whereas the entropy per particle remains unaffected. Additionally, we find that in the complex Hamiltonian case, there is no spin localization in the quantum setting. Our research also involves classical analogues and comparisons with them. It is essential to note that the complex Hamiltonian case is inherently quantum in nature and cannot be replicated in the classical setting. We demonstrate the exclusivity of the complex Hamiltonian case by investigating a classical analogue with a cosine-shaped potential and determining the conditions under which the Hamiltonian dynamics evolve from complex to real dynamics. Our research also includes references to previous studies on the Harper model, both quantum and classical. We further investigate the relationship between the Wigner function's mean value and the classical Wigner function's mean value in the classical setting. Our findings in the quantum setting are validated by means of the Lagrange multipliers of which the Wigner function is the generating function. We also investigate the classical analogue with the cosine-shaped potential and drive Hamiltonian and the related Wigner function, both numerically and analytically. Our research involves the use of numerical methods to solve the Heisenberg lattice equations in the quantum setting and the application of the Euler-Lagrange equations to derive the classical equations of the lattice parameters in the classical setting. Our results in the quantum setting are compared to those in the classical setting to highlight the differences between the two. Our research provides an assessment of the quantum equilibrium state properties through the Wigner function approach in the Harper model with a non-equilibrium drive. Our findings also highlight the exclusivity of the complex Hamiltonian case in the quantum setting and the impossibility of replicating it in the classical setting. Our research paves the way for further investigation into the Wigner function approach in the quantum setting, particularly in relation to the discussion on the mean value of the Wigner function

A new mechanism for the vacuum stability constraint in the standard model is proposed, where a minimal dark sector with a complex scalar and a fermionic dark matter particle is incorporated. This scenario observes dark parity symmetry at the explicit level but suffers from a problem due to the quantum field theoretical vacuum instability caused by the dark sector's dark matter mass. We investigate this issue within a low-scale seesaw framework and find that incorporating a Higgs portal interaction can satisfy the vacuum stability condition, with an estimated mass range (80-150TeV) for the new scalar and a corresponding dark matter mass range (10-50TeV) based on the exact solution of the consistency condition. Furthermore, we examine the potential of future 100TeV colliders to detect this new scalar and the associated dark matter particles through the $pp\to S+jet+jet \to \chi\chi$ process. We also explore the distinguishing features of the neutral pseudo-scalar and the dark matter sector's impact on the direct detection of dark matter. The proposed scenario presents a novel explanation for the cosmological dark matter density due to the correct thermal relic abundance occurring when the dark sector temperature reaches the electroweak scale. The minimal dark sector model offers potential for future particle physics and dark matter research, with the detection of a certain type of exotic Higgs decay, i.e., $h\to Z\chi\bar{\chi}$, also being feasible for the proposed parameter range. The necessity for addressing the vacuum stability issue in the standard model is highlighted, along with the potential for the proposed scenario to be tested in deep colliders or in dark matter direct detection experiments with the best current sensitivity. A fundamental concept in physics, the spin-orbit effect, results from the interaction between a particle's spin, orbital angular momentum, and momentum and gives rise to the energy level splitting we observe in transition metal oxides. In a new theory, we've investigated the impact of electron interactions and the arrangement of electrons in a crystal, known as the crystal field, on the spin-orbit effect. We found that its overall influence can be quantified by an enhanced spin-orbit coupling strength, which we calculated as a function of relevant energy levels. In particular, we determined the effective spin-orbit coupling strength in two specific materials: doped Sr$_2$IrO$_4$ and LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$. In both cases, our calculations matched previous experimental and theoretical findings. We also established that the energy gaps we observed are directly related to the dielectric properties of these materials. In addition, we predicted that the effective spin-orbit coupling strength in LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ should increase with an increase in the electron density. We tested our theory by simulating artificial stacking of these materials and found that introducing twists or defects can lead to notable changes in the spin-orbit effect, which we believe are crucial insights given the frequent occurrence of these defects in real-world samples. We believe our theory provides a critical framework for understanding the spin-orbit effect in transition metal oxides and predicts phenomena worthy of investigation through experimental methods. In the course of our study, we used a variety of methods including first-principles calculations, tight-binding models, and many-body interactions, and assumed that the electron interactions are strong but not too strong, which we believe is true for most transition metal oxides. We used two specific materials as examples but our theory is general and applicable to other transition metal oxides. We propose that the effective spin-orbit coupling strength can be an essential characteristic of these materials, influencing their physical properties, and we suggest investigating its variation with electron density, arrangement of electrons in a crystal, and defects. We also introduced the concept of an effective mass induced by the spin-orbit effect, which we believe could be valuable in understanding the behavior of these materials in different scenarios. We believe our study paves the way for a deeper understanding of the spin-orbit effect in transition metal oxides and provides a practical tool for predicting various physical properties of these materials. Given a toric complete intersection with smooth divisors, we develop methods to compute specific relative $I$-functions. Furthermore, for a particular class of variables, we establish an $A$-hypergeometric $\theta$-function approach that enables us to compare the relative $I$-functions of certain toric complete intersections with smooth divisors. Specifically, if $(Xo,Oo)$ and $(Xoo,Ooo)$ are related toric complete intersection pairs with smooth divisors, we can compute the difference of their relative $I$-functions using Milne's formula and the hypergeometric $\theta$-functions associated with $(Xo,Oo)$ and $(Xoo,Ooo)$. Moreover, if $(Xo,Oo)$ and $(Xoo,Ooo)$ share the same underlying lattice, we can compare their relative $I$-functions using the hypergeometric $\theta$-functions. As an application, we investigate relative $I$-functions of toric complete intersections arising from root systems and demonstrate the usefulness of this approach in determining the differences of their relative $I$-functions. Additionally, this comparison can be extended to the relative $I$-functions of certain toric arrangements with smooth hyperplane components. We also provide examples of these configurations based on root systems and discuss the relationships between their relative $I$-functions. Furthermore, we outline possible connections between the differences of the relative $I$-functions and the $A$-polynomials of link spaces associated with these configurations. Ohta, our research may be viewed as an initial step in exploring the relationships between the relative $I$-functions of these configurations and the $A$-polynomials of link spaces. This study explores the potential of generative models to create new pathological image representations by modifying existing ones, building on the concept of latent code manipulation. We tested this idea using two models: a convolutional neural network and a generative adversarial network. Our experiments demonstrated that these models can indeed generate novel pathological image representations by altering the latent code, even when based on limited training data. However, we also discovered that this code can be misleading as it may not accurately reflect the original disease characteristics. We propose a solution by integrating an classification module into the network, which encourages the model to prioritize semantic accuracy in generated images. Our approach is tested on two datasets: one containing lung nodules and the other containing skin lesions. We also devised two evaluation metrics to assess the semantic preservation of our proposed approach. Our results showed a significant improvement in these evaluations compared to the baseline models. Our approach was found to be particularly effective in maintaining the semantic accuracy of generated images even when the training set is minimized. Our findings have implications for using generative models in real-world applications, such as developing tools to manipulate medical image representations that healthcare professionals can trust. Our code is available online for the convolutional neural network model. We intend to make the code for the generative adversarial network model publicly accessible in the future.
